teile.einleitung: Children's rights are rights that all children in the world have. They are set out in the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child. Almost all the countries in the world have recognised it, including Switzerland.
wichtigste: The UN adopted the Convention on the Rights of the Child in 1989.
The Convention has 54 articles.
Every child has the right to a name and a nationality.
Children may give their opinion when things concern them.
Children have a right to play, rest and free time.
Switzerland recognised the Convention in 1997.
The USA is the only UN member that has not recognised it (as of 2025).

abschnitte.titel: The Convention on the Rights of the Child
abschnitte.text: On **20 November 1989** the UN General Assembly adopted the **Convention on the Rights of the Child**. It says what rights all people under 18 have. The Convention has **54 articles**. The first 41 describe children's rights; the rest govern how countries put them into practice. That is why 20 November is **Children's Rights Day**.

Under **Article 7**, every child receives a **name** and a **nationality** from birth. Children have a right to **protection** from violence and exploitation. They also have a right to **education**, meaning to go to school. And they should be able to grow up healthy, with food, a home and help from a doctor.

**Article 12** says that children may give their **opinion** on things that concern them. Adults should take this opinion seriously. This applies, for example, at school or in court. In many Swiss municipalities there are **children's and youth parliaments** for this.

**Article 31** says that every child has a right to **rest, free time and play**. Playing is important so that children develop well. Art and culture are also part of it. Children should not only have to work or learn.

Almost all the countries in the world have recognised the Convention. **Switzerland** did so in **1997**. The **USA** signed the Convention but never brought it into force (as of 2025). Countries must report regularly on how they are putting children's rights into practice. The children's fund **UNICEF** works for this around the world.

gewusst: The Convention on the Rights of the Child is the human rights treaty recognised by the most countries in the world.
Important principles are that no child is discriminated against and that the child's best interests always come first.

teile.einleitung: Horizon Europe is the European Union's large programme for research and innovation. It runs from 2021 to 2027 and has about 95 billion euros. For researchers in Switzerland, taking part was a political issue for a long time.
wichtigste: Horizon Europe is the EU's ninth framework programme for research.
It runs from 2021 to 2027.
Its budget is about 95.5 billion euros.
From 2021 to 2024 Switzerland was a non-associated third country.
Since 1 January 2025 Switzerland has been associated again, with retroactive effect.
The agreement also covers Euratom and Digital Europe.

abschnitte.text: Since 1984 the EU has funded research with **framework programmes**. The eighth programme, **Horizon 2020**, was followed by the ninth, **Horizon Europe**. It has about **95.5 billion euros**, clearly more than Horizon 2020 with about 77 billion. This makes it one of the largest research funding programmes in the world. It funds projects in medicine, climate, energy, technology and many other fields.

Countries outside the EU can **associate** themselves with Horizon Europe through an agreement. Then their researchers can take part almost in the same way as those from EU countries. The **European Research Council (ERC) grants** are especially sought after. These are grants for outstanding researchers. They are only open to researchers in member states or associated countries.

In 2021 the Federal Council broke off the negotiations on a **framework agreement** with the EU. After that the EU linked association to these institutional questions. That is why from 2021 to 2024 Switzerland counted as a **non-associated third country**. The **Confederation** funded Swiss projects directly, and the Swiss National Science Foundation created **replacement programmes**. Some researchers moved abroad.

On 10 November 2025 an agreement on the EU programmes was signed. It applies **retroactively from 1 January 2025**. That is why Swiss researchers were already able to apply for calls from 2025. Besides Horizon Europe, the agreement also covers the **Euratom programme** for nuclear research and the **Digital Europe** programme.

gewusst: Horizon Europe has about a quarter more money than the previous programme, Horizon 2020.
The EU's framework programmes for research have existed for more than 40 years.

teile.einleitung: The flag of Canada shows a red maple leaf on a white background, with a red band on the left and on the right. Many Canadians call it the “Maple Leaf”. It has the same colours as the Swiss flag.
wichtigste: In the middle of Canada's flag is a red maple leaf.
The leaf has 11 points.
There is a red band on the left and on the right, with a white field between them.
The flag is red and white, like the Swiss flag.
Canada has had this flag since 15 February 1965.
It is often called the “Maple Leaf”.

abschnitte.text: The flag of Canada has a **red band** on the **left and on the right**. Between them is a large **white field**. On this field is a **red maple leaf**. The leaf has **11 points** and is drawn in a simplified way, so that it is easy to recognise. The colours **red and white** are the same as on the Swiss flag.

The **maple** is an important sign of Canada. Many maple trees grow in the country's huge forests. In **autumn** their leaves turn a bright red. **Maple syrup**, a well-known Canadian speciality, is made from the sap of certain maple trees. That is why the leaf suits the flag well as a sign of recognition.

Before 1965 Canada used a flag that still showed the British flag. This was because Canada had long been closely linked to **Great Britain**. Many people wanted a flag of their own that was completely Canadian. After long discussions, the maple leaf flag was chosen. It was officially raised for the first time on **15 February 1965**. Today this day is **Flag Day** in Canada.

Canada lies in the **north of America**. After Russia it is the **second-largest country** on Earth. The main languages spoken in the country are **English** and **French**. So, as in Switzerland, there are several languages. The capital is called **Ottawa**.

gewusst: On many Canadian rucksacks you see small maple leaf patches, so that travellers are recognised as Canadians.
A maple leaf can also be seen on Canadian coins.

teile.einleitung: Gavi is an international vaccine alliance with its seat in Geneva. It helps poorer countries to have children vaccinated against dangerous diseases. Countries, UN organisations, foundations and companies work together in it.
wichtigste: Gavi was founded in 2000 and presented at the WEF in Davos.
Its headquarters is in Geneva.
Its work mainly benefits children in poorer countries.
WHO, UNICEF and the World Bank are important partners.
The Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation gave 750 million US dollars for its founding.
From 2020 Gavi led the COVAX initiative for coronavirus vaccines together with others.

abschnitte.text: **Gavi** is a worldwide **vaccine alliance**. An alliance is a partnership in which several partners pursue a shared aim. The name originally stood for “Global Alliance for Vaccines and Immunisation”. Gavi supports **vaccinations** in poorer countries, for example against measles or polio. According to its own figures, this has prevented many millions of deaths.

Gavi was officially launched in January 2000 at the **World Economic Forum WEF** in **Davos**. It followed an earlier initiative for children's vaccinations from 1990. The **Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation** pledged 750 million US dollars for its founding. Today Gavi has its **headquarters in Geneva**, where many other health organisations work.

Gavi is a **public-private partnership**. This means that countries and private partners work together. They include governments, the **World Health Organization WHO**, the children's fund **UNICEF**, the **World Bank**, foundations and vaccine manufacturers. In this way money and expertise are pooled. Governments pay in most of the money.

During the **COVID-19 pandemic**, from 2020 Gavi led the **COVAX** initiative together with other organisations. It was meant to share coronavirus vaccines more fairly between rich and poor countries. COVAX delivered many vaccine doses to poorer countries. But critics complained that rich countries first secured large quantities for themselves.

gewusst: By buying in bulk, Gavi can buy vaccines more cheaply than individual poor countries.
Switzerland also supports Gavi with contributions.

teile.einleitung: The Grameen Bank is a bank in Bangladesh that gives small loans to poor people. It was founded by the economics professor Muhammad Yunus. The idea of small loans became known all over the world.
wichtigste: In 1976 Muhammad Yunus gave the first small loans out of his own pocket in the village of Jobra.
Since 1983 the Grameen Bank has been an official bank under a law.
Most of its customers are poor women in the countryside.
The borrowers own most of the bank.
In 2006 Yunus and the Grameen Bank jointly received the Nobel Peace Prize.
In 2011 Yunus was removed as director.

abschnitte.text: Muhammad Yunus taught economics at a university in Bangladesh. In the village of **Jobra** he saw that poor women had large debts with moneylenders. In 1976 he lent 42 women a total of about 27 US dollars. With it they were able to free themselves from the moneylenders. This experiment became a research project that spread to other villages.

In 1983 the project became an independent bank under a law. **Grameen** means roughly “rural” or “village” in Bengali. The bank gives **microcredits**, meaning very small loans. With them people buy, for example, a cow, a sewing machine or goods for a small shop. They do not need security such as a house for this.

Most of the Grameen Bank's customers are **women**. They join together in small groups and support each other in paying back. The borrowers are also **shareholders**: they own most of the bank. Most recently, the state of Bangladesh held about a quarter of the shares.

Yunus wanted to show that companies can also have social aims. In 2006 Grameen founded the company Grameen Danone Foods with the French group **Danone**. It makes a cheap, enriched yoghurt for children to fight malnutrition. Profits are meant to stay in the company and not be paid out to owners. Something like this is called a **social business**.

In 2006 Muhammad Yunus and the Grameen Bank jointly received the **Nobel Peace Prize**. Later there was a dispute with the government of Bangladesh. In 2011 the central bank removed Yunus as director, giving the age limit as the reason. Many people saw this as a political conflict. Critics of microcredit also point out that some people still end up in debt.

gewusst: At about 27 US dollars, Yunus's first loan was smaller than a year's pocket money today.
The idea of microcredit spread from Bangladesh to many countries around the world.

teile.einleitung: The International Monetary Fund, IMF for short, is an organisation that helps countries with loans in financial crises. It is meant to keep the world's money and financial system stable. Almost all the countries in the world are members, including Switzerland.
wichtigste: The IMF helps countries with loans in financial crises.
It was agreed in 1944 at the Bretton Woods conference in the USA.
Its seat is in Washington, D.C.
It has 191 member states.
Switzerland has been a member since 1992.
In return for its loans, the IMF often demands reforms.
It is a specialised agency of the UN.

abschnitte.text: The **International Monetary Fund** is something like a fire brigade for countries' money. If a country gets into a serious financial crisis, it can borrow money from the IMF. The money comes from contributions by the member states, which are called **quotas**. The bigger a country's economy, the higher its contribution. This also gives it more voting rights.

In July 1944, while the Second World War was still going on, representatives from 44 countries met at Bretton Woods in the USA. They wanted to prevent an economic crisis like the one in the 1930s from happening again. There they decided to found the IMF and the **World Bank**. The IMF began its work in 1945 and 1946. Its headquarters is still in Washington today.

The IMF watches the economies of its members and gives them advice. When a country can no longer pay its debts, it gets loans. In return it often has to meet conditions, for example saving money or collecting taxes differently. These conditions are sometimes disputed, because poor people can suffer as a result. The IMF also has its own unit of account, the **Special Drawing Rights**.

The IMF helped, for example, during the Asian financial crisis at the end of the 1990s. After the financial crisis of 2008 it supported Greece, Ireland and Portugal, among others. Argentina has also received loans several times. During the coronavirus pandemic it quickly provided money to many poorer countries. Since 2019 the Bulgarian Kristalina Georgieva has led the IMF.

In 1992 Swiss voters said yes to joining the IMF and the World Bank. Switzerland leads its own **voting group**, which also includes Poland and several countries in Central Asia. This gives it a seat on the Executive Board, the important governing body. The Swiss National Bank and the finance department represent Switzerland. This way Switzerland has a say in important decisions.

begriffe.erklaerung: Money that you borrow and have to pay back later with interest.
A country's money, for example the Swiss franc.
The share that a country pays into the IMF, which decides its voting rights.
A time when banks, companies or countries get into serious money trouble.

gewusst: The IMF has large gold reserves and is one of the biggest owners of gold in the world.
At the Bretton Woods conference, the delegates stayed in a large hotel at the foot of the mountains of New Hampshire.

teile.einleitung: The flag of India has three horizontal stripes in saffron, white and green. In the middle there is a blue wheel with 24 spokes. Indians call it the “Tiranga”, which means three-coloured.
wichtigste: The stripes are saffron, white and green and lie horizontally.
In the middle is a dark blue wheel with 24 spokes.
The wheel is called the Ashoka Chakra, after the ancient emperor Ashoka.
The flag was adopted in July 1947.
Shortly afterwards India became independent from Great Britain.
“Tiranga” means three-coloured in Hindi.

abschnitte.text: The flag of India has three **horizontal stripes** of equal width. **Saffron** is at the top, **white** in the middle and **green** at the bottom. In Hindi the flag is called the **“Tiranga”**, which means **three-coloured**. The colours are often explained like this: saffron for courage, white for peace and truth, green for growth and the fertile land.

In the middle of the white stripe is a **dark blue wheel**. It has **24 spokes**. You can compare them with the 24 hours of a day. The wheel is called the **Ashoka Chakra**. “Chakra” means wheel. It is meant to recall movement and progress: a country should always keep developing.

The wheel is named after **Ashoka**. More than **2,000 years** ago he was a powerful emperor in India. After a terrible war he turned to **Buddhism** and worked for peace. He had large stone pillars with inscriptions put up. One of these pillars shows such a wheel, and that is where the sign on the flag comes from.

For a long time India was a **colony** of **Great Britain**. Many people fought peacefully for independence; the best known is **Mahatma Gandhi**. In **July 1947** today's flag was adopted. On **15 August 1947** India became independent. Independence Day is still celebrated on this day, with many flags all over the country.

gewusst: India is the country with the largest population in the world; it overtook China in 2023.
India's emblem also shows lions from a pillar of Emperor Ashoka.

teile.einleitung: In diplomacy, good offices are all the forms of help from a third party that open the way to talks for countries in dispute. A neutral country, an organisation or a person brings the parties to the table without taking sides. Switzerland is known worldwide for this, for example in the negotiations on Iran's nuclear programme.
wichtigste: Good offices are help from an uninvolved third party so that parties in a dispute talk to each other.
In international law they are a peaceful method of settling conflicts.
In mediation proper, the third party also contributes its own proposals for a solution.
The UN Secretary-General also offers good offices.
In the negotiations on Iran's nuclear programme, Switzerland several times provided Geneva and Lausanne as neutral places.
Good offices only work if all sides agree.

abschnitte.text: In **international law**, good offices are one of the peaceful means of settling disputes. A third party makes contact, organises meetings and provides a calm setting. In **mediation**, the third party goes a step further and makes its own proposals. Often the two forms merge into each other.

The Hague Peace Conferences of 1899 and 1907 set out good offices and mediation in treaties for the first time. The **UN Charter** of 1945 also requires countries to settle their disputes peacefully. The **UN Secretary-General** often appoints personal envoys who provide good offices. Besides Switzerland, countries such as Norway, Qatar or the Vatican are known as mediators.

From the 2000s, Iran and several great powers negotiated about **Iran's nuclear programme**. Switzerland several times provided Geneva and Lausanne as neutral places for the negotiations. In November 2013 an interim agreement was reached in Geneva. In April 2015 the main points were agreed in Lausanne, and the final **nuclear agreement** was signed in Vienna in July 2015.

The host provides security, rooms, interpreting and confidentiality. Talks often take place in hotels or remote places, so that the delegations are not disturbed. Sometimes the parties do not sit in the same room, and the mediator goes back and forth between them; this is called **shuttle diplomacy**. It is important that nothing leaks out before an agreement has been reached.

Good offices are a trademark of Swiss **foreign policy**. They strengthen Switzerland's reputation and help to prevent or end wars. Geneva, with its international organisations, offers ideal conditions for this. Switzerland stresses that it makes talks possible, but that the solution must come from the parties to the conflict themselves.

begriffe.erklaerung: Help in which an impartial person supports the search for a solution.
A group of representatives who negotiate for a country.
A mediator travels back and forth between parties who do not talk to each other directly.
Rules that apply between countries.

gewusst: In 2015 the talks on Iran's nuclear programme in Lausanne took place at the Beau-Rivage Palace hotel.
Good offices are already described in the Hague Conventions of 1899.
A mediator can only help if both sides trust them.

teile.einleitung: Since 2014 a free trade agreement has applied between Switzerland and China. It is meant to make trade between the two countries simpler and cheaper by lowering customs duties. The agreement is economically important, but it has also been criticised.
wichtigste: The agreement was signed in Beijing on 6 July 2013.
Federal Councillor Johann Schneider-Ammann signed for Switzerland.
Switzerland was the first country in continental Europe to have such an agreement with China.
Switzerland mostly removed its industrial customs duties at once; China removed many step by step over years.
Labour questions are dealt with in a separate parallel agreement.
After the EU and the USA, China is Switzerland's third-largest trading partner.

abschnitte.text: On 6 July 2013 Switzerland and China signed the agreement in **Beijing**. **Johann Schneider-Ammann**, then head of the economics department, signed for Switzerland. On the Chinese side, Commerce Minister Gao Hucheng signed. After that both countries still had to **ratify** the treaty, meaning approve it officially. In Switzerland, Parliament was responsible for this. The agreement came into force in 2014.

Switzerland was the first country in **continental Europe** to have a free trade agreement with China. It concluded it **bilaterally**, meaning directly between two countries and not through the free trade organisation EFTA. The European Union has no such agreement with China. For the Swiss economy, this was an advantage over companies from other European countries.

The agreement is **asymmetrical**, which means the two sides remove customs duties at different speeds. Switzerland quickly granted duty-free access for many industrial goods. China lowered many duties step by step with **transition periods** of up to 15 years. Swiss export goods such as **watches** and **machines** benefit from this little by little. A customs duty is a charge that must be paid when goods cross a border.

Questions about work and employment were not dealt with in the main treaty but in a **parallel agreement**. It provides for dialogue and cooperation, but no penalties for breaches. Critics complain that **human rights** are not firmly enough included. Supporters, on the other hand, stress that regular exchange with China achieves more than having no treaty.

After the **EU** and the **USA**, China is Switzerland's third-largest trading partner. Switzerland sells, among other things, watches, machines and pharmaceutical products to China. In the other direction, for example, electronics, clothes and toys come from China to Switzerland. The agreement was meant to strengthen these relations further.

gewusst: Switzerland recognised the People's Republic of China back in 1950, as one of the first Western countries.
Thanks to transition periods, many customs duties on Swiss watches in China are only falling little by little.

teile.einleitung: Kivu is a region in the east of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, on the border with Rwanda. Many armed groups have been fighting there for decades. Millions of people suffer from the conflict.
wichtigste: The conflict takes place in the provinces of North Kivu and South Kivu.
One cause is the genocide in Rwanda in 1994.
In January 2025 the rebel group M23 captured the city of Goma.
UN experts accuse Rwanda of supporting the M23.
Raw materials such as coltan, tin and gold play a big part.
The UN is in the country with its mission MONUSCO.

abschnitte.text: Kivu lies in the **east of the Democratic Republic of the Congo**, on **Lake Kivu**. The region is divided into the provinces of **North Kivu** and **South Kivu**. Important cities are **Goma** and **Bukavu**. The area has fertile soil, volcanoes and rich mineral resources. Even so, many people there live in great poverty.

In **1994** there was a genocide of the **Tutsi** in neighbouring **Rwanda**. After that more than a million Hutu fled into the eastern Congo, among them many perpetrators. Armed groups such as the **FDLR** grew out of this. The **Congo Wars** followed. So many countries took part in the Second Congo War, from 1998 to 2003, that it is called **“Africa's World War”**.

The **M23** is a rebel group. Its name stands for “Mouvement du 23 mars” and recalls a **peace agreement of 23 March 2009**. The rebels accused the government of not keeping it. In **January 2025** the M23 captured the city of **Goma**, and in February also **Bukavu**. UN experts report that **Rwanda** supports the M23. Rwanda points to the threat from the FDLR.

Valuable minerals such as **coltan**, **tin** and **gold** lie in the ground of Kivu. **Tantalum**, which is found in mobile phones and computers, is obtained from coltan. Armed groups earn money from mining and **smuggling** these raw materials. That is why some companies make sure not to buy “conflict minerals”.

The UN has been in the country with the peace mission **MONUSCO** since 2010. It grew out of the older mission MONUC and is one of the largest UN missions. Many people have had to flee their villages and live in camps. The doctor **Denis Mukwege** from Bukavu has helped victims of the war for many years. For this he received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2018.

gewusst: Rare mountain gorillas live in Virunga National Park in North Kivu.
Millions of people died in the Second Congo War through violence, hunger and disease.

teile.einleitung: The International Organisation of La Francophonie, OIF for short, is an association of countries linked by the French language. Its members share French as an official language, a school language or a language of culture. Switzerland belongs to it too, because French is spoken in the Romandy.
wichtigste: La Francophonie links countries in which French plays an important part.
Its seat is in Paris.
Its forerunner was founded in Niamey in Niger in 1970.
La Francophonie has members and observers, together about 90 states and governments.
Switzerland has been a member since 1996.
The International Day of La Francophonie is celebrated on 20 March.
More than 300 million people around the world speak French.

abschnitte.text: The word **Francophonie** means roughly the French-speaking world. The organisation OIF brings together countries in which French is spoken or learnt. They include France, Belgium, Canada, Switzerland and many countries in Africa. Some members are also countries in which only a few people speak French but which feel linked to the language. They can take part as full members, associate members or **observers**.

The idea came partly from politicians from former French colonies in Africa, such as Léopold Sédar Senghor from Senegal. In 1970 the Agency for Cultural and Technical Cooperation was founded in Niamey in Niger. Today's OIF later grew out of it. Since 1986 the heads of state and government have met regularly for a **summit**. Since 2019 the Rwandan Louise Mushikiwabo has led the organisation as Secretary General.

La Francophonie promotes the French language and the variety of cultures. It works for education, for example with teaching materials and teacher training. Democracy, human rights and peace are also among its aims. It sometimes observes elections in member countries. Its network also includes a university agency and the television channel TV5Monde.

In Switzerland about a fifth of the people speak French as their main language, mainly in the **Romandy**. Switzerland has been a member of the OIF since 1996. In 2010 the Francophonie summit took place in Montreux on Lake Geneva. Switzerland also takes part in the TV5Monde channel. In this way it shows that speaking several languages is part of its identity.

French is one of the official languages of the UN and of the International Olympic Committee. Today an especially large number of French speakers live in Africa, for example in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Experts expect their number there to keep growing strongly. French is also important in Canada, especially in Quebec. This makes French a true world language.

begriffe.erklaerung: The community of people and countries that speak French.
The French-speaking part of Switzerland in the west of the country.
A country that attends meetings but does not have all the rights of a member.
A language that a country or an organisation uses officially.

gewusst: The word Francophonie was already used around 1880 by the French geographer Onésime Reclus.
French is used as an official language on all five inhabited continents.

teile.einleitung: International schools are schools for children from many different countries. Lessons are often in English or in several languages. The oldest international school in the world is in Geneva.
wichtigste: In Geneva, children of diplomats often go to international schools.
The International School of Geneva was founded in 1924.
It is seen as the oldest international school in the world.
Lessons there are mainly in English and French.
The International Baccalaureate was developed in Geneva.
The school has three campuses and about 4,500 pupils.

abschnitte.text: At international schools, children from many countries learn together. Often their parents work for international organisations or companies and move often. So that the children can keep learning wherever they are, these schools often follow international curricula. Lessons are usually in **English** or in two languages. Many international schools charge school fees.

Many people in Geneva work at the UN and other organisations. Their children, for example children of **diplomats**, often go to an international school. The **International School of Geneva** was founded in 1924, at first for the children of staff of the **League of Nations**. It is seen as the oldest international school in the world. Lessons are mainly in English and French.

The International School of Geneva has three campuses: **La Grande Boissière**, **La Châtaigneraie** and the **Campus des Nations**. The Campus des Nations is near the UN and the other international organisations. In total about 4,500 children and young people from many countries go to the school.

In the 1960s, teachers at the International School of Geneva developed a new school-leaving qualification: the **International Baccalaureate**, IB for short. Today it is offered at schools in a great many countries. With the IB you can study at many universities all over the world. In this way an idea from Geneva became a worldwide qualification.

gewusst: The International School of Geneva is almost as old as the League of Nations, for whose staff it was founded.
Today you can take the International Baccalaureate, a qualification from Geneva, on every continent.

teile.einleitung: Henry Dunant was a businessman from Geneva who started the Red Cross. After he saw the suffering of wounded soldiers after a battle in 1859, he wanted to organise help for everyone injured in war. For his idea he received the very first Nobel Peace Prize in 1901.
wichtigste: Henry Dunant was born in Geneva on 8 May 1828.
He is the founder of the idea of the Red Cross.
In 1859 he witnessed the aftermath of the Battle of Solferino in Italy.
In 1862 he published the book “A Memory of Solferino”.
In 1863 the committee that became the International Committee of the Red Cross was formed in Geneva.
In 1901 he was one of the first people to receive the Nobel Peace Prize.
He died on 30 October 1910 in Heiden in the canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden.

abschnitte.text: Henry Dunant was born in **Geneva** on 8 May 1828 into a devout and well-off family. Even as a young man he helped poor and sick people. Later he worked as a businessman and wanted to run mills in Algeria, which belonged to France at the time. To get support for his plans, he travelled to Italy in 1859 to see the French Emperor Napoleon III.

On 24 June 1859 French and Sardinian troops fought against the Austrian army at **Solferino** in northern Italy. Tens of thousands of soldiers were killed or wounded and lay on the battlefield without help. Dunant arrived in the village of Castiglione shortly afterwards and organised care for the injured with women from the area. They helped all the wounded, no matter which side they had fought on.

In 1862 Dunant wrote the book **“A Memory of Solferino”**. In it he described the misery of the wounded and made two proposals. First, every country should have aid societies to care for the wounded. Second, countries should conclude a treaty to protect these helpers. The book was read all over Europe and moved many people.

In 1863 Dunant founded the **Committee of Five** in Geneva with four other men, including General Guillaume-Henri Dufour and Gustave Moynier. This became the International Committee of the Red Cross, ICRC for short. As early as 1864 twelve countries signed the first **Geneva Convention**, which protects the wounded and medical staff in war. As its sign they chose a red cross on a white background, meaning the reversed colours of the Swiss flag.

In 1867 Dunant's businesses went bankrupt, and he had to leave Geneva. For many years he lived poor and almost forgotten in various places in Europe. From 1887 he lived in **Heiden** in the Appenzell region, where a journalist rediscovered him in 1895. In 1901 he received the first **Nobel Peace Prize**, together with the Frenchman Frédéric Passy.

Today there are Red Cross or Red Crescent societies in almost every country in the world. The worldwide movement helps in wars, natural disasters and other emergencies. The **ICRC** still has its seat in Geneva today. Dunant's birthday, 8 May, is celebrated every year as World Red Cross Day.

begriffe.erklaerung: A worldwide aid movement that supports people in war and emergencies.
A treaty between countries that protects the wounded, prisoners and civilians in war.
The International Committee of the Red Cross, based in Geneva.
A famous prize for people who work especially hard for peace.

gewusst: In Heiden there is a Henry Dunant Museum that remembers his life.
Dunant did not spend his Nobel Prize money on himself; he lived modestly in the hospital at Heiden until his death.
The Red Cross emblem is the Swiss flag with the colours swapped, as a thank-you to Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: In a vaccination campaign, as many people as possible are vaccinated against a disease in a short time. Around the world, organisations such as the WHO and UNICEF help to make sure that children in poor countries are protected too.
wichtigste: A vaccination trains the body to defend itself against a particular germ.
The WHO makes recommendations; UNICEF buys and distributes many vaccines for children.
The vaccine alliance Gavi, based in Geneva, helps poor countries with vaccinating.
Vaccines must stay cool; this is called the cold chain.
Polio is almost wiped out thanks to vaccinations.
In Switzerland vaccinations are recorded in a vaccination certificate.

abschnitte.text: In a vaccination, the body receives a weakened or harmless part of a germ. In this way the **immune system** learns to recognise the germ. If the real germ comes later, the body can defend itself quickly. You then do not fall ill, or not so seriously. When many people are vaccinated, a disease also finds it harder to spread.

In 1796 the English doctor **Edward Jenner** vaccinated a boy with cowpox. After that the boy was protected against the dangerous real smallpox. The word “vaccine” comes from the Latin word for cow. Thanks to worldwide vaccination campaigns, smallpox is now considered wiped out.

The **WHO**, the World Health Organization, makes recommendations about which vaccinations are important. **UNICEF**, the UN children's fund, buys and distributes many vaccines for children. The vaccine alliance **Gavi** has its seat in Geneva and helps poor countries to vaccinate their children. Together they vaccinate, for example, against **measles**, a very infectious disease with red spots on the skin.

Many vaccines go off in the heat and then no longer work. That is why they must stay cool all the way, from the factory to the faraway village. They are transported in fridges and cool boxes, sometimes by motorbike, boat or drone. This unbroken cooling is called the **cold chain**.

In Switzerland children used to receive the vaccine against **polio** on a sugar lump. In German polio is called **Kinderlähmung** (“child paralysis”), because it can paralyse arms and legs. Today vaccination in Switzerland is done with an injection. All vaccinations are recorded in your **vaccination certificate**. This way you know which diseases you are protected against.

gewusst: The word “vaccine” comes from the Latin “vacca”, meaning cow, because of Jenner's vaccination with cowpox.
Smallpox is the first human disease to have been wiped out worldwide by vaccinations.

teile.einleitung: The flag of France is called the Tricolour, which means three-coloured. It has three vertical stripes in blue, white and red. It was created at the time of the French Revolution.
wichtigste: The French flag is called the Tricolour, meaning “three-coloured”.
It has three vertical stripes in blue, white and red.
Blue is next to the flagpole, red at the end that flutters.
The Tricolour dates from the time of the French Revolution, from 1789.
Blue and red were the colours of Paris, white the colour of the king.
Green does not appear on the French flag.

abschnitte.text: The flag of France has three **vertical stripes**. So they stand side by side. Next to the **flagpole** is the **blue** stripe, in the middle the **white** one and at the end that flutters the **red** one. Because the flag has three colours, it is called the **Tricolour**. “Tri” means three, and “colour” is the word for colour.

The Tricolour was created at the time of the **French Revolution**, which began in **1789**. At that time many people rose up against the great power of the king. They wore badges in **blue and red**, the old colours of the city of **Paris**. **White** was the colour of the king. Together the three colours were meant to show that the whole people belonged together.

Today France is a **republic**. The Tricolour is one of its most important signs, alongside the motto **“Liberty, Equality, Fraternity”**. On **14 July**, the French National Day, you see it everywhere. It also flies at schools and town halls. At sports events many fans paint the three colours on their faces.

The Tricolour became a **model** for many other flags. Several countries also chose three vertical stripes. A well-known example is **Italy**, with green, white and red. **Belgium** and **Ireland** also have three vertical stripes. This shows how strongly the ideas of the Revolution spread in Europe.

gewusst: The Netherlands has almost the same colours as France, but with horizontal stripes.
In French the flag is often called “le drapeau tricolore”.

teile.einleitung: Small island states often lie in the middle of the Pacific, in the Indian Ocean or in the Caribbean. Many of them are only a few metres high. That is why the rising sea level threatens them especially.
wichtigste: Many islands lie only a few metres above the sea.
The sea level is rising because water is warming and land ice is melting.
From 1901 to 2018 it rose by about 20 centimetres.
The Maldives are seen as the flattest country in the world.
In the AOSIS alliance, the island states fight for climate protection.
Vanuatu took the climate question to the International Court of Justice.

abschnitte.text: The **sea level** is rising for two main reasons. Warmer water **expands** and takes up more space. In addition, **meltwater** from glaciers and ice sheets flows into the sea. According to the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, the sea level rose by about **20 centimetres** from 1901 to 2018. The rise is also getting faster and faster.

Many islands, especially **atolls**, lie only a few metres above the sea. If the water rises, **floods** threaten. Salt water gets into the groundwater and the fields. Then **drinking water** becomes scarce and plants grow less well. The **Maldives** in the Indian Ocean are seen as the flattest country in the world; their highest natural point is only just over 2 metres high.

The small island states have joined together in the **AOSIS** alliance. This stands for “Alliance of Small Island States”. It was founded in **1990**. At the climate conferences, the island states call for **strict climate protection**. Alone they are small, but together they have many votes.

abschnitte.titel: Pictures that went round the world
abschnitte.text: In **2009** the government of the Maldives held a meeting **under water**. The ministers dived to the seabed with equipment and signed a declaration there. In 2021 the Foreign Minister of **Tuvalu**, **Simon Kofe**, stood knee-deep in the sea in a suit. In this way he spoke to the climate conference by video and showed how threatened his home is.

On the initiative of **Vanuatu**, the UN General Assembly asked the **International Court of Justice** in 2023 for an advisory opinion on countries' climate obligations. The opinion was published in July 2025. In 2014 **Kiribati** bought a large piece of land on the island of Vanua Levu in **Fiji**. In this way it wanted to secure its food supply.

gewusst: Switzerland has no coast, but its melting glaciers also contribute a little to the rise in sea level.
The International Court of Justice has its seat in The Hague in the Netherlands.

teile.einleitung: The Geneva Conventions are international treaties that lay down rules for wars. They protect the wounded, prisoners of war and civilians, meaning people who are not fighting or are no longer fighting. They are the most important part of international humanitarian law and have a close link to Switzerland.
wichtigste: The Geneva Conventions govern the protection of the wounded, prisoners and civilians in wars.
The first Geneva Convention was signed in Geneva in 1864.
The four conventions in force today date from 1949.
Additional protocols were added in 1977 and 2005.
All the countries in the world have recognised the Geneva Conventions.
Switzerland is the depositary state: it keeps the treaties.
The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) watches over their observance.

abschnitte.text: A **convention** is a treaty between countries. The Geneva Conventions lay down how armies must behave in war. For example, they ban torture, killing prisoners and attacks on hospitals. Together they form the core of **international humanitarian law**, which is also called the law of war.

The impulse came from the Genevan **Henry Dunant**, who saw the suffering of the wounded after the Battle of Solferino in 1859. In 1863 what later became the International Committee of the Red Cross was founded in Geneva. As early as 1864, twelve countries signed the first convention in Geneva to protect wounded soldiers. It also introduced the **red cross** on a white background as a protective emblem.

After the Second World War, the rules were rewritten and extended in 1949. The first convention protects the wounded and sick on land, the second the shipwrecked at sea. The third governs the treatment of **prisoners of war**, and the fourth protects civilians. In 1977 two additional protocols were added, and in 2005 a third, which created the red crystal as a further protective emblem.

Those protected are people who are not fighting, meaning **civilians**, doctors, nurses and helpers. Soldiers who are wounded or have surrendered may also no longer be attacked. Prisoners of war must be treated humanely, get enough food and be allowed contact with their families. Vehicles and buildings with the red cross or the **red crescent** must not be attacked.

As the **depositary state**, Switzerland keeps the original treaties and calls conferences. The ICRC, based in Geneva, visits prisoners of war, searches for missing people and reminds the parties to a war of their duties. The Geneva Conventions are among the few treaties that have been ratified by every country in the world. Sadly they are still broken in many wars; serious breaches count as war crimes.

begriffe.erklaerung: Rules that are meant to protect people in war and limit suffering.
A soldier who has been captured by the enemy.
The country that keeps and manages an international treaty.
A sign such as the red cross that protects helpers and hospitals from attack.
A serious breach of the rules of war.

gewusst: The red cross on a white background is the Swiss flag reversed, in honour of Switzerland.
The first Geneva Convention of 1864 had only ten articles.
The four Geneva Conventions were adopted on 12 August 1949.

teile.einleitung: A peace treaty officially ends a war. In it, countries agree that the fighting is over and what should apply afterwards. Some peace treaties have also shaped the history of Switzerland.
wichtigste: A peace treaty officially ends a war.
It becomes valid when the representatives of the countries sign it.
Before that there are often long negotiations.
A ceasefire is only a pause in the fighting.
The Peace of Westphalia of 1648 ended the Thirty Years' War.
The Treaty of Versailles of 1919 settled peace with Germany after the First World War.

abschnitte.text: With a **ceasefire**, the fighting stops, but the war is not yet officially over. Often long **negotiations** follow. In them the countries look for a solution that everyone can accept. At the end comes the **peace treaty**. The representatives of the countries sign it and so promise to keep to it.

Peace treaties often lay down where the **borders** between countries run. They also settle other disputed questions, for example what happens to prisoners. Sometimes a country that has lost the war has to pay money. Such payments are called **reparations**.

The **Peace of Westphalia** was concluded in 1648 in the cities of **Münster** and **Osnabrück**. It ended the **Thirty Years' War** in Europe. It was especially important for Switzerland: it recognised that the **Swiss Confederacy** no longer belonged to the Holy Roman Empire. The mayor of Basel, Johann Rudolf Wettstein, worked hard for this.

The **Treaty of Versailles** was signed in France in 1919. It settled peace with Germany after the **First World War**. Germany lost territory and had to pay high reparations. Many Germans felt the treaty was unfair. Historians see it as one of the reasons for the tensions of the following years.

gewusst: In the Korean War only a ceasefire was agreed in 1953; there is still no peace treaty today.
Since 1953 Swiss officers have helped to monitor this ceasefire in Korea.

teile.einleitung: Interpol is an organisation that links up the police authorities of different countries. It helps to find criminals who flee or operate across borders. Its headquarters is in Lyon in France.
wichtigste: Interpol links up the police of 196 member states.
It was founded in Vienna in 1923.
Since 1989 its headquarters has been in Lyon.
Interpol has no police officers of its own who arrest people.
Its notices are well known, for example the red notice for wanted people.
Interpol may not get involved in political, military or religious cases.
In Switzerland the Federal Office of Police, fedpol, is the link to Interpol.

abschnitte.text: The name **Interpol** is short for International Criminal Police Organization. It is one of the largest international organisations in the world. Almost every country is a member. Interpol makes sure that the police of different countries can exchange information quickly and safely. This is because crimes such as drug trafficking, human trafficking or cybercrime do not stop at borders.

Interpol was founded in Vienna in 1923 as the International Criminal Police Commission. During the Second World War it came under the control of the National Socialists. After the war it was rebuilt in 1946 and moved to Paris. Since 1956 it has had its present name. In 1989 the headquarters moved to **Lyon**.

Every member country has a **National Central Bureau** that is connected to Interpol. Interpol runs large databases, for example with fingerprints, stolen passports and stolen works of art. Police officers can search these data in seconds. But it is always the police of the country concerned that must make an arrest. Interpol itself has no agents like in films who arrest people.

Interpol sends **notices** in different colours to all its members. A red notice asks for a wanted person to be found and provisionally arrested. A yellow notice helps in the search for missing people, often children. A black notice is used to identify unknown dead people. There are other colours too, for example for warnings about dangerous objects.

Switzerland has been a member of Interpol for many decades. Its National Central Bureau is at the Federal Office of Police, **fedpol**, in Bern. Experts work there round the clock. They pass requests from abroad on to the cantonal police forces, and the other way round. Switzerland makes sure that no one who is politically persecuted is handed over.

begriffe.erklaerung: The police search for a person or a thing.
When one country hands over a wanted person to another country.
A large, ordered collection of information on a computer.
All criminal offences, meaning actions that break the law.

gewusst: Interpol has four official languages: Arabic, English, French and Spanish.
Millions of stolen and lost travel documents are stored in the Interpol database.

teile.einleitung: The Good Friday Agreement is a peace agreement for Northern Ireland. It was signed in Belfast on 10 April 1998. It was meant to end a conflict that had lasted for decades.
wichtigste: The agreement was concluded on Good Friday, 10 April 1998.
Because it was signed in Belfast, it is also called the Belfast Agreement.
It was meant to end the Northern Ireland conflict, known as “The Troubles”.
More than 3,500 people had died since the late 1960s.
In May 1998 both parts of Ireland approved it in referendums.
Since then Northern Ireland has been governed by a government of both communities.
John Hume and David Trimble received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1998.

abschnitte.text: In Northern Ireland two groups faced each other. The **unionists** were mostly Protestant and wanted Northern Ireland to belong to Great Britain. The **nationalists** were mostly Catholic and wanted a united Ireland. From the late 1960s there was violence and there were attacks. This period is called **“The Troubles”**.

The talks were led by the former US Senator **George Mitchell**. At the end he set a deadline, which led to the breakthrough. Prime Minister **Tony Blair** signed for Great Britain, and the head of government **Bertie Ahern** for Ireland. Parties from both communities in Northern Ireland also took part. After long negotiations through the night, agreement was reached on Good Friday.

On 22 May 1998 the people in **Northern Ireland** and in the **Republic of Ireland** voted on the same day. In both parts there was a clear majority in favour. This gave the agreement a strong foundation. An important principle is that Northern Ireland stays part of Great Britain as long as the majority there wants this.

The agreement provides for **power-sharing**. Unionists and nationalists must sit together in the regional government. Northern Ireland got its own parliament, the **Northern Ireland Assembly**. Cooperation between Northern Ireland and Ireland was also strengthened. Armed groups were to hand over their weapons.

In 1998 **John Hume** and **David Trimble** received the Nobel Peace Prize. Hume led a moderate nationalist party, and Trimble the largest unionist party. Both worked for peace despite great differences. Later the peace was not without difficulties, but the large-scale violence ended.

gewusst: Good Friday is the Friday before Easter, which is where the agreement's name comes from.
After the agreement, Ireland changed its constitution and gave up its claim to Northern Ireland.

teile.einleitung: After a natural disaster, many people need help quickly. Disaster relief brings rescue, water, food and a roof over people's heads. Switzerland also helps in many countries.
wichtigste: Earthquakes, floods and hurricanes are natural disasters.
After an earthquake, help must come very quickly.
Anyone who has lost their house needs a tent or emergency shelter.
Clean drinking water is especially important after floods.
Swiss Rescue searches for people buried under rubble abroad.
Relief supplies are often brought by aeroplane.

abschnitte.text: A **natural disaster** is a great catastrophe caused by nature. These include **earthquakes**, **floods**, **hurricanes** or volcanic eruptions. A **tsunami** is a huge sea wave, which is often caused by an earthquake under the sea. Such events can put many people in need all at once.

After an earthquake, people are sometimes trapped under collapsed houses. They can usually survive there for only a few days. That is why help must come **very quickly**. **Swiss Rescue** is made up of experts, doctors and **search dogs**. It can fly abroad within hours and search for people buried under rubble.

Anyone who no longer has a house needs a safe place to sleep. That is why aid organisations bring **tents**, **blankets** and tarpaulins. Sometimes whole **emergency shelters** are set up in sports halls or camps. A **relief package** often contains blankets, food and things for personal hygiene. This way people can get through the first few days.

After a flood the water is often **polluted**. Anyone who drinks it can fall ill. A **water filter** holds back dirt and many germs. Helpers also bring tablets that can be used to clean water. That is why clean water is one of the most important forms of help of all.

Over long distances the **aeroplane** is fastest. That is why relief supplies are often flown straight into the disaster area. On the spot, lorries, boats or helicopters distribute the goods further. Many organisations help, for example the **Red Cross**. In Switzerland, **Swiss Solidarity** (the Glückskette) collects donations after major disasters.

gewusst: Search dogs can find people under rubble with their sensitive noses.
The Red Cross was founded in Geneva; its founder Henry Dunant was Swiss.

teile.einleitung: Human Rights Watch is an international organisation that investigates human rights violations and makes them public. It was founded in 1978 and has its headquarters in New York. It is one of the best-known human rights organisations in the world.
wichtigste: Human Rights Watch was founded in 1978 under the name Helsinki Watch.
Since 1988 it has been called Human Rights Watch.
Its headquarters is in New York.
Every year it publishes a World Report on the state of human rights.
According to its own statements, it accepts no money from governments.
It was a founding member of the campaign against landmines, which received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1997.

abschnitte.text: In 1975 countries from East and West signed the **Helsinki Final Act**. In it they also promised to respect human rights. In 1978 **Helsinki Watch** was founded. The group was meant to monitor whether the countries of the **Eastern Bloc** were keeping this promise. Later other “Watch” groups were set up for the Americas, Asia and the Middle East. In 1988 they were united under the name **Human Rights Watch**.

Experts travel to **crisis areas**, interview witnesses and collect **evidence**. This leads to reports on human rights violations. These are made public, so that pressure builds on governments. At the start of every year the **World Report** is published. It describes the situation in about 100 countries. Some governments criticise the reports as one-sided.

Human Rights Watch wants to stay **independent**. That is why, according to its own statements, it accepts **no money from governments**. It is funded by private **donations** and foundations. Besides the headquarters in **New York**, it has offices in many cities around the world. In **Geneva** the organisation presents its investigations to the **UN Human Rights Council**, which meets there several times a year.

Human Rights Watch was a founding member of the **International Campaign to Ban Landmines**. After wars, landmines often stay in the ground for years and injure people. In 1997 the campaign achieved the **Ottawa Treaty**, which bans such mines. In the same year it received the **Nobel Peace Prize** for this.

gewusst: The Helsinki Final Act of 1975 was also signed by Switzerland.
Human Rights Watch's World Report runs to several hundred pages every year.

teile.einleitung: Peace is a state in which people and countries live together without war and violence. There are disagreements in peacetime too, but they are settled with words, negotiations and rules. Peace is one of the most important aims of world politics.
wichtigste: Peace between countries means that there is no war and that disputes are settled without violence.
A distinction is made between negative peace, meaning the absence of war, and positive peace with justice.
The UN was founded in 1945 to secure world peace.
The Nobel Peace Prize has been awarded every year since 1901.
The International Day of Peace is on 21 September.
Switzerland has not fought a war since the Sonderbund War of 1847.
Geneva is seen as an important city for peace negotiations.

abschnitte.text: The German word for peace, Frieden, originally meant protection and sparing; in Latin it is **pax**. Peace starts in small ways, for example when children settle an argument in the playground with words. Between countries, peace means that they do not use weapons against each other. The Norwegian peace researcher Johan Galtung distinguished between **negative peace**, meaning no war, and **positive peace**, in which injustice and poverty are also reduced.

Wars often end with a **peace treaty**. A famous example is the Peace of Westphalia of 1648, which ended the Thirty Years' War. After the First World War, the League of Nations was founded in 1920 with its seat in Geneva. After the Second World War, the UN was created in 1945; its most important aim is to secure world peace.

Countries make treaties, negotiate with each other and keep to **international law**. The UN can send peacekeeping troops, the so-called Blue Helmets, into crisis areas. Disarmament, meaning reducing weapons, is also meant to prevent wars. Trade and cooperation make countries depend on each other, which can make war less likely.

Switzerland is a **neutral** country and does not take part in wars between other states. It offers its good offices, mediates between parties to a conflict and provides places for negotiations such as Geneva. Geneva is home to the International Committee of the Red Cross and the European seat of the UN. Swiss experts help to build peace in many countries.

Since 1901 the **Nobel Peace Prize** has honoured people and organisations that work for peace. Among the first winners was the Genevan Henry Dunant, the founder of the Red Cross. Organisations such as the Red Cross or the UN have also received the prize. Every year on 21 September, the world celebrates the International Day of Peace.

begriffe.erklaerung: A conflict fought with weapons and violence between countries or groups.
A treaty that officially ends a war.
A country stays out of other countries' wars.
Reducing or getting rid of weapons.

gewusst: The Nobel Peace Prize is awarded not in Stockholm but in Oslo.
The Peace of Westphalia of 1648 was negotiated in the cities of Münster and Osnabrück.
The League of Nations, a forerunner of the UN, had its seat in Geneva.

teile.einleitung: Integration means that people who move to Switzerland can live, work and take part well here. The Confederation, the cantons and the municipalities support this together. At the same time, the newcomers are expected to make an effort themselves.
wichtigste: Switzerland's integration policy follows the principle “support and demand”.
The Foreign Nationals and Integration Act, AIG for short, has had this name since 2019.
Since 2019 there has been the Swiss Integration Agenda of the Confederation and the cantons.
The Confederation pays the cantons a one-off sum of 18,000 francs per refugee.
The cantons and municipalities carry out integration on the spot.
Ordinary naturalisation usually requires ten years of residence.

abschnitte.text: The state supports newcomers, for example with **language courses** and advice. But it also expects them to make their own efforts, for example in learning a national language. So both sides carry responsibility. Since 2019 the law on this has been called the **Foreign Nationals and Integration Act**, AIG for short. The new name shows how important integration has become.

Integration mainly happens in everyday life: at school, at work, in clubs and in the neighbourhood. The **cantons and municipalities** carry out the support on the spot. For this the cantons run **cantonal integration programmes**. The Confederation and the cantons pay for them together.

Since 2019 the **Swiss Integration Agenda** has applied. It sets shared goals for refugees and people with provisional admission. One goal is that three years after arriving, they have basic knowledge of a national language at level **A1**. For this the Confederation tripled the integration lump sum from 6,000 to **18,000 francs** per person. The money goes, for example, into language courses and education.

Work is an important part of integration. Since 2018 there has been the **pre-apprenticeship for integration**. It lasts one year and specifically prepares refugees for an apprenticeship. The participants work in a company and at the same time attend language and school lessons.

Anyone who wants to become Swiss can apply for naturalisation. Since 2018, **ordinary naturalisation** has usually required ten years of residence and a **permanent residence permit C**. Years between your 8th and 18th birthdays count double. In addition, the municipality and the canton check whether someone is well integrated.

gewusst: In Switzerland the Confederation, the canton and the municipality all have a say in naturalisation, which is why there are three levels of citizenship.
Years that you spend in Switzerland as a child or teenager count double for naturalisation.

teile.einleitung: The flag of Liechtenstein has a blue stripe at the top and a red stripe at the bottom. In the top left is a golden princely hat, a kind of crown. Liechtenstein is a small neighbour of Switzerland to the east.
wichtigste: The flag of Liechtenstein is blue and red.
The two stripes are horizontal, with blue at the top.
In the top left is the golden princely hat.
The princely hat stands for the prince, because Liechtenstein is a principality.
The crown was added to the flag in 1937.
The reason was that Haiti had almost the same flag at the 1936 Olympic Games.

abschnitte.text: The flag of Liechtenstein has two **horizontal stripes**. **Blue** is at the top, **red** at the bottom. In the top left, on the blue stripe, is a **golden princely hat**. This is a special crown. The flag is simple and yet easy to recognise.

Liechtenstein is a **principality**. At the head of the state is a **prince**. He governs together with the people and the parliament, the **Landtag**. The **princely hat** on the flag stands for the prince and the princely house. So it shows that the country is a monarchy.

In **1936** the Olympic Games took place in **Berlin**. There people noticed that **Haiti** had almost the same blue and red flag as Liechtenstein. This could lead to confusion. That is why the **princely hat** was added to Liechtenstein's flag in **1937**. Since then it has been easy to tell the two flags apart.

Liechtenstein lies **east of Switzerland**, on the **Rhine**. It borders the cantons of **St Gallen** and the **Grisons** and Austria. The capital is called **Vaduz**. Liechtenstein and Switzerland are closely linked: in Liechtenstein people pay with the **Swiss franc**. Both countries also belong to **EFTA**.

gewusst: Liechtenstein is one of the smallest countries in the world and has no army of its own.
Since 1923 a customs treaty has linked Switzerland and Liechtenstein.

t19hxz6p.t: International Red Cross and Red Crescent Museum

teile.einleitung: The International Red Cross and Red Crescent Museum is in Geneva. It tells how people are helped in wars and disasters. The museum opened in 1988.
wichtigste: The museum is in Geneva, right next to the seat of the ICRC.
It is at 17 Avenue de la Paix; “paix” means peace.
It opened in 1988.
It owns the medal of the first Nobel Peace Prize, from 1901.
The collection includes about 30,000 objects.
About 120,000 visitors come every year.

abschnitte.text: The museum shows how people in need are helped, for example in wars, after earthquakes or in floods. It is in **Geneva** at 17 **Avenue de la Paix**, right next to the seat of the **ICRC**. “Paix” means “peace” in English. The museum opened in 1988. About 120,000 people visit it every year.

A special treasure is the medal of the first **Nobel Peace Prize**, from 1901. This prize went to the Genevan **Henry Dunant**, the founder of the Red Cross. In 1859 Dunant had witnessed the Battle of Solferino and seen that wounded soldiers were left without help. This gave him his idea of a neutral aid organisation.

abschnitte.titel: Index cards from the First World War
abschnitte.text: In the **First World War**, the Red Cross in Geneva collected information about **prisoners of war**. Millions of index cards were written for this. In this way families could find out where their relatives were and find them again. In the museum you can see how huge this card index was.

The collection includes about **30,000 objects**, for example photos, posters, letters and relief supplies. The exhibition shows not only history but also today's questions. Visitors can try things out for themselves and think about what humanity means. The museum is one of the well-known museums of the city of Geneva.

gewusst: The card index of prisoners of war from the First World War is part of UNESCO's Memory of the World.
Henry Dunant, the first winner of the Nobel Peace Prize, came from Geneva, the museum's city.

teile.einleitung: Humanitarian aid saves lives and relieves suffering. It helps people after wars, natural disasters or famines. Clear principles apply, so that the aid reaches everyone in need.
wichtigste: Humanitarian aid helps everyone in need, no matter where they come from.
Humanitarian workers are neutral and do not side with any party to a war.
In a famine, food and clean water are needed first.
After wars, landmines have to be removed.
The Red Cross emblem is protected by the Geneva Conventions.
World Humanitarian Day is on 19 August.

abschnitte.text: **Humanitarian aid** is help for people in acute need. It comes after an earthquake, a flood, a war or a famine. The aim is to **save lives** and relieve suffering. It does not ask about origin, religion or opinion. Every person in need should get help.

Humanitarian workers work according to fixed principles. They are **neutral**: they do not side with any party to a war. They are **impartial**: whoever needs help most gets it first. And they are **independent** of governments. That is why both sides of a conflict often trust them and let them reach the victims.

In a famine, **food** and clean **water** are needed first. Severely malnourished children are often given a special **peanut paste** made of peanuts, milk powder and vitamins. It is very nourishing and keeps for a long time. After a war, experts search for **landmines** and make them harmless. These often stay hidden in the ground for many years.

The **Red Cross emblem** is protected by the **Geneva Conventions**. Anyone who wears it and helps must not be attacked in war. In many countries the **Red Crescent** is used instead. The International Committee of the Red Cross has its seat in **Geneva**. It helps victims of war all over the world.

Many aid organisations work with **volunteers**. They give their time without being paid for it. Without them, many organisations could not work at all. Every year on **19 August** is **World Humanitarian Day**. It honours everyone who helps others in need, sometimes in great danger.

gewusst: World Humanitarian Day recalls an attack on the UN headquarters in Baghdad on 19 August 2003.
The peanut paste for starving children can be eaten without cooking and without clean water.

teile.einleitung: The Nobel Peace Prize is one of the best-known prizes in the world. It honours people or organisations that have done a great deal for peace. The very first winner came from Switzerland.
wichtigste: The prize is named after the Swede Alfred Nobel.
The Nobel Peace Prize is presented in Oslo in Norway.
The ceremony is held every year on 10 December, the anniversary of Nobel's death.
In 1901 the Genevan Henry Dunant received the first Nobel Peace Prize.
The ICRC has received the prize three times: in 1917, 1944 and 1963.
In 2014 Malala Yousafzai was the youngest winner, at 17.

abschnitte.text: **Alfred Nobel** was born in 1833 in **Stockholm**, the capital of Sweden. He was a chemist and inventor and became rich through **dynamite**. In his **will** he laid down that prizes should be awarded every year with his money. He died on 10 December 1896. Since then there have been prizes for physics, chemistry, medicine, literature and peace, among others.

Most Nobel Prizes are awarded in Stockholm. The **Nobel Peace Prize**, on the other hand, is presented in **Oslo** in Norway. A committee in Norway chooses the winners. The ceremony takes place on **10 December**. Whoever receives the prize gets a gold **medal**, a diploma and prize money.

The very first Nobel Peace Prize went in 1901 to **Henry Dunant** from Geneva, the founder of the Red Cross. He shared it with the Frenchman Frédéric Passy. The **International Committee of the Red Cross** (ICRC) received the prize in 1917, 1944 and 1963. No other organisation has received it so often.

The prize is normally awarded **once a year**. In some years, for example in times of war, nobody received it. In 2014 it went to **Malala Yousafzai**, who campaigns for all girls to be allowed to go to school. At 17 she was the youngest winner. Nelson Mandela and Martin Luther King also received the Nobel Peace Prize.

gewusst: The Nobel Peace Prize can also go to organisations, not only to individual people.
In his old age Henry Dunant lived in Heiden in the canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden, where a museum remembers him today.

teile.einleitung: A refugee is a person who has had to leave their home because of war or persecution. They cannot go back, because they would be in danger there. Today more people around the world are fleeing than at any time for decades.
wichtigste: A refugee is a person who has had to leave their home because of war or persecution.
The Geneva Refugee Convention of 1951 lays down who counts as a refugee.
Refugees must not be sent back to a country where they face persecution.
The UN refugee agency UNHCR has its seat in Geneva.
In 2024 more than 100 million people around the world had fled or been driven from their homes.
Many refugees stay in their own country; they are called internally displaced people.
World Refugee Day is on 20 June.

abschnitte.text: According to the **Geneva Refugee Convention** of 1951, a refugee is a person who has left their country because they are being persecuted. The reasons can be their religion, origin, nationality, political opinion or membership of a particular group. People fleeing war also usually receive protection. Someone who flees within their own country is called an **internally displaced person**.

According to the UN refugee agency, more than 100 million people around the world had fled or been driven from their homes in 2024. In recent years there have been large movements of refugees, for example from Syria, Afghanistan, Ukraine, Sudan and Myanmar. Most refugees live in countries neighbouring their home, not in rich countries. Countries such as Turkey, Iran or Colombia have taken in especially large numbers of people.

An important principle is the **ban on sending people back**, also called non-refoulement. It means that nobody may be sent back to a country where they face torture or persecution. Recognised refugees have, for example, the right to school, work and protection by the law. At the same time they must keep to the laws of their new country.

Anyone seeking protection in Switzerland makes an **asylum application**. The State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) examines whether the person is recognised as a refugee. Some are given provisional admission if a return is too dangerous at the moment. In 2022, for people from Ukraine, Switzerland introduced **protection status S** for the first time.

Over the course of history Switzerland has taken in refugees again and again, for example Huguenots from France in the 17th century. After the Hungarian uprising of 1956, thousands of people came from Hungary, and later also from Tibet, Czechoslovakia and Vietnam. During the Second World War, however, Switzerland also turned away many Jewish refugees at the border. Today this is remembered as a dark chapter of Swiss history.

begriffe.erklaerung: Protection that a state grants to a person who is being persecuted.
When people are threatened, locked up or harmed because of their origin, religion or opinion.
The refugee agency of the United Nations, with its seat in Geneva.
People who have had to flee but have stayed in their own country.

gewusst: The UN refugee agency UNHCR has received the Nobel Peace Prize twice, in 1954 and 1981.
About 40 per cent of all refugees worldwide are children.

teile.einleitung: Cross-border commuters live in one country and work in another. They regularly travel across the border to work and back home again. There are a great many of them in Switzerland.
wichtigste: A cross-border commuter lives in one country and works in the neighbouring country.
Cross-border commuters in Switzerland receive permit G.
In summer 2026 about 400,000 cross-border commuters were working in Switzerland.
More than half of them live in France.
Most cross-border commuters work in the canton of Geneva, followed by Ticino and Vaud.
In Ticino almost all cross-border commuters come from Italy.

abschnitte.text: Cross-border commuters are **commuters**: in the morning they travel to work in the neighbouring country, and in the evening they go back home. Some take the car, others the train, the bicycle or the tram. Because many people are on the move at the same time, there are often **traffic jams** at border crossings in the morning, for example near Basel or Geneva. Cross-border commuters must regularly return to their home abroad.

Anyone who lives abroad and works in Switzerland gets a **cross-border commuter permit**, **permit G**. The G stands for Grenzgänger, the German word for cross-border commuter. Since Switzerland agreed the **free movement of persons** with the EU, it has become easier for people from EU countries to work in Switzerland. Cross-border commuters work, for example, in hospitals, factories, shops and on building sites.

Most cross-border commuters come from **France**, more than half of them. They are followed by **Italy** and **Germany**, plus some from Austria. The canton of **Geneva** has the most cross-border commuters; many live in the French border area around the city. Almost all of those who come to **Ticino** are from Italy. Around **Basel**, many commute from Germany and France.

In Ticino, cross-border commuters are called **“frontalieri”** in Italian. The word comes from “frontiera”, the border. In Geneva and the rest of French-speaking Switzerland, people say **“frontaliers”** in French. Cross-border commuters are important for many companies, because they bring skills. At the same time, politicians debate what effects they have on wages and traffic.

gewusst: In the canton of Geneva, a large share of employees are cross-border commuters from France.
Basel lies at the point where three countries meet: Switzerland, Germany and France.

teile.einleitung: The free trade agreement of 1972 governs trade in industrial goods between Switzerland and the European Economic Community, today's EU. It is one of Switzerland's most important agreements with Europe and still applies today.
wichtigste: The agreement was signed in Brussels on 22 July 1972.
On 3 December 1972, 72.5 per cent of voters said yes.
It has applied without interruption since 1 January 1973.
It removes customs duties and quantity limits for industrial products.
Farm products are not covered in principle.
Switzerland had already been a founding member of EFTA since 1960.

abschnitte.text: With **free trade**, goods are traded across the border without **customs duties** and without **quotas**. A quota is a maximum amount that may be imported. Otherwise, though, the countries involved stay independent. They make their own laws and have no shared government. That is what makes a free trade agreement different from membership of the EU.

In 1960 several countries founded the **European Free Trade Association EFTA**; Switzerland was part of it from the start. Alongside it there was the **European Economic Community EEC**. In 1973 important EFTA partners such as **Great Britain** and Denmark moved to the EEC. Without a new agreement, Swiss exports to those countries would have been subject to customs duties again. That is why the treaty was so important for Switzerland.

The agreement was signed on 22 July 1972 in **Brussels**, the seat of the EEC. After that the Swiss people were allowed to vote on it. On 3 December 1972, **72.5 per cent** of voters said yes. Turnout was just under 53 per cent. On **1 January 1973** the agreement came into force.

abschnitte.titel: What applies and what does not
abschnitte.text: The agreement mainly covers **industrial products** such as machines, chemicals or watches. For these goods, customs duties between Switzerland and the EEC were dropped. **Farm products** are not covered in principle. Separate rules apply to them, so that Swiss farmers stay protected. Later further treaties were added, for example the **bilateral agreements**.

gewusst: The 1972 agreement has applied without interruption for more than 50 years.
The EU is still Switzerland's most important trading partner today.

t1cfn64n.t: Trade conflict between China and the USA

teile.einleitung: Since 2018 the USA and China have been arguing fiercely about trade and technology. Both countries charge customs duties on each other's goods and restrict exports. Because they are the two largest economies in the world, the dispute affects many other countries.
wichtigste: In 2018 the USA introduced customs duties against China, based on Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974.
China responded with counter-duties, especially on US soya beans.
In 2019 the USA put Huawei on the so-called Entity List.
Since 2022 the USA has restricted the export of advanced computer chips to China.
In 2023 China restricted the export of gallium and germanium.
In May 2025 the two countries agreed in Geneva on a temporary cut in customs duties.

abschnitte.text: In 2018 the US government imposed **customs duties** on many goods from China. A customs duty is a charge that has to be paid when goods are imported. The USA based this on **Section 301** of the Trade Act of 1974. It accused China of forced technology transfer and of violating **intellectual property**. China rejected the accusations and responded with duties of its own.

China was the largest buyer of American **soya beans**. With counter-duties, China deliberately hit farming in the USA. Many farmers lost income. That is why the US government gave them **aid payments**. This shows that a trade conflict also hits people who are not directly involved at all.

In 2019 the USA put the Chinese company **Huawei** on the **Entity List**. Since then companies have needed a permit to supply Huawei with US technology.
