From October 2022 the USA restricted the export of advanced **semiconductors**, meaning computer chips, and of the machines used to make them. The aim is to slow down China's progress in artificial intelligence and military technology. In 2023 China responded with export restrictions on the metals **gallium** and **germanium**.

In 2025 customs duties rose sharply. At times the USA demanded additional duties of 145 per cent, and China counter-duties of 125 per cent. In May 2025 representatives of both countries met in **Geneva**. After that the USA lowered its additional duties to **30 per cent** for 90 days, and China lowered its own to 10 per cent. Switzerland acted as **host**.

In politics two paths are being discussed. **Decoupling** means a far-reaching separation of the economies. **De-risking** means reducing risk: the aim is to reduce dependence on China without cutting off trade completely, for example by using suppliers in other countries. Which path is right is disputed.

gewusst: China is by far the largest producer of gallium and germanium, which are important for chips.
A customs duty is paid by the importer in their own country, not by the country the goods come from.

t1cly98g.t: Court of Justice of the European Union

teile.einleitung: The Court of Justice of the European Union has its seat in Luxembourg. It makes sure that EU law is interpreted and applied in the same way in all member states. It is made up of two courts: the Court of Justice and the General Court.
wichtigste: Its seat is in the city of Luxembourg.
Each of the 27 member states provides one judge at the Court of Justice.
The judges are appointed for six years, and they can be reappointed.
Eleven Advocates General give independent opinions before judgments.
In the preliminary ruling procedure, national courts ask what EU law means.
The EU Commission can take member states to court if they do not apply EU law.
The Court of Justice of the EU is not the same as the European Court of Human Rights.

abschnitte.text: The **Court of Justice of the European Union** is in **Luxembourg**. Its main task is to interpret **EU law** and check whether it is being kept. This way it applies in the same way in all member states. It is made up of the **Court of Justice**, often called the CJEU, and the **General Court**. The General Court deals, for example, with cases brought by companies against decisions of the EU.

Each of the 27 member countries provides **one judge** at the Court of Justice. The governments of the member states appoint the judges together for **six years**, and they can be reappointed. There are also **eleven Advocates General**. Before a judgment, they present an independent opinion. The judges do not have to follow it, but they often do.

If a court in a member state is unsure what EU law means, it refers the question to the Court of Justice. This is called the **preliminary ruling procedure**, set out in Article 267 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU. The answer then applies to all courts. If a member state does not apply EU law, the **EU Commission** can start **infringement proceedings**. If the country loses, it must apply the law, or else it faces fines.

The Court of Justice of the EU is often confused with the **European Court of Human Rights**. That court is in **Strasbourg** and belongs to the **Council of Europe**, not to the EU. Switzerland is a member of the Council of Europe, so cases from Switzerland can be heard in Strasbourg. This is not possible in principle at the Court of Justice of the EU in Luxembourg, because Switzerland is not an EU member.

In the negotiations on new treaties between Switzerland and the EU, the role of the Court of Justice was a major point of dispute. The plan is that an **arbitration tribunal** decides in disputes. If the dispute is about interpreting EU law, the tribunal is to ask the Court of Justice of the EU for its interpretation. Supporters see this as a fair solution; opponents fear foreign judges.

gewusst: Cases at the Court of Justice are heard in all the official languages of the EU, but internally it mostly works in French.
The Court of Justice was founded in 1952, at that time for the European Coal and Steel Community.

teile.einleitung: A border separates two countries, cantons or municipalities from each other. It shows where one area ends and the next begins. Switzerland has borders with five neighbouring countries.
wichtigste: Switzerland borders Germany, France, Italy, Austria and Liechtenstein.
Borders often run along rivers, lakes or mountain ridges.
On Lake Geneva the border with France runs through the middle of the lake.
In the Jura, the Doubs forms part of the border with France.
Büsingen is a German exclave that is completely surrounded by Swiss territory.
The border is watched over by Swiss customs.

abschnitte.text: A **border** is a line that separates two areas. It is drawn on maps, but in nature you often cannot see it. Sometimes **boundary stones** mark where it runs. There are borders between countries, but also between cantons and municipalities. Up to the border, one country's laws apply; beyond it, those of the neighbouring country.

Many borders follow nature. Over long stretches the **Rhine** separates Switzerland from Germany and Austria. In the Jura flows the **Doubs**, which forms part of the border with France. On **Lake Geneva** the border runs through the middle of the water. In the Alps the border often lies on mountain ridges and passes, for example on the **Great St Bernard** between the Valais and the Aosta Valley.

The town of **Chiasso** in Ticino lies right on the border with Italy. The southernmost point of Switzerland is also near Chiasso. Every day many cars, lorries and trains cross the border here. That is why Chiasso is an important place for traffic between north and south.

An **exclave** is a piece of land that belongs to one country but is completely surrounded by the territory of another country. A well-known example is **Büsingen** on the High Rhine. The village belongs to Germany but is surrounded on all sides by Switzerland. **Campione d'Italia** on Lake Lugano is also an exclave: it belongs to Italy and lies in the middle of Ticino.

In the past, **border guards** watched over the border, including away from the large crossings. This “green border” runs through woods and fields and over mountains. Today these officers belong to the **Federal Office for Customs and Border Security**. Since Switzerland joined the Schengen Agreement, people are no longer checked every time they enter. But goods are still checked.

gewusst: In Büsingen people often pay with francs, even though the village belongs to Germany.
On the Great St Bernard there is a hospice where the famous St Bernard dogs used to be bred.

teile.einleitung: The institutional framework agreement was a planned treaty between Switzerland and the European Union. It was meant to govern how the bilateral agreements would be adapted to new law and how disputes would be settled. In 2021 the Federal Council broke off the negotiations.
wichtigste: The negotiations began on 22 May 2014.
A finished draft treaty was ready in November 2018.
The agreement was to apply to five market access agreements.
The main points of dispute were wage protection, the Citizens' Rights Directive and state aid.
On 26 May 2021 the Federal Council broke off the negotiations.
There was never a popular vote on it.

abschnitte.text: Switzerland is not a member of the EU, but it has many **bilateral agreements** with it. The framework agreement was meant to form a shared roof over five market access agreements, including the free movement of persons and land and air transport. It was about **adopting law**, monitoring and **settling disputes**. Schengen and Dublin would not have been covered, because they have their own rules.

If the EU changes its law in an area covered by the agreements, Switzerland would have been expected to adapt its law regularly. This is called **dynamic adoption of law**. Switzerland would have kept the right to a **referendum**. In disputes, an **arbitration tribunal** was to decide. If it was about interpreting EU law, it would have had to ask the **Court of Justice of the European Union** in Luxembourg.

Three points were especially disputed in Switzerland. Trade unions feared that **wages** would be less well protected. The **Citizens' Rights Directive** governs, among other things, EU citizens' access to social benefits; there were fears of higher costs for social assistance. On **state aid**, people were worried about state guarantees for cantonal banks or cantonal energy companies. Supporters, on the other hand, stressed secure access to the EU single market.

On 26 May 2021 the **Federal Council** ended the negotiations. After that the EU stopped updating, for example, the agreement on technical barriers to trade for **medical devices**. Since then Swiss medical technology companies have needed additional approvals in the EU. Later Switzerland and the EU started new talks on a package of agreements.

gewusst: The framework agreement was negotiated for about seven years, but the people never voted on it.
Arbitration tribunals have existed for a long time: two parties in a dispute choose together who will decide their dispute.

teile.einleitung: The KlimaSeniorinnen Schweiz (Senior Women for Climate Protection Switzerland) are an association of women of pension age. They took Switzerland to court because, they said, it was doing too little for climate protection. In 2024 the European Court of Human Rights ruled in their favour.
wichtigste: The association was founded in August 2016.
Its members are women of pension age.
The association was set up on the initiative of Greenpeace Switzerland.
The Federal Supreme Court rejected their appeal in 2020.
The court in Strasbourg ruled in their favour on 9 April 2024.
In June 2024 the Swiss Parliament declared that Switzerland did not need to take any further action on the judgment.

abschnitte.text: The association **KlimaSeniorinnen Schweiz** brings together older women who campaign for more **climate protection**. It was founded in **August 2016**. The idea came from the environmental organisation **Greenpeace Switzerland**, which also supported the association later. Together the women demand that politicians do more against climate change.

The association based its case on **heat**. Studies show that older people, and especially **older women**, fall ill or die more often during heatwaves. Because climate change makes heatwaves more frequent, the women saw their **health** as threatened. They felt that the state had to protect them better.

abschnitte.titel: The long road through the courts
abschnitte.text: In 2016 the women submitted a request to the **federal authorities**. It was rejected, and they took the case further. In **2020** the **Federal Supreme Court** in Lausanne also rejected the appeal. It found that the women were not affected strongly enough. That is why they went to the European Court of Human Rights in **Strasbourg**.

The **European Court of Human Rights** belongs to the **Council of Europe**, not to the EU. On **9 April 2024** its Grand Chamber announced its judgment. It found that Switzerland had done too little for climate protection and had therefore violated a right under the **Convention on Human Rights**. It was the first judgment of this court that accused a country of too little climate protection.

The judgment was hotly debated in Switzerland. In **June 2024** both chambers of **Parliament** adopted a declaration. It said that the court had gone too far and that Switzerland was already meeting its climate obligations. Others welcomed the judgment as an important step for climate protection. The question of how far courts should have a say in climate policy remains disputed.

gewusst: The KlimaSeniorinnen judgment is followed closely by experts on climate cases around the world.
Strasbourg is in France, near the border with Germany.

teile.einleitung: The Group of Twenty, G20 for short, is an association of important industrialised and emerging countries. Its members are the 20 economically most important countries or groups of countries in the world, namely 19 countries plus the EU, and since 2023 also the African Union. Every year the heads of state and government meet for a summit.
wichtigste: The G20 is an association of the economically most important countries in the world.
Its members are 19 countries, the European Union and, since 2023, the African Union.
The G20 was founded in 1999 after the Asian financial crisis.
Since 2008 the heads of state and government have met at summits.
Together the members produce most of the world economy.
Switzerland is not a member, but it is invited to some meetings.

abschnitte.text: The **G20** is a forum in which important countries talk about the economy, finance and global problems. It is not an organisation with its own seat or its own administration. Every year a different member takes over the **presidency** and organises the summit. Decisions of the G20 are not binding, but they carry great weight.

The members include the USA, China, India, Japan, Germany, France, Brazil, South Africa and Saudi Arabia. In addition there is the **European Union** as a whole. In 2023 the **African Union** was admitted as the 21st member. Together the members stand for about two thirds of the world's population and about 85 per cent of the world's economic output.

The G20 was created in 1999 as a meeting of finance ministers and central bank governors after the **Asian financial crisis**. During the global financial crisis of 2008, the heads of state and government met for the first time in Washington. Since then a **summit** has taken place every year, for example in Hamburg in 2017 or in Johannesburg in 2025, the first summit in Africa. Before that, the smaller G7 was the most important meeting place of rich industrialised countries.

The G20 talks about **economic growth**, banks and taxes. Now it also deals with climate protection, health, food and digitalisation. Around the summits there are many meetings of ministers and experts. Critics say that the other roughly 170 countries in the world have no say in these decisions.

Switzerland is not a member, even though it has an important **financial centre**. But for some years it has regularly been invited to the meetings of finance ministers and central bank governors. This way it can contribute its experience in banking questions. Switzerland also works to make sure that important questions are discussed at the UN too, where all countries are represented.

begriffe.erklaerung: A meeting of the top politicians of several countries.
A country on the way from being a developing country to an industrialised country.
The country that leads and organises the meetings for a year.
A group of seven large industrialised countries, including the USA, Japan and Germany.

gewusst: Although it is called the G20, the group has actually had 21 members since 2023.
The first G20 summit in Africa took place in Johannesburg in 2025.
The G20 has no office of its own; the host country takes over the organisation each time.

teile.einleitung: International relations are all the connections between different countries, meaning politics, trade and treaties, but also disputes and war. This is because “international” means between different countries. The study of international relations asks why countries work together or fight each other.
wichtigste: “International” means between different countries.
The modern system of sovereign states began with the Peace of Westphalia in 1648.
Realism sees countries as players who strive for power and security in an anarchic system.
Kenneth Waltz founded neorealism in 1979.
Alexander Wendt's constructivism stresses that ideas and norms shape world politics.
Soft power means influence through culture, values and policies.
In the Cold War there was a bipolar order with two superpowers.

abschnitte.text: When countries negotiate with each other, trade or make treaties, this is called **international relations**. Those involved are mainly countries, but also international organisations such as the UN, large companies and aid organisations. Looking after these relations through ambassadors is called **diplomacy**. The study of it is a separate subject at universities, part of political science.

In 1648 the **Peace of Westphalia**, concluded in Münster and Osnabrück, ended the Thirty Years' War in Europe. It is seen as the starting point of the modern system of **sovereign states**, which do not have to obey anyone above them. It was especially important for Switzerland, because the Swiss Confederacy was released from the Holy Roman Empire. This had been negotiated by the mayor of Basel, Johann Rudolf Wettstein.

**Realism** is an important theory: it sees the world as an anarchic system, because there is no world government above the countries. That is why countries strive above all for power and security. In 1979 Kenneth Waltz developed neorealism from this with his book “Theory of International Politics”. A typical problem is the **security dilemma**: if one country arms itself for protection, others feel threatened and arm themselves too.

Other theories are more optimistic and stress cooperation, trade and international organisations. The **democratic peace theory** says that democracies hardly ever wage war on each other. The philosopher Immanuel Kant had already prepared this idea in 1795 in his essay “Perpetual Peace”. Alexander Wendt's **constructivism** says that ideas and norms decide how countries behave. His sentence from 1992 says: anarchy is what states make of it.

In the **Cold War**, from about 1947 to 1991, there was a bipolar order with two superpowers, the USA and the Soviet Union. After the collapse of the Soviet Union, the USA was for a time the only superpower. Today many experts speak of a multipolar world with several strong powers, such as the USA, China and the EU. The American Joseph Nye coined the term **soft power**: influence through the attraction of culture, values and policies instead of through weapons or money.

Switzerland is a **neutral** country and does not join military alliances. It often offers its good offices, meaning mediation in conflicts and meeting places for negotiations. For example, since 1980 it has represented the interests of the USA in Iran as what is called a **protecting power**. Many international organisations have their seat in Geneva, which is why the city is a centre of diplomacy.

begriffe.erklaerung: A country is sovereign when it decides its own affairs.
The art of looking after relations between countries through talks and negotiations.
A state without a higher government that can give orders to everyone.
When one country's arming threatens others and leads them to arm in return.
A country's influence through culture, values and example instead of force.

gewusst: The independence of the Swiss Confederacy from the Holy Roman Empire was only officially recognised in 1648 in the Peace of Westphalia.
Films, music and sport can be important means of soft power for a country.
As a protecting power, Switzerland has represented the interests of the USA in Iran for more than 40 years.

teile.einleitung: All people should have equal rights, no matter where they come from or what their skin colour or sex is. This idea is in the Swiss Federal Constitution and in human rights. Many people had to fight for it for a long time.
wichtigste: Article 8 of the Federal Constitution says: “Every person is equal before the law.”
Since 1981 equal rights for men and women have been in the Federal Constitution.
Discrimination means treating people unfairly and putting them at a disadvantage.
In 1955 Rosa Parks stayed in her seat on a bus in Montgomery.
In 1963 Martin Luther King gave the speech “I have a dream”.
Nelson Mandela fought for equal rights in South Africa.
On 14 June 1991 hundreds of thousands of women in Switzerland went on strike for equality.

abschnitte.text: **Article 8** of the Swiss **Federal Constitution** says: “Every person is equal before the law.” This means that the same rules apply to everyone. For example, nobody may be put at a disadvantage because of their origin, language, religion or a disability. The **Universal Declaration of Human Rights** of 1948 also begins with the idea that all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights.

Anyone who treats someone worse because of their origin, skin colour or sex is **discriminating** against them. So discrimination means putting people at an unfair **disadvantage**. It can happen in everyday life, at school, at work or when looking for a flat. Laws are meant to protect against it, but every single person can also help by being fair.

Women in Switzerland only got the right to vote and stand for election at federal level in 1971. In **1981** the people approved the article on **equal rights for men and women**. Because there were still many differences in everyday life, for example in wages, hundreds of thousands of women took part in the **women's strike** on **14 June 1991**. In 1996 the Gender Equality Act came into force.

In parts of the USA, black and white people had to sit separately for a long time, for example on buses. In 1955 **Rosa Parks** refused to give up her seat for a white man in **Montgomery**. This became an important sign against **racial segregation**. In 1963 **Martin Luther King** gave the famous speech **“I have a dream”**. He dreamt of a country in which all people are treated equally.

In **South Africa** there was **apartheid** for a long time, a strict separation of black and white people. **Nelson Mandela** fought against it and was in prison for many years because of this. He was released in 1990 and received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1993. In 1994 he became South Africa's first black **president**.

gewusst: In the canton of Appenzell Innerrhoden, women have only been allowed to vote at cantonal level since 1990, after a ruling by the Federal Supreme Court.
In 2019 there was another large women's strike in Switzerland on 14 June.

teile.einleitung: The flag of Greece is blue and white. It has nine horizontal stripes and, in the top left, a white cross on a blue field. Its stripes recall a famous cry from the struggle for independence.
wichtigste: The Greek flag is blue and white.
It has nine horizontal stripes, five blue and four white.
The top and bottom stripes are blue.
In the top left is a white cross on a blue field.
The stripes are said to stand for the syllables of the cry “Freedom or death”.
The cross stands for the Christian faith.

abschnitte.text: The flag of Greece has **nine horizontal stripes**. **Five** of them are **blue** and **four** are **white**. They alternate, and the top and bottom stripes are blue. In the top left corner is a **blue field** with a **white cross**. This cross has four arms of equal length.

It is said that the nine stripes stand for the **nine syllables** of a cry. In Greek it is **“Eleftheria i thanatos”**, meaning “Freedom or death”. The Greeks used this cry in the **War of Independence** from **1821**. At that time Greece wanted to free itself from the rule of the **Ottoman Empire**. After some years, a Greek state of its own was created.

The **cross** stands for the **Christian Orthodox faith**. Many people in Greece belong to the Orthodox Church. The **blue** is often linked with the **sea** and the **sky**. Greece has a great many islands and a long coastline. To some people, the **white** recalls the waves and the white houses on the islands.

The striped flag was used soon after the start of the fight for independence, at first mainly on **ships**. For a long time there was also another flag with a simple cross. Since **1978** the striped flag has been the only **national flag** of Greece. At celebrations, for example on the National Day on **25 March**, it can be seen everywhere.

gewusst: At the opening of the Olympic Games, Greece always enters first, because the Games come from Greece.
Over the course of history, the blue of the Greek flag has sometimes been lighter and sometimes darker.

teile.einleitung: Japan is today the only country in the world whose head of state is an emperor. But the emperor has no political power. He is a symbol of the state and the unity of the people.
wichtigste: Japan is the only country with an emperor as head of state.
Since 2019 Naruhito has been Emperor of Japan (as of 2026).
He succeeded his father Akihito.
The Imperial Palace is in the middle of Tokyo.
The sign of the imperial house is a golden chrysanthemum.
The government is led by the Prime Minister, not the emperor.

abschnitte.text: China and Korea also used to have emperors, but today there is only one, in Japan. In Japanese he is called the **Tennō**. Since 2019 **Naruhito** has been emperor (as of 2026). He succeeded his father **Akihito**, who gave up the throne during his lifetime. His wife is Empress **Masako**; the two have been married since 1993.

The **Constitution of Japan** calls the emperor the **symbol of the state and of the unity of the people**. He does not make laws or take political decisions. The government is led by the **Prime Minister**, who is elected by Parliament. The emperor mainly has ceremonial tasks; for example, he receives guests from other countries. This is a little like kings and queens in Europe.

The **Imperial Palace** is in the middle of **Tokyo**, the capital of Japan. It is surrounded by moats and walls and by large gardens. The emperor lives and works there. Parts of the gardens are open to visitors.

The emblem of the imperial house is a golden **chrysanthemum** with 16 petals. That is why the throne is also called the **Chrysanthemum Throne**. The emperor's birthday is a national **holiday** in Japan. For Naruhito it is 23 February. With each new emperor, a new era with its own name also begins in Japan; since 2019 it has been called **Reiwa**.

gewusst: In Japan years are also counted by the emperor: 2019 was the first year of the Reiwa era.
The Japanese imperial house is seen as the oldest hereditary monarchy in the world that still exists.

t1exo0co.t: Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights

teile.einleitung: The Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, OHCHR for short, works for human rights around the world. It was created in 1993 and has its headquarters in Geneva. It is led by a High Commissioner.
wichtigste: The World Conference on Human Rights in Vienna in 1993 recommended creating the post.
The UN General Assembly created it in the same year.
Its headquarters is the Palais Wilson in Geneva.
The first High Commissioner was José Ayala-Lasso from Ecuador.
The OHCHR supports the Universal Periodic Review of the Human Rights Council.
Since 2022 the Austrian Volker Türk has been High Commissioner (as of 2025).

abschnitte.text: In 1993 countries from all over the world met in **Vienna** for the **World Conference on Human Rights**. In the Vienna Declaration they called for a separate office for human rights at the UN. The **General Assembly** created it in the same year. The office is meant to promote human rights, point out violations and advise countries. Its basis is the **Universal Declaration of Human Rights** of 1948.

The office has its headquarters in the **Palais Wilson** in **Geneva**. The building on Lake Geneva used to be the seat of the secretariat of the **League of Nations**, the organisation that came before the UN. The **UN Human Rights Council** also meets in Geneva. That is why the city is an important centre for human rights.

Since 2008 there has been the **Universal Periodic Review**. In it, the human rights situation in every UN member state is reviewed by the Human Rights Council about every four and a half to five years. Other countries make **recommendations**. The OHCHR supports this process. Switzerland is also reviewed regularly in this way.

The first High Commissioner, from 1994, was **José Ayala-Lasso** from Ecuador. From 1997 to 2002 the post was held by **Mary Robinson**, the former President of Ireland. The Brazilian **Sérgio Vieira de Mello** died in 2003 in an attack on the UN headquarters in Baghdad. From 2008 to 2014 the South African **Navi Pillay** led the office. In October 2022 **Volker Türk** succeeded Michelle Bachelet.

gewusst: The anniversary of Sérgio Vieira de Mello's death, 19 August, is now World Humanitarian Day.
Navi Pillay had previously been a judge at the Rwanda Tribunal and at the International Criminal Court.

teile.einleitung: Hybrid warfare combines military and non-military means. These include false information, cyber attacks, economic pressure and covert troops. Often it remains unclear whether there is a war at all.
wichtigste: Hybrid warfare mixes military and non-military means.
It often stays below the threshold of open war.
This area between peace and war is called the grey zone.
In 2007 Estonia was the target of large cyber attacks.
In 2014 soldiers without national insignia appeared in Crimea.
Since 2017 there has been a centre of excellence against hybrid threats in Helsinki.

abschnitte.text: In **hybrid warfare**, a country uses many different means at the same time. These include **disinformation**, meaning false information spread on purpose. **Cyber attacks** on computers, economic pressure and covert troops are also part of it. Often the attacker denies being involved. This makes it difficult to prove anything against them.

Hybrid actors often operate in the **grey zone** between peace and open war. Their actions deliberately stay below the threshold of an **armed attack**. This makes a clear military response harder. That is why neutral countries such as Switzerland also deal with protection against cyber attacks and disinformation.

In 2007 **Estonia** was the target of massive **cyber attacks** after a dispute over a Soviet war memorial, the Bronze Soldier. Websites of the government, banks and media were paralysed. In 2014 soldiers in uniforms without markings appeared on the Ukrainian peninsula of **Crimea**. They were called **“little green men”**. At first Russia denied being involved; later President Putin admitted that Russian troops had been used.

abschnitte.titel: Migration as a means of pressure
abschnitte.text: In 2021 the regime in **Belarus** let migrants enter the country and brought them to the borders with **Poland** and Lithuania. The people were meant to get into the EU this way. The EU saw this as a **hybrid attack** with which Belarus wanted to exert political pressure. Many of those affected were stuck at the border in the cold.

In 2013 the Russian Chief of the General Staff **Valery Gerasimov** published an article that is often quoted. It described the growing importance of non-military means in conflicts. After that, people in the West spoke of a “Gerasimov doctrine”, but the term is disputed. In 2017 the **European Centre of Excellence for Countering Hybrid Threats** was founded in **Helsinki**. It is supported by EU and NATO countries.

gewusst: The expression “little green men” was a reference to aliens, because officially nobody knew where the soldiers came from.
Today Estonia is seen as one of the countries with the best protection against cyber attacks.

teile.einleitung: The flag of South Africa is one of the most colourful in the world. It has six colours and a green band in the shape of a Y lying on its side. It was introduced in 1994, when the first free elections for everyone took place in South Africa.
wichtigste: The flag has six colours: red, blue, green, black, yellow and white.
A green band forms a Y lying on its side.
On the left is a black triangle with a narrow yellow border.
At the top is a red field, at the bottom a blue one.
South Africa has had this flag since 27 April 1994.
The country is also called the Rainbow Nation.

abschnitte.text: The flag of South Africa has **six colours**: **red, blue, green, black, yellow and white**. At the top is a **red field**, at the bottom a **blue field**. Between them runs a broad **green band**. It is edged with white on both sides. On the left is a **black triangle** pointing towards the middle, surrounded by a narrow **yellow border**.

The green band starts on the left with **two arms**. Towards the right they join into **one band**. This makes a **Y lying on its side**. It is explained like this: **two paths become one**. The different people in the country are meant to go into the future together.

For a long time **apartheid** ruled in South Africa. This was a system that separated people according to their skin colour. The black majority had far fewer rights and was not allowed to vote. At the end of April **1994**, the **first free elections for everyone** took place. On **27 April 1994** the new flag was also introduced. **Nelson Mandela** then became the country's first black president.

People with many different **languages**, origins and traditions live in South Africa. The country even has **more than ten** official languages. That is why South Africa is often called the **Rainbow Nation**. Like the many colours on the flag, the many people are meant to form one country together. Today 27 April is a public holiday, **Freedom Day**.

gewusst: The term Rainbow Nation became well known through the Nobel Peace Prize winner Desmond Tutu.
At first the flag was only meant as a temporary solution, but people liked it so much that it stayed.

teile.einleitung: Jean Monnet was a French businessman and politician. He is seen as one of the **founding fathers of Europe**, because he did a great deal to push forward cooperation between European countries after the Second World War.
wichtigste: Jean Monnet was born in Cognac in 1888.
From 1920 to 1923 he was Deputy Secretary-General of the League of Nations in Geneva.
From 1946 he led the Monnet Plan for rebuilding France.
He was the first President of the High Authority of the European Coal and Steel Community.
In 1976 he became the first Honorary Citizen of Europe.
His foundation, with his archive, is in Lausanne.

abschnitte.titel: Origins and the League of Nations
abschnitte.text: Jean Monnet was born in **Cognac** in 1888. His family traded in the brandy of the same name, and Monnet travelled abroad as a merchant early on. After the First World War he became **Deputy Secretary-General of the League of Nations**, from 1920 to 1923. This organisation had its seat in Geneva and was meant to secure peace.

After the Second World War, from 1946 Monnet led the Planning Commission in France. He designed the **Monnet Plan** for rebuilding the French economy. He focused on coal, steel, energy and transport. This experience shaped his ideas for Europe.

Monnet relied on **small, concrete steps** of cooperation in particular areas. Greater unity was to grow out of them little by little. His ideas went into Robert Schuman's plan to manage coal and steel together. This led to the **European Coal and Steel Community** (ECSC), also called the **Montan Union**. Monnet became the first President of its **High Authority**.

After stepping down from the High Authority, in 1955 Monnet founded the **Action Committee for the United States of Europe**. It brought together politicians and trade unions from several countries. Together with Robert Schuman, Konrad Adenauer and others, he is one of the founding fathers of European unity. In 1976 the heads of state and government of the European Communities made him the first **Honorary Citizen of Europe**.

In 1978 Monnet founded the **Fondation Jean Monnet pour l'Europe** and handed over his archives to it. The foundation is on the grounds of the University of **Lausanne**. Monnet died in 1979. For his 100th birthday in 1988, his remains were moved to the **Panthéon** in Paris, where France honours important figures.

gewusst: Jean Monnet was never a head of government or a minister, and yet he became one of the most important builders of Europe.
Monnet's archive is in Switzerland, even though Switzerland is not a member of the EU.

teile.einleitung: The flag of Nepal is very special: it is the only national flag in the world that is not four-sided. It is made up of two red triangles with a blue border. On it you can see a white moon and a white sun.
wichtigste: The flag of Nepal is made up of two triangles, one above the other.
It is the only national flag that is not four-sided.
The background colour is a dark crimson.
A blue border runs round the whole flag.
There is a white moon at the top and a white sun at the bottom.
Since 1962 the flag has been laid down in the constitution with exact measurements.

abschnitte.text: Almost all national flags are **rectangles**. Switzerland and Vatican City have a **square**. Only **Nepal** has a flag that is **not four-sided**. It is made up of **two triangles**, one above the other. Such triangular flags are also called pennants.

The background colour is a dark **crimson**. It is the colour of the **rhododendron**, Nepal's **national flower**. This flower grows on many mountainsides there. A **blue border** runs round the whole flag. It is often explained as a sign of **peace**.

In the upper triangle is a **white moon**, in the lower one a **white sun**. The sun and moon have existed for a very long time. People wish that their country may **last as long** as they do. To many people, the two points of the flag recall the peaks of the **Himalayas**. Nepal lies in these mountains, and on its border stands **Mount Everest**, the highest mountain on Earth.

The shape of the flag is very old. But in **1962** it was laid down with **exact measurements** in the **constitution**. There it says step by step how to draw the flag with lines and angles. It is almost like a geometry problem. This way every flag of Nepal looks the same.

gewusst: Nepal's constitution contains exact construction instructions for drawing the flag step by step.
In Nepali, Mount Everest is called Sagarmatha.

teile.einleitung: The flag of the United States is often called the “Stars and Stripes”. It has 13 red and white stripes and, in the top left, a blue field with 50 white stars. Each star stands for a state.
wichtigste: The US flag has 13 stripes in red and white.
The 13 stripes recall the first 13 colonies.
In the top left is a blue field with white stars.
Each of the 50 stars stands for a state.
Since 4 July 1960 the flag has had 50 stars.
There is a red stripe at the top and at the bottom.

abschnitte.text: The flag of the USA has **13 stripes** that alternate between **red and white**. It begins and ends with a **red stripe**. That is why there are **seven red** and **six white** stripes. In the top left is a **blue field** with **white stars**. That is why the flag is often called the **“Stars and Stripes”**.

The 13 stripes recall the **13 colonies** from which the USA was formed. These territories on the east coast of America used to belong to **Great Britain**. In **1776** they declared themselves **independent**. That is why the USA celebrates its Independence Day every year on **4 July**. The first flag had 13 stripes and 13 stars.

Each star stands for a **state**. When new states joined, the flag got **new stars**. But the stripes stayed at 13. The last state to join was **Hawaii**, in **1959**. So from **4 July 1960** the flag had **50 stars**. Nothing has changed since then.

The US flag is one of the **best-known flags** in the world. In the USA it hangs on many houses, schools and sports grounds. Many children recite a pledge of allegiance to the flag at school every morning. During the **Moon landings** from **1969**, astronauts put up US flags on the Moon. Another nickname for the flag is **“Old Glory”**.

gewusst: Over its history the flag has had more than 25 different arrangements of stars.
Switzerland and the USA are both federal states: Switzerland has cantons, and the USA has states.

teile.einleitung: An international organisation is a group in which several countries work together. It has fixed rules, its own office and staff. Well-known examples are the UN, NATO, the OSCE and the Council of Europe.
wichtigste: International organisations are created by treaties between countries.
The largest is the UN, with 193 member states.
In the UN Security Council, a decision on substance needs 9 of 15 votes and no veto.
Germany is not a permanent member of the Security Council.
In 2026 NATO has 32 member states.
In 2026 Switzerland holds the chairmanship of the OSCE.
Switzerland has been a member of the Council of Europe since 1963.

abschnitte.text: An **international organisation** is an association of several countries with a shared aim. Its basis is a treaty that all the members sign. The organisation has a seat, a leadership and staff. There are also **non-governmental organisations** such as Greenpeace, in which private people instead of countries work together. These are called NGOs for short.

The United Nations was founded in 1945 after the Second World War and has its headquarters in New York. Its most important aim is peace in the world. 15 countries sit on the **Security Council**. Five of them are always there: the USA, Russia, China, Great Britain and France. These five have a right of veto, with which they can block a decision on their own.

NATO is a defence alliance founded in 1949, which has 32 members in 2026. The OSCE, the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe, has its seat in Vienna. It has 57 member countries from Europe, North America and Asia. Every year a different country takes over the **chairmanship**. In 2026 it is Switzerland, which already led the OSCE in 1996 and 2014.

The Council of Europe was founded in 1949 and has its seat in Strasbourg in France. It works for human rights, democracy and the rule of law in Europe. The European Court of Human Rights belongs to it. Switzerland has been a member since 1963. The Council of Europe is not the same as the European Union.

Although Switzerland is neutral, it works in many organisations. It has been a member of the UN since 2002, after the people said yes in a **vote**. In 2023 and 2024 it sat on the Security Council as a non-permanent member. Switzerland does not belong to NATO or the EU, however. Instead, Geneva is home to many international organisations.

begriffe.erklaerung: An objection with which a single country can block a decision.
A country that has joined an organisation.
An organisation that is run not by governments but by private people.
The task of leading an organisation for a certain time.

gewusst: The ten non-permanent members of the Security Council are each elected for two years.
Switzerland only joined the UN in 2002, even though many UN offices had stood in Geneva for a long time.

t1i29vv.t: Community of Latin American and Caribbean States

teile.einleitung: The Community of Latin American and Caribbean States, CELAC for short, is an association of all 33 countries of Latin America and the Caribbean. It was founded in 2011 and serves political cooperation in the region. The USA and Canada are not part of it.
wichtigste: CELAC was founded in Caracas in December 2011.
It has 33 member states.
The USA and Canada do not belong to it.
Its most important forerunner was the Rio Group of 1986.
The presidency passes from member to member every year.
Brazil suspended its participation from 2020 to 2023.

abschnitte.text: The decision in principle to create **CELAC** was taken in Mexico in 2010. It was formally founded in December 2011 at the summit in **Caracas** in Venezuela. All the independent countries of Latin America and the Caribbean are members, **33 countries** in all. The **USA** and **Canada** are deliberately not included. This makes CELAC different from the **Organization of American States** (OAS), in which both take part.

Its most important forerunner is seen as the **Rio Group**, a forum for political coordination among Latin American countries since 1986. It merged into CELAC together with the CALC summit. CELAC has **no permanent secretariat**. One member state takes over the **pro tempore presidency** for a year at a time, for example Colombia in 2025. “Pro tempore” is Latin and means “for the time being”.

Under President **Jair Bolsonaro**, **Brazil** withdrew from CELAC in 2020. After **Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva** took office, the country returned in 2023. Because the members are politically very different, reaching agreement is often difficult. Decisions are usually taken by **consensus**, meaning when nobody objects.

CELAC is also a partner for talks with other world regions. In July 2023 CELAC and the **European Union** met in **Brussels** for a joint summit. It was the first meeting of this kind since 2015. It was meant to revive relations between Europe and Latin America, for example on trade and climate protection.

gewusst: CELAC includes large countries such as Brazil and Mexico, but also small island states in the Caribbean.
In CELAC every member has the same weight, no matter how big it is.

teile.einleitung: The INF Treaty was a disarmament treaty between the USA and the Soviet Union. It banned land-based nuclear missiles and cruise missiles of intermediate and shorter range. It is seen as one of the most important steps towards the end of the Cold War.
wichtigste: The INF Treaty was signed in Washington on 8 December 1987.
It was signed by Ronald Reagan for the USA and Mikhail Gorbachev for the Soviet Union.
It banned land-based missiles and cruise missiles with a range of 500 to 5,500 kilometres.
For the first time, a whole class of nuclear weapons was completely abolished.
By 1991 about 2,700 missiles had been destroyed, checked by inspectors on the spot.
On 2 August 2019 the treaty ended after the USA had withdrawn.

abschnitte.text: In the 1970s the Soviet Union deployed new intermediate-range missiles of the **SS-20** type. They could reach targets all over Western Europe. In 1979 NATO responded with the **NATO Double-Track Decision**: it offered negotiations and at the same time threatened to deploy its own missiles. Because the talks failed, American **Pershing II** missiles and cruise missiles were stationed in the Federal Republic of Germany from 1983. Many people demonstrated against this in large peace rallies.

INF is short for “Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces”. Ronald Reagan and Mikhail Gorbachev signed the treaty in Washington on 8 December 1987, and it came into force in 1988. It only covered weapons launched **from the ground**. Missiles on ships, submarines and aircraft remained allowed, as did intercontinental missiles with a longer range.

Earlier agreements such as **SALT** had only set upper limits for weapons. The INF Treaty, on the other hand, required all the weapons in a whole category to be destroyed. The **checks on the spot** were also new: inspectors from the other side were allowed to watch the destruction. By the deadline of 1 June 1991, 2,692 missiles had been destroyed, most of them Soviet. In this way the Pershing II missiles also disappeared from Germany again.

In the 2010s the USA accused Russia of having developed the cruise missile **9M729**, which it said broke the treaty. Russia denied this. The USA gave notice of withdrawal from the treaty, and it ended on 2 August 2019. Many experts regretted this, because an important building block of arms control in Europe was lost.

gewusst: The INF Treaty was the first treaty that did not just limit a whole group of nuclear weapons but abolished it completely.
Inspectors from the USA and the Soviet Union were allowed to watch in their former opponent's country as missiles were destroyed.

teile.einleitung: Italy is a country in the south of Europe and one of Switzerland's neighbours. It is famous for its long history, famous buildings and good food. The capital is Rome.
wichtigste: The capital of Italy is Rome, where the Colosseum stands.
In the middle of Rome lies Vatican City, a small country of its own.
The canton of Ticino borders Italy and speaks Italian.
The Matterhorn stands on the border between the Valais and Italy.
Campione d'Italia is an Italian village in the middle of Ticino.
Etna on Sicily is the highest active volcano in Europe.

abschnitte.text: **Rome** is the capital of Italy and used to be the centre of the Roman Empire. The **Colosseum** is an oval building almost 2,000 years old; gladiators used to fight there. In the middle of Rome lies **Vatican City**, the smallest country in the world. The Pope lives there, and the **Swiss Guard** protects him.

Italy and Switzerland share a long border through the Alps. The canton of **Ticino** is in the south of Switzerland, and people speak Italian there. The **Matterhorn** stands exactly on the border with the Valais; in Italian it is called Monte Cervino. Most of **Lake Maggiore** lies in Italy, but its northern end with Locarno belongs to Ticino. On Lake Lugano lies **Campione d'Italia**, an Italian village completely surrounded by Switzerland.

**Venice** is built on many small islands. Instead of cars, boats and gondolas travel along its canals. In **Pisa** stands the famous **Leaning Tower**, a bell tower. Because the ground beneath it is soft, it leans. Other well-known cities are Milan, Florence and Naples.

Many popular dishes come from Italy. **Pizza** comes especially from the area around **Naples** and is eaten all over the world today. Pasta, risotto and gelato are also Italian specialities. In Switzerland, especially in Ticino, Italian cooking is very widespread.

Italy is shaped like a boot and is surrounded by sea almost everywhere. Large islands such as **Sicily** and Sardinia belong to Italy. On Sicily stands **Etna**, the highest active volcano in Europe. It erupts again and again. Near Naples there is another famous volcano, **Vesuvius**.

gewusst: Vatican City is the smallest country in the world and lies entirely within the city of Rome.
In Campione d'Italia people usually pay with francs, even though the village belongs to Italy.

teile.einleitung: The International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, also called the **Rwanda Tribunal**, was a UN court. It was meant to bring to trial those responsible for the genocide in Rwanda in 1994.
wichtigste: The UN Security Council set up the tribunal in November 1994 with Resolution 955.
It was responsible for acts committed in 1994.
The tribunal's seat was Arusha in Tanzania.
In 1994 an estimated 800,000 to one million people were killed in about 100 days.
In 1998 it handed down the first judgment by an international court for genocide.
The “Media Trial” was about the hate radio station RTLM.

abschnitte.text: Between April and July 1994, an estimated **800,000 to one million** people were killed in Rwanda in only about 100 days. Most of the victims belonged to the **Tutsi** population group; moderate Hutu were also killed. A **genocide** is a crime with the aim of destroying a group in whole or in part. At the time the world hardly stepped in, which was heavily criticised later.

In November 1994 the **UN Security Council** adopted **Resolution 955**, based on Chapter VII of the UN Charter. This created the tribunal, responsible for acts from 1994. It sat in **Arusha** in Tanzania, meaning outside Rwanda. There the safety of witnesses and accused people could be better guaranteed.

In 1998 the tribunal convicted **Jean-Paul Akayesu**, a former mayor. It was the first judgment by an international court for genocide under the **Genocide Convention** of 1948. The judgment also stated that serious violence against women can be part of a genocide, a milestone in international criminal law. In the same year **Jean Kambanda**, the prime minister of the interim government, pleaded guilty. He was the first head of government to plead guilty to genocide before an international court.

At the centre of the so-called **Media Trial** was the radio station **Radio Télévision Libre des Mille Collines** (RTLM). It had stirred up hatred against Tutsi and called for violence. In 2003 the tribunal convicted leading media figures of **incitement to genocide**. The businessman **Félicien Kabuga** is said to have financed militias and the station. He was arrested near Paris in 2020 after a long time on the run, but he was later declared unfit to stand trial because of dementia.

gewusst: The Rwanda Tribunal was the first international court to convict someone of genocide.
The Media Trial showed that words on the radio can also support a terrible crime.

teile.einleitung: The flag of Italy has three vertical stripes in green, white and red. Italians call it “Il Tricolore”, the three-coloured one. Italy is Switzerland's neighbour to the south.
wichtigste: The Italian flag has three vertical stripes.
Green is next to the flagpole, white in the middle and red at the end that flutters.
The flag is called “Il Tricolore”, meaning “the three-coloured one”.
Mexico has the same colours, but with an eagle emblem in the middle.
Ireland has a similar flag with orange instead of red.
Italy borders Switzerland to the south.

abschnitte.text: The flag of Italy has three **vertical stripes** standing side by side. Next to the **flagpole** is **green**, in the middle **white** and at the end that flutters **red**. Because it has three colours, it is called **“Il Tricolore”**, meaning “the three-coloured one”. The colours are sometimes linked with green meadows, the white snow of the Alps and red passion. But this is a popular explanation.

The green, white and red flag was created at the end of the **18th century**. At that time French troops came to Italy, and the French **Tricolour** was a model. For a long time Italy was made up of many separate states. In the **19th century** the country was united, and the Tricolore became its sign. It used to carry the coat of arms of the royal family in the middle. Since Italy became a **republic** in **1946**, it has had no coat of arms.

Some flags look very like the Italian one. **Mexico** has the same colours in the same order, but shows a coat of arms with an **eagle** in the middle. **Ireland** also has three vertical stripes, but with **orange** instead of red. So if you look closely, you can tell the flags apart easily.

Italy lies **south of Switzerland**. The cantons of **Ticino**, the **Grisons** and the **Valais** border on Italy. **Italian** is one of Switzerland's four national languages. In Ticino and in some valleys of the Grisons, most people speak Italian. That is why the Tricolore is a familiar sight to many people in Switzerland.

gewusst: In Italy there is a Tricolour Day on 7 January, because the flag was first adopted on that day in 1797.
At sports events, Italian teams are often called the “Azzurri”, the Blues, even though blue is not on the flag.

teile.einleitung: The EFTA countries and India have concluded a trade and partnership agreement, TEPA for short. It lowers customs duties and, for the first time, includes a target for investment and jobs. For Switzerland it opens up access to the country with the largest population in the world.
wichtigste: The agreement was signed in New Delhi in March 2024.
It has been in force since 1 October 2025.
EFTA is made up of Switzerland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Iceland.
The EFTA countries want to invest 100 billion US dollars in India within 15 years.
This is meant to create one million direct jobs in India.
Negotiations had been going on since 2008.

abschnitte.text: The **Trade and Economic Partnership Agreement** between **EFTA** and **India** is called **TEPA** for short. It was signed in **New Delhi** on **10 March 2024**. **Federal Councillor Guy Parmelin** signed for Switzerland. A **referendum** could have been called against the agreement in Switzerland, but none came about. On **1 October 2025** the agreement came into force. Since then customs duties on many Swiss exports to India have been falling.

The **European Free Trade Association** was founded in **1960**. Today it has **four members**: **Switzerland**, **Liechtenstein**, **Norway** and **Iceland**. These countries do not belong to the EU. They conclude free trade agreements with other countries **together**. This gives them more weight in negotiations than a single small country.

The agreement is the **first free trade agreement** with an **investment target**. The EFTA countries want to increase their **direct investment** in India by **100 billion US dollars** within **15 years**. This is meant to create **one million direct jobs** in India. India attached great importance to this. However, the countries can only **encourage** investment by private companies, not order it.

The agreement contains a special **mechanism**. If the investment target is not reached, there are first **consultations**, meaning talks. After that India may **temporarily withdraw customs concessions**. This is meant to keep the balance between the two sides. Supporters see this as a fair solution; others think the target will be hard to reach.

The **negotiations** began back in **2008**. They were interrupted for years, because the two sides could not agree on important questions. Only after about **16 years** could the agreement be concluded. India is a large and growing market. That is why access is especially important for Swiss companies, for example in the machine industry.

gewusst: In 2023 India overtook China as the most populous country in the world.
The agreement with India was something new for EFTA, because it combines trade with targets for investment.

teile.einleitung: The flag of the United Kingdom is usually called the Union Jack. It combines three crosses in red, white and blue. Each cross stands for a part of the country.
wichtigste: The British flag is officially called the Union Flag, but usually the Union Jack.
Its colours are red, white and blue.
In the Union Jack, three crosses lie on top of one another.
The upright red cross stands for England, the white diagonal cross for Scotland.
The red diagonal cross stands for Ireland.
Wales cannot be seen in the Union Jack.

abschnitte.text: The flag of the United Kingdom is officially called the **Union Flag**. But it is usually called the **Union Jack**. It is made up of **red and white crosses** on a **blue background**. In fact there are **three crosses** laid on top of one another. “Union” means joining together, and that is exactly what the flag shows.

The **upright red cross** on white is the **Cross of St George**, the flag of **England**. The **white diagonal cross** on blue is the **Cross of St Andrew**, the flag of **Scotland**. The **red diagonal cross** is the **Cross of St Patrick** and stands for **Ireland**. First England and Scotland were combined in one flag. Later the cross for Ireland was added.

One part of the country is missing from the Union Jack: **Wales**. When the flag was created, Wales had long been joined to **England**. That is why it did not get a sign of its own. But Wales has its own very striking flag. It shows a **red dragon** on **white and green**.

Great Britain used to have many **colonies** all over the world. Some countries that are closely linked to Great Britain still carry the Union Jack on their flag today. A well-known example is **Australia**: the Union Jack is in the top left, with white **stars** on a blue background. **New Zealand** also shows the Union Jack in the top left.

gewusst: The Union Jack is not completely symmetrical, which is why it can also be flown upside down.
Today only Northern Ireland belongs to the United Kingdom; the Republic of Ireland is a separate country.

teile.einleitung: The Glückskette, known in English as Swiss Solidarity, is a Swiss foundation that collects donations for people in need. It mainly calls for collections after disasters. It began in 1946 as a radio programme in French-speaking Switzerland.
wichtigste: Swiss Solidarity collects donations for people in need.
It began in 1946 as a programme on French-speaking Swiss radio.
It works closely with the radio and television of the SRG.
The money goes to Swiss partner aid organisations that help on the spot.
The most money was collected after the tsunami in Asia in 2004.
It also helps in Switzerland, for example after severe storms.

abschnitte.text: The **Glückskette** (literally “chain of good fortune”) began in **1946** as a programme on French-speaking Swiss radio. It was founded by **Roger Nordmann**, Paul Valloton and the entertainer **Jack Rollan**. In French it is called the **Chaîne du Bonheur**, in Italian the **Catena della Solidarietà**. Today it is a **foundation**.

Swiss Solidarity works closely with the **radio and television of the SRG**. After earthquakes, floods or wars, a lot of money is needed quickly. Then Swiss Solidarity organises a **day of collection**. Radio and television spread the appeal, and many people donate by telephone or bank transfer.

Swiss Solidarity does not help on the spot itself. It passes the money on to **Swiss partner aid organisations**. They carry out the projects, for example rebuilding houses or providing water and food. Swiss Solidarity checks whether the money is being used sensibly.

After the **tsunami in Asia** in December 2004, about **227 million francs** were collected. That is still Swiss Solidarity's record (as of 2026). It also helps in **Switzerland**, for example after the severe storms in the Valais and Ticino in October 2000. From 2009 to 2018 the campaign **“Jeder Rappen zählt”** (“Every rappen counts”) ran with SRF every year before Christmas.

gewusst: Swiss Solidarity was founded shortly after the Second World War, when many people in Europe needed help.
During “Jeder Rappen zählt”, presenters spent days in a glass house on a town square.

teile.einleitung: The global minimum tax is meant to make sure that large international corporations pay at least 15 per cent tax on their profits everywhere. It was drawn up by the OECD and the G20 countries. Switzerland has been applying it since 2024.
wichtigste: The minimum tax rate is 15 per cent.
It affects corporations with an annual turnover of at least 750 million euros.
On 18 June 2023 the Swiss people approved putting it into effect, with about 79 per cent yes.
The top-up tax has applied in Switzerland since 1 January 2024.
75 per cent of the revenue goes to the cantons, 25 per cent to the Confederation.
In the OECD project, the minimum tax is called “Pillar Two”.
In June 2025 the G7 agreed on exceptions for US corporations.

abschnitte.text: Many countries try to attract companies with **low taxes on profits**. This is called **tax competition**. The minimum tax is meant to put a floor under this competition. Countries should no longer undercut each other with ever lower taxes. Large corporations should bear a **minimum tax burden** everywhere, no matter where they declare their profits.

The minimum tax rate is **15 per cent**. It applies only to large groups of companies with an annual turnover of at least **750 million euros**. The vast majority of small and medium-sized businesses in Switzerland are not affected. If a corporation's tax in a country is below 15 per cent, a **top-up tax** can be charged.

The minimum tax came out of the OECD/G20 project **BEPS**. This stands for “Base Erosion and Profit Shifting”. It is aimed at tax tricks with which corporations shift profits to **low-tax countries**. The project has two pillars. **Pillar One** redistributes taxing rights to the countries where goods are sold. **Pillar Two** governs the minimum tax.

abschnitte.titel: Putting it into effect in Switzerland
abschnitte.text: To put it into effect, the **Federal Constitution** had to be changed. On **18 June 2023**, about **79 per cent** of voters approved the proposal. The top-up tax has applied since **1 January 2024**. **75 per cent** of the revenue goes **to the cantons** and **25 per cent to the Confederation**. The cantons get three quarters because they are responsible for company taxes and compete with each other on taxes.

The **USA** has its own rules for a minimum tax and rejected parts of the OECD solution. In June 2025 the **G7** agreed on a “side-by-side” approach. Under it, US corporations are exempted from parts of the global minimum tax. In return, the USA dropped planned retaliatory taxes. What happens next is still being negotiated internationally.

gewusst: In 2021 more than 130 countries agreed to the principle of a global minimum tax.
It is mainly cantons with many international corporations, such as Zug or Basel-Stadt, that receive revenue from the top-up tax.

teile.einleitung: Free trade means that goods are traded between countries with no customs duties or only a few. Switzerland is a small country with many exports and so depends heavily on open trade. At the same time it protects some areas, above all farming.
wichtigste: Customs duties are charges on imported goods and are often meant to protect home-grown products.
Since 1 January 2024 Switzerland has no longer charged customs duties on industrial products.
There are still customs duties on many farm products such as meat.
The World Trade Organization WTO has its seat in Geneva and was founded in 1995.
Switzerland is a founding member of EFTA.
Since 1972 a free trade agreement with the EU has applied to industrial goods.

abschnitte.text: A **customs duty** is a charge you have to pay when you bring goods into a country. Customs duties make foreign goods **more expensive**. This way **home producers** have less competition. The state also takes in money. **Free trade** means the opposite: customs duties and other barriers to trade are removed, so that goods can cross borders more easily.

Since **1 January 2024** Switzerland has **no longer charged customs duties** on **industrial products** such as bicycles, clothes or cars. This is meant to make goods cheaper for companies and consumers. It is different for **farming**: on many **agricultural products**, for example **meat** or dairy products, there are still customs duties, some of them high. In this way Switzerland wants to protect its **farms**.

The **World Trade Organization WTO** sets rules for world trade. It has its seat in **Geneva**. The WTO was founded in **1995** and replaced the **GATT**, an agreement on tariffs and trade from **1947**. When countries argue about trade, the WTO can help to **settle the dispute**. Most countries in the world are members.

The **European Free Trade Association EFTA** was founded in **1960**. Switzerland is a **founding member**. Today its members are Switzerland, **Norway**, **Iceland** and **Liechtenstein**. Through EFTA, Switzerland concludes many **free trade agreements** with other countries. In **1972** it concluded a **free trade agreement** for industrial goods with what was then the European Economic Community. The people approved it clearly in December 1972.

Supporters say that free trade makes goods cheaper and creates jobs in exporting companies. Critics fear that home businesses come under pressure or that environmental standards suffer. How important open markets are became clear in **2025**: from **7 August 2025** the **USA** charged a customs duty of **39 per cent** on many Swiss goods, for example machines and watches. After negotiations the rate was lowered to **15 per cent** in November 2025.

gewusst: Switzerland earns a large part of its prosperity from exports, for example of medicines, machines and watches.
The 1972 agreement with today's EU still applies today.

teile.einleitung: An aid organisation is an organisation that helps people in need. Aid organisations collect donations and use the money for projects. In Switzerland there are many well-known aid organisations that work at home and abroad.
wichtigste: Aid organisations help people in need, in Switzerland and abroad.
Pro Juventute runs the number 147 for children and young people.
Terre des hommes was founded in Lausanne in 1960.
The Pestalozzi Children's Village has stood in Trogen since 1946.
Caritas belongs to the Catholic Church, HEKS to the Reformed Church.
The ZEWO seal of approval shows that an aid organisation handles donations carefully.

abschnitte.text: Aid organisations collect **money** and use it to help people in need. Some help after disasters; others support children, families or mountain farmers. Many work with **donations** from private people. Often **volunteers**, who are not paid, also help. Most aid organisations are organised as an association or a foundation.

**Pro Juventute** works for children and young people in Switzerland. On the number **147** they can get advice and help round the clock. **Terre des hommes** was founded in Lausanne in 1960 by Edmond Kaiser and helps children in need. The **Pestalozzi Children's Village** was founded in 1946 in Trogen in the canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden. At first, children who had lost their parents in the war lived there.

Some aid organisations belong to churches. **Caritas** is the aid organisation of the Catholic Church. It helps poor people in Switzerland and abroad. **HEKS** is the aid organisation of the Protestant Reformed Church of Switzerland. HEKS also works at home and abroad. Both help everyone, regardless of their religion.

**Swiss Mountain Aid** supports farming families and businesses in the mountains. This way people can go on living and working there. The **Swiss Red Cross**, for example, helps older people or trains babysitters. **Swiss Solidarity** (the Glückskette) collects money after disasters and passes it on to Swiss aid organisations.

The **ZEWO** foundation checks aid organisations. Those that carry its **seal of approval** use donations honestly and carefully. Children can also help, for example with a **sponsored run**. Adults pay an amount for every lap run. The money then goes to an aid project.

gewusst: Pro Juventute's number 147 can also be reached by chat and text message.
Today children from different countries meet at the Pestalozzi Children's Village in Trogen for exchange projects.

teile.einleitung: Canada is a huge country in the north of America. After Russia it is the second-largest country on Earth, but it has far fewer inhabitants. Its capital is Ottawa.
wichtigste: Canada has two official languages: English and French.
The head of state is the British king, since 2022 Charles III.
The government is led by the Prime Minister.
Parliament stands on Parliament Hill in Ottawa.
Ottawa is in the province of Ontario, right on the border with Quebec.
The country is made up of 10 provinces and 3 territories.
The flag shows a red maple leaf.

abschnitte.text: In Canada, **English** and **French** are official languages. Most people speak English. But in the province of **Quebec**, most people speak French. That is why federal laws and many federal signs exist in both languages. This is a little like Switzerland, where several languages also live side by side.

Canada is a **monarchy** and belongs to the Commonwealth. The British King **Charles III** is also King of Canada. But he does not live there. In Canada he is represented by a **Governor General**. The real politics is done by the government under the **Prime Minister**, who is supported by Parliament.

Parliament stands on **Parliament Hill**, a hill above the Ottawa River. The buildings with their towers look like a castle. Parliament has two chambers: the **House of Commons**, which is elected by the people, and the **Senate**. An eternal flame burns in front of Parliament.

In 1857 **Queen Victoria** chose Ottawa as the capital. The city lay between the English-speaking and the French-speaking parts of the country. This way neither side had to feel left out. The **Rideau Canal** flows through Ottawa. In winter it freezes and becomes one of the longest skating rinks in the world.

Canada has huge **forests**, countless lakes and, in the north, the Arctic. Long before the Europeans, the **First Nations** and the **Inuit** lived here. Later the French and the British came. In **1867** several colonies joined together to form Canada. That is why **Canada Day** is celebrated on 1 July.

gewusst: The Rideau Canal has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2007.
Canada has the longest coastline of any country in the world.
The maple leaf has been on the Canadian flag since 1965.

t1lpjbrj.t: International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia

teile.einleitung: The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia was a UN court in The Hague. It was meant to prosecute serious crimes committed during the wars in collapsing Yugoslavia. It worked from 1993 to 2017.
wichtigste: The UN Security Council set up the court in 1993 with Resolution 827.
It was the first international criminal court since Nuremberg and Tokyo.
The tribunal charged a total of 161 people.
The first chief prosecutor was the South African Richard Goldstone.
The first trial, against Duško Tadić, ended with a judgment in 1997.
At the end of December 2017 the tribunal was dissolved.

abschnitte.text: In the 1990s there were terrible wars in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, with many crimes against the civilian population. In 1993 the **UN Security Council** created the court with **Resolution 827**, based on Chapter VII of the UN Charter. It was the first international criminal court since the trials at **Nuremberg** and **Tokyo** after the Second World War. Its seat was in **The Hague** in the Netherlands.

The first chief prosecutor, from 1994 to 1996, was the South African judge **Richard Goldstone**. At the same time he was responsible for the Rwanda Tribunal. From 1999 to 2007 the Swiss **Carla Del Ponte** was chief prosecutor. The first trial was against **Duško Tadić**, a Bosnian Serb camp guard, and ended with a judgment in 1997. It settled many basic questions, for example whether the court had jurisdiction at all.

The tribunal charged a total of **161 people**. All those wanted were eventually caught or died before that. The former President of the Bosnian Serbs, **Radovan Karadžić**, lived under a false name for a long time. With a beard, he posed as a healer called “Dragan Dabić” until he was arrested in Belgrade in 2008. He was later sentenced to life imprisonment. A dramatic moment came in 2017 at the appeal judgment against the Croatian general **Slobodan Praljak**, who drank poison in the courtroom and died shortly afterwards.

At the end of December 2017 the tribunal finished its work. Its remaining tasks were taken over by the **International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals**, which the Security Council had created in 2010. It deals with appeals, retrials and the protection of witnesses. It also works for the former Rwanda Tribunal. The Yugoslavia Tribunal is seen as an important step towards today's International Criminal Court.

gewusst: In the end nobody escaped the Yugoslavia Tribunal: all 161 people charged were caught or had died.
With Carla Del Ponte, a woman from Ticino led the prosecution in The Hague for eight years.

teile.einleitung: Climate migration means that people leave their homes because of the effects of climate change. Reasons include droughts, storms or the rising sea level. Most of them stay in their own country.
wichtigste: Most people move within their own country.
Under the Geneva Refugee Convention they usually do not count as refugees.
Switzerland and Norway started the Nansen Initiative in 2012.
Since 2016 the Platform on Disaster Displacement has continued this work.
The World Bank expects up to 216 million internal migrants by 2050.
Low-lying island states in the Pacific are especially threatened.

abschnitte.text: Most people who leave their homes because of environmental changes stay **in their own country**. They often move from the countryside to the **city** or to a nearby region. Some return when the situation improves. Only a few cross borders. They are then called **internally displaced people** or internal migrants.

The **Geneva Refugee Convention** protects people who are **persecuted** for particular reasons, for example because of their religion or political opinion. Droughts, storms or rising seas are not among them. That is why **“climate refugee”** is not a legal term. Anyone who flees only because of the effects of climate change is usually not recognised as a refugee under the Convention.

In **2012** **Switzerland** and **Norway** started the **Nansen Initiative**. It is named after the Norwegian polar explorer **Fridtjof Nansen**. The aim was to protect people driven from their homes by natural disasters better. Since **2016** the **Platform on Disaster Displacement** has been putting the recommendations into practice. Its secretariat is in **Geneva**.

Many **atolls** in the Pacific lie only a few metres above the sea. If the **sea level** rises, soil and drinking water become salty, and land is lost. **Ioane Teitiota** from **Kiribati** sought protection in New Zealand as a climate refugee, but without success. In 2020, however, the UN Human Rights Committee stated that the effects of climate change could in future forbid sending people back.

In **2023** **Tuvalu** concluded the **Falepili Agreement** with **Australia**. Every year Australia offers a right of residence to a limited number of people from Tuvalu. The World Bank's **Groundswell report** of 2021 expects up to **216 million** people to move within their own country because of the climate by 2050. With effective climate protection, the number could be much smaller.

gewusst: Fridtjof Nansen received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1922 for his help for refugees.
Many climate migrants only move away for a while.

teile.einleitung: The Group of Seven, G7 for short, is a meeting of seven large industrialised countries with democratic governments. Their heads of state and government meet every year for a summit. There they talk about the economy, security and global problems.
wichtigste: The G7 is made up of the USA, Japan, Germany, France, Great Britain, Italy and Canada.
The European Union also takes part in the meetings.
The first summit took place in 1975 at the Château de Rambouillet near Paris.
The G7 is an informal forum with no founding treaty and no permanent secretariat.
Russia was part of it for a time but was excluded in 2014 after the annexation of Crimea.
The 2026 summit took place in Évian on Lake Geneva.

abschnitte.text: In 1975 the French President **Valéry Giscard d'Estaing** and the German Chancellor **Helmut Schmidt** invited leaders to a meeting. It took place at the **Château de Rambouillet** near Paris, with six countries at the time. The background was the **oil crisis** and the end of the Bretton Woods system of fixed exchange rates. A year later Canada joined, and so the G7 was created.

abschnitte.titel: From G7 to G8 and back
abschnitte.text: In the 1990s **Russia** was admitted to the group, which was then called the **G8**. After the annexation of the Ukrainian peninsula of **Crimea** in 2014, the other members suspended Russia's participation. Since then the group has met as the G7 again. Besides the G7, since 1999 there has been the **G20**, which also includes large emerging economies such as China, India and Brazil.

The G7 is not an international organisation like the WTO or the UN. It has **no founding treaty** and no permanent secretariat.
