A branch of the olive tree, which has long been a sign of peace.
UN soldiers who help on peacekeeping missions.
The UN, an organisation of almost all the countries in the world for peace and cooperation.

gewusst: The colour of the UN flag is often called UN blue and is a shade of its own.
The map of the world on the UN emblem does not show Antarctica.
The UN has 193 member states, and in front of the headquarters in New York a flag flies for each of them.

teile.einleitung: The Climate Protection Act lays down how Switzerland wants to reduce its emissions of greenhouse gases. The people approved it on 18 June 2023. The big goal is net zero by 2050.
wichtigste: Voters said yes on 18 June 2023, with about 59 per cent.
The SVP had called the referendum.
By 2050 Switzerland is to have net zero greenhouse gas emissions.
The law was drawn up as a counter-proposal to the Glacier Initiative.
For replacing old heating systems, 2 billion francs are available over ten years.
The law has been in force since 1 January 2025.

abschnitte.text: It all began with the **Glacier Initiative**. It wanted to ban fossil fuels such as oil and gas in the long term. **Parliament** drew up a **counter-proposal**: the Climate Protection Act. After that the people behind the initiative withdrew it. The official name is the **Federal Act on Climate Protection Targets**.

The **SVP** called a **referendum** against the law. It feared higher costs and shortages of electricity. That is why there was a popular vote. On **18 June 2023**, about **59 per cent** of voters said yes. So a clear majority agreed.

The goal is called **net zero by 2050**. This means that Switzerland should not emit more greenhouse gases than are **removed** again. Doing without any emissions at all is hardly possible, for example in farming. These remaining emissions are to be stored in **forests**, **soils** or with technology. Overall, the total is then zero.

Many houses are still heated with **oil**, **gas** or direct electric heating. The law provides a total of **2 billion francs** over ten years, meaning 200 million a year. Homeowners receive contributions if they replace old heating systems with climate-friendly ones, for example a **heat pump**. Companies that use new climate-friendly technologies are also supported.

The law contains **interim targets** and guideline values for **buildings**, **transport** and **industry**. This is meant to show whether Switzerland is on course. After the vote, **ordinances** still had to be drawn up. They govern the details of putting the law into practice. That is why the law only came into force on **1 January 2025**.

gewusst: Swiss glaciers have lost a lot of ice in recent decades, which gave the Glacier Initiative its name.
The Confederation itself and the cantons are also meant to set an example in climate protection.

teile.einleitung: The International Day of Peace is celebrated every year on 21 September. The United Nations introduced it so that people around the world think about peace. On this day even the weapons are meant to fall silent.
wichtigste: The UN's day of peace takes place on 21 September.
The UN General Assembly decided on the day in 1981.
At first it fell on the third Tuesday in September.
Since 2002 the fixed date has been 21 September.
On this day the UN calls for a worldwide ceasefire.
In New York the Peace Bell is rung at the UN headquarters.
Schools and municipalities mark the day with activities and minutes of silence.

abschnitte.text: The **International Day of Peace** is a UN day of remembrance and action. It is meant to remind us that peace cannot be taken for granted. Events take place all over the world on this day. People pray, sing, paint or discuss peace. Every year the UN sets a theme of its own.

The UN General Assembly introduced the day in 1981. It was celebrated for the first time in 1982, at that time on the third Tuesday in September. That day was the opening day of the yearly General Assembly. In 2001 the UN decided to fix the day on 21 September. At the same time it declared it a day of worldwide **ceasefire**.

At the UN headquarters in New York hangs a **Peace Bell** from Japan. It was given in 1954 and cast from coins donated by people from many countries. On the Day of Peace, the UN Secretary-General rings this bell. A minute of silence follows. This remembers all the victims of war.

Even today there are many armed conflicts in the world. That is why the UN sends **peacekeeping troops** to crisis areas, who can be recognised by their blue helmets. On the Day of Peace, aid organisations sometimes have the chance to vaccinate children in war zones. Peace does not only mean that there is no war. It also includes justice, security and respect.

Switzerland is a neutral country and offers its help with peace talks. Negotiations between hostile parties take place in Geneva again and again. Many Swiss schools use 21 September to talk about settling disputes. Everyone can contribute to peace in everyday life. Anyone who settles arguments fairly and respects others is already taking the first step.

begriffe.erklaerung: A time during which the parties to a war do not fight.
The assembly of all UN member states, in which each country has one vote.
UN soldiers who help to keep the peace in crisis areas.
A minute of quiet to remember someone or something.

gewusst: The Japanese Peace Bell carries the words “Long live absolute world peace” in Japanese characters.
The dove of peace with an olive branch is one of the best-known symbols of peace.

teile.einleitung: The Gaza war began on 7 October 2023 with a major attack by Hamas on Israel. After that Israel waged a war in the Gaza Strip. The war has claimed a very large number of victims and is highly disputed politically.
wichtigste: On 7 October 2023 armed fighters of Hamas and other groups attacked Israel.
About 1,200 people were killed and about 250 were taken away as hostages.
Hamas has controlled the Gaza Strip alone since 2007.
Before the war about 2 million people lived in the Gaza Strip.
Qatar, Egypt and the USA mediated between Israel and Hamas.
South Africa brought a case against Israel at the International Court of Justice.
In 2024 the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants against Israeli politicians and a Hamas leader.

abschnitte.text: The **Gaza Strip** is a narrow area on the Mediterranean between Israel and Egypt. Before the war about **2 million people** lived on only about 360 square kilometres. It is one of the most densely populated areas in the world. **Hamas** won the Palestinian parliamentary elections in 2006 and drove out Fatah by force in 2007. Since then Hamas has governed in Gaza and the **Palestinian Authority** in the West Bank.

On 7 October 2023 armed fighters of Hamas and other groups broke into **Israel** from the Gaza Strip. About **1,200 people** were killed, most of them civilians, including many people at a music festival. About **250 people** were taken to Gaza as **hostages**. It was the day on which more Jews were killed than on any day since the Holocaust.

Israel responded with air strikes and a ground offensive in the Gaza Strip. The aim was to destroy Hamas and free the hostages. In the war, **tens of thousands of people** were killed in Gaza, and a great many buildings were destroyed. Almost the whole population had to flee, and there was a shortage of food, water and medicines. The **Rafah** border crossing to Egypt was important for aid deliveries.

Israel and Hamas do not negotiate directly with each other. That is why **Qatar**, **Egypt** and the **USA** mediated. There were several **truces**, during which hostages were exchanged for Palestinian prisoners. Many countries and aid organisations called for more humanitarian aid for Gaza. Switzerland supported aid for the civilian population and called on all sides to respect international law.

In December 2023 **South Africa** brought a case of genocide against Israel at the **International Court of Justice** in The Hague. Israel rejects the accusation. In 2024 the court ordered provisional measures; a judgment was still pending (as of 2025). In November 2024 the **International Criminal Court** issued arrest warrants for war crimes against **Benjamin Netanyahu** and **Yoav Gallant**. An arrest warrant was also issued against the Hamas military leader Mohammed Deif.

gewusst: Rafah is the only border crossing of the Gaza Strip that does not lead into Israel.
In 2024 the Swiss Parliament passed a law banning Hamas in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: Greta Thunberg is a climate activist from Sweden. At 15 she began going on strike from school to demand more climate protection. This grew into a worldwide youth movement.
wichtigste: Greta Thunberg was born in Stockholm in 2003.
In August 2018 she began her school strike in front of the Swedish parliament.
Her strikes gave rise to the Fridays for Future movement.
In January 2019 she spoke at the World Economic Forum in Davos.
In 2019 she sailed across the Atlantic to the UN climate summit in New York.
The magazine “Time” named her Person of the Year in 2019.

abschnitte.titel: A sign in front of parliament
abschnitte.text: In August 2018 Greta Thunberg, then 15, did not go to school. Instead she sat down with a sign in front of the **Riksdag** in Stockholm, Sweden's parliament. The sign said “School strike for the climate” in Swedish. She wanted politicians to do more against **climate change**. Soon other young people joined in.

Because the strikes took place on Fridays, the movement called itself **Fridays for Future**. Young people all over the world took to the streets. In Switzerland this led to the **Climate Strike**. In many cities tens of thousands of young people demonstrated for more climate protection.

In January 2019 Greta Thunberg spoke to business leaders at the **World Economic Forum** in Davos. She said that people should act as if their own house were on fire. In September 2019 she gave a speech at the **UN climate summit** in New York. With the cry **“How dare you!”** she accused the heads of state of letting young people down.

Greta Thunberg does not fly, because aeroplanes emit a lot of **CO2**. In 2019 she crossed the Atlantic on the racing yacht **“Malizia II”**. The voyage took about two weeks. That same year the US magazine **“Time”** named her Person of the Year. At 16 she was the youngest person ever to receive this honour.

Many people admire Greta Thunberg for her courage and determination. Others criticise the way she presents herself or her demands. She still stands up for other political causes too. What is undisputed is that she has got many young people to take an interest in the **climate**.

gewusst: Greta Thunberg's first strike was completely on her own, with just a home-made sign.
She is still the youngest Person of the Year in the history of “Time” magazine.

teile.einleitung: The International Civil Aviation Organization, **ICAO** for short, is a specialised agency of the UN. It sets rules for safe flying around the world. Its seat is in Montreal in Canada.
wichtigste: The ICAO has its seat in Montreal.
It is based on the Chicago Convention of 7 December 1944.
It officially began its work on 4 April 1947.
Swiss airports have ICAO codes beginning with LS; Zurich is LSZH.
The radio alphabet with “Alfa, Bravo, Charlie” comes from the ICAO.
With CORSIA, international flights are meant to offset their CO2.

abschnitte.text: While the Second World War was still going on, countries met in **Chicago**. On 7 December 1944 they signed the Convention on International Civil Aviation, the **Chicago Convention**. It came into force on 4 April 1947, and with that the ICAO officially began its work. Soon it became a **specialised agency of the UN**. Today 7 December is marked as **International Civil Aviation Day**.

The ICAO's main task is to draw up **standards and recommendations**. They concern safety, navigation and environmental protection in aviation. The member states put them into their laws. This way similar rules apply all over the world. The ICAO also lays down what **machine-readable passports** must look like, so that passports can be read in the same way at every border.

Every airport has a four-letter **ICAO code**. Swiss airports begin with **LS**: Zurich is LSZH, Geneva LSGG and Bern LSZB. On luggage tags, on the other hand, you see the three-letter IATA code, ZRH for Zurich. The **international spelling alphabet**, with words such as “Alfa, Bravo, Charlie”, also comes from the ICAO. With it, pilots and air traffic controllers spell clearly, for example “Zulu” for Z.

Flying produces a lot of **CO2**. In 2016 the ICAO adopted the **CORSIA** programme. With it, international flights are meant to offset their CO2 emissions, for example through climate protection projects. Experts debate how well such offsetting measures work.

gewusst: Montreal is home not only to the ICAO but also to IATA, the association of airlines.
Thanks to the ICAO, a Swiss passport can be read by a machine at almost any border in the world.

teile.einleitung: In November 1985 the US President Ronald Reagan and the Soviet party leader Mikhail Gorbachev met in Geneva. It was their first meeting, in the middle of the Cold War. The summit is seen as the start of an easing of tension between the two superpowers.
wichtigste: The summit lasted from 19 to 21 November 1985.
Reagan represented the USA, Gorbachev the Soviet Union.
The President of the Confederation, Kurt Furgler, received the guests for Switzerland.
Nuclear weapons were at the centre of the talks.
The statement declared that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought.
In 1986 the two met again in Reykjavik.

abschnitte.titel: In the middle of the Cold War
abschnitte.text: The summit took place during the **Cold War**. This is the name for the long period of tension between the **USA** and the **Soviet Union** after the Second World War. Both sides had huge numbers of **nuclear weapons**. **Ronald Reagan** was President of the USA, and **Mikhail Gorbachev** was General Secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union.

Switzerland made Geneva available as a neutral meeting place. The President of the Confederation, **Kurt Furgler**, welcomed Reagan before the summit and stressed Switzerland's role as host. On the first day of talks, the two met at the **Villa Fleur d'Eau**. It is in the municipality of **Versoix**, right on the shore of Lake Geneva.

Reagan and Gorbachev held a one-to-one talk in a pool house in front of a **fire**. That is why the meeting is also called the **Fireside Summit**. The two got to know each other personally. This is seen as important for the trust of the following years.

At the centre was the limiting of **nuclear weapons**. No disarmament treaty was reached in Geneva yet. But in their joint statement, both sides declared that **a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought**. This sentence is still often quoted today. The next meeting took place in October 1986 in **Reykjavik** in Iceland.

gewusst: In 1987 Reagan and Gorbachev signed the INF Treaty on intermediate-range missiles in Washington.
On the last day of the Geneva Summit, the two held a joint press conference.

t4j7mse.t: Convention on the Rights of the Child

teile.einleitung: The Convention on the Rights of the Child is a UN treaty that sets out basic rights of children around the world, for example to education and protection. Its official name is the Convention on the Rights of the Child. It applies to everyone under 18 and has been recognised by almost all the countries in the world.
wichtigste: The Convention on the Rights of the Child sets out basic rights of children worldwide, for example to education and protection.
The UN General Assembly adopted it on 20 November 1989.
It applies to all children and young people under 18.
It has 54 articles.
196 countries have ratified it; only the USA has not.
It has applied in Switzerland since 1997.
20 November is International Children's Rights Day.

abschnitte.text: The **Convention on the Rights of the Child** is an international treaty. It says what rights every child in the world has. Countries that sign and ratify the treaty commit themselves to protecting these rights. The Convention applies to everyone under 18, no matter where they come from. It is the human rights treaty with the most states party to it.

As early as 1924 the League of Nations adopted the Geneva Declaration of the Rights of the Child. It went back to the Briton Eglantyne Jebb, the founder of Save the Children. After long negotiations, the UN adopted today's Convention on 20 November 1989. It came into force on 2 September 1990. Later three **optional protocols** were added, for example against the use of children as soldiers.

The Convention is based on four **basic principles**. No child may be discriminated against, for example because of origin, religion or sex. In all decisions, the child's interests must come first; this is called the **best interests of the child**. Every child has a right to life and development. And children have the right to give their opinion and be heard.

Children have a right to education and so to go to school. They have a right to health, to free time and to play. They must be protected from violence, exploitation and dangerous child labour. A name, a nationality and privacy are also among their rights. Children with disabilities have a right to special support.

Switzerland ratified the Convention in 1997. Since then it has had to report regularly to the **UN Committee on the Rights of the Child** in Geneva on how children in the country are doing. This committee then makes recommendations. In Switzerland there are, for example, children's parliaments and youth councils in which young people have a say. If they have problems, children can turn to Pro Juventute's helpline 147.

begriffe.erklaerung: A treaty between many countries.
To make a treaty officially valid, so that a country has to keep to it.
What is best for a child.
The UN children's fund, which works for children around the world.

gewusst: The USA signed the Convention on the Rights of the Child but is the only UN member never to have ratified it.
There is a child-friendly version of the Convention, which many schools use in lessons.

teile.einleitung: The Hague Conventions of 1907 are treaties between many countries. Among other things, they lay down how neutral countries must behave in war. They are still very important for neutral Switzerland today.
wichtigste: The Hague Conventions were adopted in 1907 at the Second Hague Peace Conference.
The Hague is in the Netherlands.
Two conventions govern neutrality: one in war on land, one in war at sea.
A neutral country does not take part in other countries' wars.
Foreign soldiers who flee into a neutral country are disarmed and interned.
A neutral country may defend itself against attacks.

abschnitte.text: **The Hague** is the seat of government of the **Netherlands**. In 1899 and 1907 representatives of many countries met there for the **Hague Peace Conferences**. They wanted to set rules so that wars would be less cruel and disputes could be settled peacefully. In 1907 a total of 13 conventions were adopted. Some of them still apply today.

Two of the conventions govern **neutrality**. One applies to **war on land**, the other to **war at sea**. Aircraft played no part in 1907, which is why there are no separate rules for them. Being neutral means that a country does not take sides in a war between other countries.

A neutral country may not take part in a war. It may not let its own **soldiers** fight for a party to the war. In the other direction, parties to a war may not march **troops** through the territory of a neutral country. This territory is **inviolable**. If a neutral country restricts the export of war material, it must **treat** all parties to the war **equally**.

If soldiers of a party to the war flee onto neutral territory, the neutral country must **disarm** and **intern** them. This means they are housed in a particular place and can no longer take part in the war. Switzerland knew this even earlier: in 1871 it took in the French **Bourbaki Army** and looked after the soldiers.

A neutral country may defend itself if it is attacked. The Hague Convention states that resisting a violation of neutrality is **not a hostile act**. That is why Switzerland has an **army**. It is meant to protect the country and be able to defend its neutrality.

gewusst: In The Hague stands the Peace Palace, where the UN's International Court of Justice sits today.
The Hague Conventions of 1907 are more than a hundred years old and still apply.

teile.einleitung: The International Atomic Energy Agency, IAEA for short, is an international organisation with its seat in Vienna. It deals with the peaceful use and the control of nuclear energy around the world. Its inspectors check that no country is secretly building nuclear weapons.
wichtigste: The IAEA looks after the peaceful use and the control of nuclear energy around the world.
It was founded in 1957.
Its seat is in Vienna in Austria.
It belongs to the United Nations family and reports to the UN General Assembly and the Security Council.
Inspectors check nuclear facilities in many countries.
In 2005 the IAEA received the Nobel Peace Prize together with its head, Mohamed ElBaradei.
Switzerland has been a member since its founding in 1957.

abschnitte.text: **IAEA** stands for International Atomic Energy Agency. It is an independent organisation that works closely with the UN. About 180 countries are members (as of about 2025). Its motto means roughly atoms for peace and development.

After the atomic bombs were dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in 1945, many people feared a nuclear war. In 1953 US President Dwight D. Eisenhower gave his famous speech **“Atoms for Peace”** to the UN. He proposed founding an organisation to promote the peaceful use of nuclear power. In 1957 the IAEA was then founded in **Vienna**.

One of the IAEA's main tasks is monitoring, so that no material is diverted for **nuclear weapons**. For this it sends inspectors to nuclear facilities, who take samples, set up cameras and attach seals. The main basis for this is the **Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty**, which came into force in 1970. The inspections became well known, for example, in Iran and North Korea.

Nuclear energy is not only used in nuclear power stations to produce electricity. In **medicine**, radiation helps with X-rays and the treatment of cancer. In farming, insects that have been made infertile with radiation are released to fight pests. The IAEA mainly supports poorer countries in using such techniques safely.

The IAEA develops safety standards for **nuclear power stations** and for handling radioactive waste. After accidents such as Chernobyl in 1986 and Fukushima in 2011, it helped to investigate the consequences. Since 2022 IAEA experts have been at the Ukrainian nuclear power station of Zaporizhzhia, which was occupied in the war. They watch the situation, so that there is no disaster.

Switzerland has been a member of the IAEA since 1957. In Switzerland, the **ENSI**, the Swiss Federal Nuclear Safety Inspectorate, monitors nuclear facilities. In 2017 the people approved the Energy Strategy 2050, under which no new nuclear power stations may be built. The Mühleberg nuclear power station in the canton of Bern was shut down in 2019.

begriffe.erklaerung: Energy that is released when atomic nuclei are split, for example in a nuclear power station.
An expert who checks on the spot whether rules are being kept.
A treaty in which countries commit themselves not to spread nuclear weapons.
Invisible radiation that comes from certain substances and can be dangerous.

gewusst: IAEA inspectors seal containers of nuclear material in such a way that you can see straight away if someone has opened them.
With radiation techniques, the IAEA also helps to fight harmful insects such as the tsetse fly.
The IAEA has its seat in the Vienna International Centre, which is also called UNO City.

teile.einleitung: The HIPC Initiative is a programme that cancels debts for very poor and heavily indebted countries. It was launched in 1996 by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank. The money saved is meant to be used to fight poverty.
wichtigste: HIPC stands for “Heavily Indebted Poor Countries”.
The IMF counts 39 countries that are eligible or possibly eligible.
33 of them are in Africa south of the Sahara.
At the decision point, a country is admitted to the programme.
For full debt relief, a poverty reduction strategy is needed.
From 2005 the MDRI added full cancellation of certain debts to the initiative.

abschnitte.text: Over the decades, many poor countries had taken on large **debts** with other countries and international banks. The interest and repayments ate up a large part of their money. There was hardly anything left for schools, hospitals or roads. That is why the **IMF** and the **World Bank** started the HIPC Initiative in 1996. It is meant to reduce the burden of debt to a bearable level.

The road to debt relief has several stages. At the **decision point**, the IMF and the World Bank decide that a country may take part. After that it already receives some temporary relief. The country must present a **poverty reduction strategy** and carry it out for at least a year. At the **completion point**, it then receives full debt relief.

The IMF counts **39 countries** that are eligible or possibly eligible. 33 of them are in **Africa south of the Sahara**. They are joined by Afghanistan and some countries in Latin America and the Caribbean, for example **Bolivia**, Honduras, Nicaragua, Guyana and Haiti. Bolivia was one of the first countries to complete the process. Almost all the countries have made great progress today.

In 2005 an addition was prepared at the G8 summit: the **Multilateral Debt Relief Initiative**, **MDRI** for short. Countries that have completed the HIPC process receive **full cancellation** of certain debts through it. These are debts to the IMF, the World Bank and the African Development Fund.

Some countries joined only late. **Sudan** reached the decision point in 2021, after the long-time ruler Omar al-Bashir had been overthrown. The war in Sudan from 2023 slowed down the further process. **Eritrea** is the only country that has not yet started the process and has so far received no HIPC relief.

gewusst: Around the year 2000, churches and aid organisations in many countries called for debt relief for poor countries with the “Jubilee” campaign (in German, “Erlassjahr”).
Almost all of the 39 HIPC countries have now completed the whole process.

teile.einleitung: A capital city is the city where a country's government has its seat. Often the parliament works there too. The capital is not always the largest city in a country.
wichtigste: A country's government sits in the capital.
In Switzerland, Bern is officially called the federal city.
The largest Swiss city is Zurich.
Every canton has a capital where the cantonal government sits.
Berlin is the largest capital among Switzerland's neighbouring countries.
Vienna is both a city and an Austrian federal state.

abschnitte.text: In the **capital** there are usually the **government** and the **parliament** of a country. Often there are also embassies of other countries there. The capital is not always the largest city. In Canada, Ottawa is the capital, not Toronto. In Australia it is Canberra, not Sydney. In the USA too, Washington is much smaller than New York.

The Swiss Federal Constitution does not name a capital. **Bern** is officially called the **federal city**, because the **Federal Council** and **Parliament** sit there. They work in the **Federal Palace**. But the largest city in Switzerland is **Zurich**, with the most inhabitants. Switzerland did not want to place one town above the others.

Every canton also has a place where its government sits. It is called the **cantonal capital**. In the Grisons, for example, it is **Chur**, in the Valais **Sion**. The cantonal government and usually the cantonal parliament work there. Sometimes the capital has the same name as the canton, for example Zurich, Bern or Lucerne.

The largest capital among the neighbouring countries is **Berlin**, with about 3.7 million people (as of 2024). The **Spree** flows through Berlin, past the Reichstag building. **Vienna** is the capital of Austria and also a **federal state** of its own. One of its landmarks is the **Giant Ferris Wheel** in the Prater, from 1897. Other capitals are Paris, Rome and Vaduz.

The capital of China is **Beijing**, once also called Peking. There stands the famous **Forbidden City**, the former imperial palace. Some countries have built a new capital, for example Brazil with **Brasília**. Bolivia even has two: according to the constitution the capital is Sucre, but the government sits in La Paz.

gewusst: Bern was chosen as the federal city in 1848, shortly after the modern federal state was founded.
Vaduz, the capital of Liechtenstein, is one of the smallest capitals in Europe.

teile.einleitung: The Cold War was a long conflict between the USA and the Soviet Union, which lasted from about 1947 to 1991. Politically the world was split into a bloc led by the USA and a bloc led by the Soviet Union. It was called cold because the two superpowers never fought each other directly.
wichtigste: The Cold War began shortly after the Second World War.
In the West stood the USA and its allies, in the East the Soviet Union.
The West relied on democracy and a market economy, the East on communism.
Both sides built huge numbers of nuclear weapons.
The Berlin Wall, from 1961 to 1989, was a symbol of division.
In 1962 the Cuban Missile Crisis brought the world close to nuclear war.
With the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991, the Cold War ended.

abschnitte.text: After the Second World War, the USA and the **Soviet Union** were the two most powerful countries. But they had completely different ideas about how a country should be governed. The West, with the USA, relied on free elections and a market economy. In the East, under the leadership of the Soviet Union, communism ruled with only one party. In 1946 the British politician Winston Churchill spoke of an **Iron Curtain** dividing Europe.

In 1949 Western countries founded the defence alliance NATO. As its counterpart, the **Warsaw Pact** was created in the East in 1955. Both sides built thousands of nuclear weapons and missiles. This was called the arms race. Because a nuclear war would have destroyed both sides, neither dared to attack directly.

Germany was divided into the Federal Republic in the west and the GDR in the east. In 1948 and 1949 the Soviet Union cut off West Berlin, and the Western powers supplied the city by plane with an **airlift**. In 1961 the GDR built the Berlin Wall to stop people fleeing to the West. On 9 November 1989 the Wall fell. A year later Germany was reunited.

abschnitte.titel: Crises and the race into space
abschnitte.text: In 1962 the Soviet Union stationed nuclear missiles on Cuba, close to the USA. In the **Cuban Missile Crisis** the world stood on the brink of nuclear war for a few days. In other countries such as Korea and Vietnam, the blocs fought proxy wars. There was also a race in space: in 1957 the Soviet Union sent the first satellite, Sputnik, into space. Then in 1969 Americans became the first people to land on the Moon.

Switzerland remained neutral but felt closer to the West. Out of fear of a nuclear war, it built **shelters** for almost all its inhabitants. Geneva became an important place for talks between East and West. In 1985 Ronald Reagan and Mikhail Gorbachev met there for a famous summit. After reforms in the Soviet Union and peaceful revolutions in Eastern Europe, the Soviet Union broke apart in December 1991.

begriffe.erklaerung: A system of government in which factories and land belong to the state and one party rules.
A country with very great military and economic influence.
When countries compete to build more and more weapons.
A war in which great powers support other countries or groups instead of fighting directly themselves.

gewusst: From 1963 there was a hotline between Washington and Moscow, a direct teleprinter link for crises.
Switzerland still has so many shelters that almost all its inhabitants can find room in them.

teile.einleitung: The Geneva Refugee Convention is the most important international treaty for protecting refugees. It lays down who counts as a refugee and what rights these people have. It was adopted in Geneva in 1951.
wichtigste: The Convention was adopted in Geneva on 28 July 1951.
It came into force in 1954, and Switzerland ratified it in 1955.
At first it applied only to events before 1951; the New York Protocol of 1967 removed this limit.
It names five grounds of persecution.
A refugee must be outside their home country.
The principle of non-refoulement forbids sending refugees back to a country where they would be persecuted.

abschnitte.text: The Convention relating to the Status of Refugees was drawn up under the impression of the huge **movements of refugees** in the Second World War. It was adopted in **Geneva** on **28 July 1951**. It only came into force in **1954**, when enough countries had **ratified** it, meaning approved it officially. **Switzerland** became a party in 1955 and so is one of the early members.

abschnitte.titel: From a cut-off date to worldwide validity
abschnitte.text: At first the Convention only protected people who had fled because of events **before 1 January 1951**, mainly in Europe. With the **New York Protocol** of 1967, this limit in time and place was dropped. Since then the Convention has applied **worldwide** and with no cut-off date. Most countries in the world have signed it or the Protocol.

A refugee in the sense of the Convention is **outside their home country**. Someone who flees within their own country does not fall under this definition. The Convention names **five grounds of persecution**: race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group and **political opinion**. Poverty or natural disasters on their own are not grounds of persecution.

A core part of the protection is the principle of **non-refoulement**. The word comes from the French “refouler”, which means to push back. Under **Article 33**, a refugee must not be expelled to a country where they face persecution. The exclusion clause in **Article 1F** excludes from protection people who have committed serious crimes such as **war crimes**. The protection is not meant to benefit perpetrators.

gewusst: The UN refugee agency UNHCR watches over the Convention and has its seat in Geneva.
In Switzerland, the Asylum Act governs how the Convention is applied in everyday life.

teile.einleitung: In Colombia the guerrilla group FARC fought against the state for more than 50 years. In 2016, after long negotiations, the government and the FARC concluded a peace agreement. The road to it was difficult, and the peace is still not complete today.
wichtigste: The FARC was founded in 1964 and fought against the Colombian state.
From 2012 to 2016 negotiations took place in Havana in Cuba.
On 2 October 2016 the people narrowly rejected the first agreement.
Congress approved a revised version in November 2016.
President Juan Manuel Santos received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2016.
The FARC became a political party, which today is called Comunes.
The guerrilla group ELN remained active.

abschnitte.text: The **FARC** was founded in 1964. A **guerrilla** group is an armed group that does not belong to a country's army. For more than 50 years the FARC fought against the Colombian state. The conflict claimed more than 200,000 lives, and millions of people had to leave their homes.

From 2012 to 2016 the government and the FARC negotiated in **Havana**, the capital of Cuba. **Cuba** and **Norway** accompanied the talks as **guarantor countries**. They helped to keep both sides at the table. The talks were about land, the victims and how the fighters could return to normal life, among other things.

On 2 October 2016 the people voted on the first agreement. About **50.2 per cent** said no. Many felt that the fighters were being treated too leniently. After that the treaty was renegotiated. In November 2016 **Congress**, meaning the parliament, approved the new version.

President **Juan Manuel Santos**, in office from 2010 to 2018, received the **Nobel Peace Prize** in 2016. The FARC laid down its weapons. The former fighters founded a **political party** and were given guaranteed seats in parliament for some years. Today the party is called **Comunes**.

The guerrilla group **ELN**, the National Liberation Army, was not part of the agreement. Negotiations with it have not yet brought lasting peace. Other armed groups also remain active in some regions. Even so, the agreement with the FARC is seen as an important step.

gewusst: The agreement was signed with a ballpoint pen made from a bullet.
On the pen it said: “Bullets wrote our past, education our future”.

teile.einleitung: International Women's Day is celebrated every year on **8 March**. This day is about women's rights and equality between women and men. Switzerland was part of the very first Women's Day.
wichtigste: International Women's Day is on 8 March.
In 1910 Clara Zetkin proposed a yearly Women's Day.
The first Women's Day took place on 19 March 1911.
In 1911 women celebrated in Germany, Austria-Hungary, Denmark and Switzerland.
At that time they were fighting mainly for the right to vote.
In Switzerland women have been able to vote and stand for election at national level since 1971.

abschnitte.text: At an international conference in 1910, the German politician **Clara Zetkin** proposed celebrating a Women's Day every year. At that time women had fewer rights than men in many countries. They were often not allowed to vote in elections or in popular votes. Women's Day was meant to draw attention to this injustice.

On 19 March 1911 the first Women's Day took place. It was celebrated in **Germany, Austria-Hungary, Denmark and Switzerland**. Many women took to the streets and above all demanded the **right to vote**. Later 8 March became the fixed date. Today it is officially called **International Women's Day**.

In Switzerland it took a long time before women were allowed to have a say. On 7 February 1971 Swiss men voted yes to **women's suffrage** at federal level. Since then women have been able to vote and stand for election at national level. In some cantons women only got the vote later; the last canton was Appenzell Innerrhoden in 1990.

Today there are rallies, events and discussions in many countries on 8 March. Topics include equal pay for equal work or sharing family work. In the federal state of **Berlin**, 8 March has been an official public holiday since 2019. Do not confuse it: **Mother's Day** is a different day, in May.

gewusst: In 1911 Switzerland was one of the first four countries to celebrate a Women's Day, but it only gave women the national vote 60 years later.
Appenzell Innerrhoden only introduced women's suffrage in 1990, after a ruling by the Federal Supreme Court.

teile.einleitung: The Indochina Conference took place in **Geneva** in 1954. It ended the war between France and the Vietnamese fighters for independence. Vietnam was divided into two parts for the time being.
wichtigste: The conference met in Geneva from 26 April to 21 July 1954.
Shortly before, France lost the Battle of Điện Biên Phủ.
Vietnam was divided for the time being at the 17th parallel.
Elections for the whole of Vietnam were planned for 1956 but never took place.
Great Britain and the Soviet Union jointly chaired the conference.
Laos and Cambodia were confirmed as independent.

abschnitte.text: Indochina was the name of the former French colonial territory in South-East Asia, with Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia. After the Second World War, Vietnamese fighters for independence fought against France. On 7 May 1954 the French fortress of **Điện Biên Phủ** fell. This happened while the conference in Geneva was already under way, and it greatly weakened France's position.

With Geneva, Switzerland provided a neutral place for the negotiations. The conference was jointly chaired by the British Foreign Secretary **Anthony Eden** and the Soviet Foreign Minister **Vyacheslav Molotov**. The People's Republic of China was also there with **Zhou Enlai**, as were the USA, France and representatives from Indochina. In June 1954 **Pierre Mendès France** became French Prime Minister. He promised to reach a ceasefire within 30 days, and he only just managed it.

The **Geneva Accords** brought a ceasefire. Vietnam was divided for the time being at the **17th parallel** into a north and a south. Elections in the whole of Vietnam were planned for 1956, to unite the country again. In addition, the independence of **Laos** and **Cambodia** was confirmed, and foreign troops were to withdraw.

The USA took part in the conference but did not sign the final declaration. It only declared that it would not use force against the agreements. The planned elections never took place, because South Vietnam and the USA rejected them. The dividing line, which was only meant to be temporary, remained the border between North and South Vietnam until 1975.

gewusst: The fortress of Điện Biên Phủ fell on 7 May 1954, one day before the talks on Indochina began in Geneva.
A line that was only meant to be temporary ended up dividing Vietnam for more than 20 years.

teile.einleitung: **Jus cogens** (also written ius cogens) is Latin and means “compelling law”. It refers to the most important rules of international law, from which no country may depart, not even with a treaty. They include, for example, the ban on slavery and on genocide.
wichtigste: Jus cogens is peremptory international law, from which no departure is allowed.
Art. 53 of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties declares treaties that conflict with it void.
Such a norm can only be changed by a later norm of the same kind.
Recognised examples are the bans on slavery, torture, genocide and wars of aggression.
In Switzerland a popular initiative is invalid if it violates peremptory international law.

abschnitte.text: In international law, countries can change most rules among themselves through treaties. With **jus cogens** this is not possible. These are norms that are recognised by the community of states as a whole. The **Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties** (VCLT) defines the term in **Art. 53**: a treaty that conflicts with a peremptory norm when it is concluded is **void**. Such a norm can only be changed by a later norm of the same legal character.

The recognised core includes the **ban on slavery**, the **ban on torture**, the **ban on genocide** and the **ban on aggression**, meaning the ban on wars of aggression. Questions such as customs rates or visa rules, on the other hand, are freely negotiable. If a new peremptory norm emerges, then under **Art. 64 VCLT** an existing treaty that conflicts with it becomes void and ends. In a dispute about this, the **International Court of Justice** can be called on under **Art. 66 VCLT**.

For a long time the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in The Hague avoided the term. In 1970, in the **Barcelona Traction** case, it distinguished duties towards individual countries from duties **erga omnes**, meaning towards all countries. In 2006, in the case **Democratic Republic of the Congo v. Rwanda**, it called the ban on genocide a norm of jus cogens explicitly for the first time. Many jus cogens norms create such duties towards everyone.

Peremptory international law also plays a part in Switzerland. Under **Art. 139 para. 3 of the Federal Constitution**, the **Federal Assembly** declares a popular initiative wholly or partly invalid if it violates peremptory international law. This happened in 1996 with an asylum initiative, because it broke the **principle of non-refoulement**. This principle forbids sending people back to a country where they face torture or serious persecution.

gewusst: Not even the Swiss people can abolish peremptory international law with an initiative.

teile.einleitung: The International Labour Organization, ILO for short, is a specialised agency of the United Nations with its seat in Geneva. It works for fair working conditions around the world. These include fair wages, safe workplaces and the ban on child labour.
wichtigste: The ILO deals with fair working conditions around the world.
It was founded in 1919 after the First World War.
Its seat is in Geneva in Switzerland.
Since 1946 it has been a specialised agency of the UN.
In the ILO, governments, employers and employees have a say together.
It adopts international conventions, for example against child labour and forced labour.
In 1969 the ILO received the Nobel Peace Prize.

abschnitte.text: **ILO** is short for International Labour Organization. It is an international organisation in which almost all the countries of the world are members, namely 187 countries. Its aim is **decent work** for all people. This means, for example, a fair wage, protection from accidents and enough free time.

The ILO was founded in 1919 with the **Treaty of Versailles** after the First World War. At the time people were convinced that lasting peace was only possible with social justice. Since 1920 it has had its seat in **Geneva**. It survived the Second World War and in 1946 became the first specialised agency of the newly founded UN.

What is special about the ILO is its **tripartite structure**. Each country sends not only government representatives but also representatives of employers and employees, meaning the trade unions. Every June they all meet in Geneva for the International Labour Conference. New rules are discussed and adopted there.

abschnitte.titel: Rules for the world of work
abschnitte.text: The ILO draws up international **conventions**, which countries can sign. Its very first convention, in 1919, governed working hours in industry, with a maximum of eight hours a day. The **core labour standards** are especially important: the ban on child labour and forced labour, no discrimination, and the right to organise in trade unions. The ILO regularly checks whether countries are keeping these rules.

Around the world many millions of children still have to work instead of going to school. The ILO has created its own programmes and conventions on this. Every year on 12 June, the **World Day Against Child Labour** draws attention to this problem. When buying clothes or chocolate, you can also check whether fair working conditions were kept.

Switzerland has been a member of the ILO since 1920. The ILO's large headquarters stands in Geneva, near the Palais des Nations. In this way the ILO adds to Geneva's reputation as a city of international organisations. Swiss trade unions and employers' associations take an active part in the ILO.

begriffe.erklaerung: An independent organisation that works with the UN and looks after a particular topic.
An association of employees that stands up for their rights.
Work done by children that harms them or keeps them from going to school.
A treaty that countries sign and must then keep to.

gewusst: The ILO is older than the UN itself; it was founded back in 1919.
In 1969, on its 50th birthday, the ILO received the Nobel Peace Prize.
In the ILO, not only governments but also trade unions and employers have a say.

teile.einleitung: The flag of Mexico has three vertical stripes in green, white and red. In the middle is the coat of arms with an eagle sitting on a cactus and holding a snake in its beak. The picture recalls an old Aztec legend.
wichtigste: The flag of Mexico is green, white and red.
Mexico's coat of arms is in the middle, white stripe.
The coat of arms shows an eagle on a cactus with a snake in its beak.
The legend behind it comes from the Aztecs.
The city of Tenochtitlan, today Mexico City, was built at this spot.
Italy has the same colours, but no coat of arms.

abschnitte.titel: Three stripes and a coat of arms
abschnitte.text: The flag of Mexico has three **vertical stripes**. **Green** is on the left, **white** in the middle and **red** on the right. In the **middle stripe** is Mexico's **coat of arms**. This makes it different from the flag of **Italy**, which has the same colours in the same order but no coat of arms.

The coat of arms shows an **eagle**. It sits on a **prickly pear cactus** and holds a **snake** in its beak. The cactus grows on a **rock** that rises out of the water of a lake. At the bottom, the coat of arms is surrounded by a wreath of branches. The picture looks strong and proud.

The **Aztecs** were an ancient people in Mexico. According to their **legend**, they wandered for a long time looking for a place for a new city. Their god is said to have told them: build the city where you see an **eagle on a cactus**. They are said to have found this sign on an island in a lake. There they founded the city of **Tenochtitlan**.

Tenochtitlan became a large and splendid city. After the **Spanish** arrived in the 16th century, it was destroyed and rebuilt. Today **Mexico City**, the country's **capital**, stands on this spot. The lake of those days has mostly disappeared. But the legend lives on in the flag.

gewusst: Mexico celebrates a Flag Day every year on 24 February.
The name Mexico goes back to the Mexica, which is what the Aztecs called themselves.

teile.einleitung: The identity card is an official identity document. With it you can show who you are. In Switzerland it is usually just called the **ID**.
wichtigste: The identity card, ID for short, is an official identity document.
It is the size of a bank card and fits into a purse or wallet.
The ID shows, among other things, your name, date of birth, height and place of origin, as well as a photo.
With the Swiss ID you can travel to most countries in Europe.
Even babies can get their own ID; their parents apply for it.
If you lose your ID, you must report it to the police.

abschnitte.text: The word **identity** means who someone is. The identity card proves this officially, meaning with the confirmation of the state. You need it, for example, at the border, at the post office, at the bank or when opening an account. In Switzerland people usually just say “ID”. It is a stiff card the size of a bank card.

The Swiss ID shows your name, date of birth, height and **place of origin**. The place of origin is the municipality where you hold citizenship, and not necessarily where you live. There is also a photo of your face. Special patterns and marks make the card hard to forge.

With the Swiss ID you can travel to all **EU** countries and to other European countries. For many other countries, such as the USA, you need a **passport**. The passport is a small booklet with pages for stamps and visas. The ID, on the other hand, is a card without pages. Before a trip it is worth checking which document is required.

You can get an ID from birth. For children, the parents apply for the document, usually at their municipality or the cantonal passport office. The ID is only valid for a certain time and must then be renewed. Anyone who loses their ID reports it to the **police**. This way nobody else can misuse the card, and you can order a new one.

gewusst: The Swiss ID does not show your place of birth but your place of origin, meaning the municipality your family comes from.
Even a baby can have its own identity card with a photo.

teile.einleitung: The flag of Ukraine is made up of two stripes of equal width: blue at the top and yellow at the bottom. The colours are often explained as a blue sky above yellow fields of grain. Ukraine is a large country in the east of Europe.
wichtigste: The Ukrainian flag is blue and yellow.
It has two horizontal stripes of equal width.
Blue is at the top, yellow at the bottom.
Blue is often explained as the sky, yellow as fields of grain.
On 23 August Ukraine celebrates National Flag Day.
The coat of arms of Ukraine shows a golden trident on blue.

abschnitte.text: The flag of Ukraine is very simple. It has **two horizontal stripes** that are **exactly the same width**. **Blue** is at the top, **yellow** at the bottom. The flag is a rectangle that is wider than it is tall. Because it is so clear, it is easy to recognise.

The colours are often explained like this: the **blue** is the wide **sky**, and the **yellow** is ripe **fields of grain**. Ukraine has very fertile soil. A lot of **wheat** and other grain is grown there. That is why the country is sometimes called the **breadbasket of Europe**. The colours blue and yellow were used in the region a long time ago.

For a long time Ukraine was part of the **Soviet Union**. In **1991** it became **independent**. **Independence Day** is on **24 August**. The day before, on **23 August**, the country celebrates **National Flag Day**. On this day flags are raised all over the country.

The coat of arms of Ukraine shows a **golden trident** on a **blue background**. In Ukrainian it is called the **Tryzub**. The sign is very old and was already known more than a thousand years ago. So the coat of arms and the flag have the same colours. The capital of Ukraine is called **Kyiv**.

gewusst: By area, Ukraine is the largest country that lies entirely in Europe.
Since 2022 the blue and yellow flag has also been seen in many Swiss municipalities as a sign of sympathy.

teile.einleitung: The **Human Development Index**, HDI for short, compares how well people live in the countries of the world. It measures not only money but also health and education.
wichtigste: The HDI is published by the UN Development Programme, the UNDP.
It appeared for the first time in 1990.
The HDI lies between 0 and 1; the closer to 1, the higher the development.
It measures health, education and standard of living.
In the 2025 report, Switzerland is in 3rd place, behind Iceland and Norway.
In the 2025 report, South Sudan is in last place out of 193 countries.

abschnitte.text: In the past, countries were mainly compared using **gross domestic product**, meaning the value of all goods and services. The Indian economist **Amartya Sen** criticised this as showing development only poorly. He helped to develop the HDI. Sen received the Nobel Prize in Economics in 1998. Since 1990 the HDI has appeared in the **UNDP**'s Human Development Report.

For **health**, what counts is life expectancy at birth. For **education**, since 2010 it has been counted how many years adults have on average spent at school and how many years a child is expected to go to school. For **standard of living**, gross national income per person, adjusted for purchasing power, is used. Each area is converted to a scale from 0 to 1 and then combined.

The 2025 report compares 193 countries and territories with data from 2023. In it, **Switzerland** is in 3rd place, behind Iceland and Norway. In the two reports before that it was in 1st place. At the bottom of the list is **South Sudan**. Somalia, the Central African Republic and Chad are also far down.

Some experts criticise the HDI for not taking **environmental effects** into account. A country can have a very high value and still put a heavy strain on the environment. That is why since 2020 there has also been a **planetary pressures-adjusted HDI**, which also includes CO2 emissions and the use of raw materials. Others complain that averages hide differences within a country.

gewusst: In the HDI reports before 2025, Switzerland was in 1st place in the world twice in a row.
The HDI is always based on data that are already one to two years old.

teile.einleitung: In front of the Palais des Nations in Geneva is the Allée des Drapeaux, the avenue of flags. There the flags of the UN member states fly side by side. It shows that all countries have equal rights in the UN.
wichtigste: The avenue of flags is in front of the Palais des Nations in Geneva.
The flags of the UN member states fly there.
In French it is called the “Allée des Drapeaux”.
At the entrance is the visitor centre, the Portail des Nations.
All the flags are equally important, because all member states have equal rights.

abschnitte.text: The **Palais des Nations** is a large building in **Geneva**. It was built for the **League of Nations**, a forerunner of the UN. Today it is an important seat of the **United Nations**, **UN** for short. In front of the building is the **avenue of flags**. In French it is called the **“Allée des Drapeaux”**, because “drapeau” means flag.

Along the avenue stand many **flagpoles** in long rows. The flags of the **UN member states** fly on them. Every flag is **the same size** and hangs at the same height. This shows that in the UN **every member country has one vote**. Small and large countries have **equal rights**. The **Swiss flag** also flies there, because Switzerland has been a member of the UN since **2002**.

At the entrance to the Palais des Nations, along the avenue of flags, is the **visitor centre, the Portail des Nations**. The **guided tours** of the building start there. You can see halls where experts from all over the world negotiate. That is why Geneva is an important city for **international cooperation**. Many other organisations have their seat here.

gewusst: Switzerland joined the UN after a popular vote in 2002.
Opposite the Palais des Nations, on the Place des Nations, stands a huge wooden sculpture: a chair with a broken leg.

teile.einleitung: The International Court of Justice, ICJ for short, is the court in The Hague that decides disputes between countries. It is the most important court of the United Nations. Instead of going to war, countries can have their disputes settled peacefully here.
wichtigste: The ICJ decides disputes between countries, not cases about individual people.
It has its seat in the Peace Palace in The Hague in the Netherlands.
It is one of the six main bodies of the UN.
The court is made up of 15 judges.
They are elected for nine years.
The ICJ began its work in 1946.
It can also give opinions on questions of international law.

abschnitte.text: The **International Court of Justice** was created in 1945 with the Charter of the United Nations. It is the most important court of the UN. Only countries can bring cases before it or have cases brought against them. It judges according to **international law**, meaning the rules that apply between countries. It cannot punish individual people; for that there is the International Criminal Court.

The ICJ sits in the Peace Palace in The Hague. This splendid building was opened in 1913. The American businessman Andrew Carnegie paid for it with his money. The ICJ's predecessor, the Permanent Court of International Justice, already worked there from 1922. That is why The Hague is often called the city of peace and justice.

15 **judges** from different countries work at the court. They are elected for nine years by the UN General Assembly and the Security Council together. No country may provide two judges at the same time. A case can take several years, because both sides present their arguments in detail. The judgments are binding on the countries involved.

Countries often argue about borders, islands or fishing grounds at sea. But cases are also about environmental protection, the treatment of citizens abroad or genocide. The UN can also ask the ICJ for an **advisory opinion**, for example on questions of climate protection. Such an opinion is not binding, but it carries great weight. One problem is that the ICJ has no police to enforce its judgments.

Switzerland has recognised the jurisdiction of the ICJ since 1948. It had joined the Statute of the court even before it joined the UN. As a country that relies on law rather than power, it supports the peaceful settlement of disputes. Switzerland has itself taken a case to the ICJ. Peaceful solutions to conflicts are an important aim of Swiss foreign policy.

begriffe.erklaerung: The rules that apply between countries, for example in treaties.
When someone asks a court to decide a dispute.
An assessment by experts on a legal question.
A court's decision at the end of proceedings.

gewusst: The Peace Palace in The Hague has a huge library on international law.
The official languages of the ICJ are English and French.

teile.einleitung: The flag of Japan is white with a red circle in the middle. The circle represents the sun. In Japanese the flag is called the “Hinomaru”, which means roughly circle of the sun.
wichtigste: Japan's flag shows a red circle on a white background.
The red circle stands for the sun.
The circle is exactly in the middle of the rectangular flag.
“Hinomaru” means roughly circle of the sun.
The flag has only been official by law since 1999.
Japan is also called the “Land of the Rising Sun”.

abschnitte.text: The flag of Japan is very simple. It is a **white rectangle** with a **red circle** exactly in the **middle**. The flag is wider than it is tall. Because of its simple shape, it is very easy to recognise even from far away. In Japanese it is called the **“Hinomaru”**, which means roughly **circle of the sun** or sun disc.

abschnitte.titel: The Land of the Rising Sun
abschnitte.text: The red circle is a **sun**. Japan lies in the far **east of Asia**. Seen from there, the sun rises over the wide Pacific. The Japanese name of the country, **Nihon** or **Nippon**, means roughly **“origin of the sun”**. That is why Japan is also called the **Land of the Rising Sun**. A sun goddess plays an important part in old Japanese legends.

The sun flag has been used in Japan for a very long time. Even so, for a long time there was **no law** that made it the official national flag. Only in **1999** was such a law passed. It also lays down the exact measurements. For example, the circle must be exactly in the middle.

The flag of **Bangladesh** looks similar to the Japanese one. It also shows a **red circle**, but on a **green** background. There the circle is moved a little towards the flagpole. When the flag flutters in the wind, it then looks as if it were in the middle again. Both flags show how powerful a simple sign can be.

gewusst: At sports events, Japanese fans often wave small Hinomaru flags.
Japan is made up of thousands of islands; the four largest are called Honshu, Hokkaido, Kyushu and Shikoku.

tcmnehp.t: International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement

teile.einleitung: The International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement is the largest humanitarian network in the world. It helps people in wars, disasters and emergencies. Its roots are in Switzerland, and many of its institutions have their seat in Geneva.
wichtigste: The Movement is made up of three parts.
They are the ICRC, the International Federation and the national societies.
There are 191 national societies, only one in each country.
The Movement has seven principles, proclaimed in 1965.
The Swiss Red Cross was founded in 1866 and has its seat in Bern.
The International Conference meets about every four years.

abschnitte.text: The Movement is made up of the **International Committee of the Red Cross** (ICRC), the **International Federation** of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies and the **national societies**. The ICRC helps mainly in armed conflicts. The Federation coordinates the help of the national societies, especially in natural disasters and health crises. It was founded in Paris in 1919 as the **League of Red Cross Societies**. Since 1991 it has been called the International Federation and has had its seat in Geneva.

In 1965 the Movement proclaimed seven principles: **humanity, impartiality, neutrality, independence, voluntary service, unity and universality**. Impartiality means that only need counts: origin, religion or political opinion play no part. Neutrality means that the Movement does not take sides in conflicts. This way it keeps the trust of all sides and can help everywhere.

In about 190 countries there is a national Red Cross or Red Crescent society; the Federation counts 191. There may be only one such society in each country. Many volunteers work there, for example in the ambulance service, for blood donations or in care. Depending on the country, the emblem is a **red cross** or a **red crescent** on a white background.

Switzerland's national society is called the **Swiss Red Cross** (SRC). It was founded in 1866 and has its seat in **Bern**. The SRC helps in Switzerland and abroad, for example with ambulance services, courses and support for older people. It is part of the worldwide Movement.

The highest body of the Movement is the **International Conference of the Red Cross and Red Crescent**. As a rule it meets about every four years. All parts of the Movement and the states party to the **Geneva Conventions** take part. Joint decisions on humanitarian aid are taken there.

gewusst: The Red Cross emblem is the Swiss flag with the colours reversed, in honour of Switzerland.
At the International Conference, aid organisations and governments sit at the table together.

teile.einleitung: For a long time Geneva has been a place where countries negotiate about peace. That is why Geneva is often called the “City of Peace”. Switzerland helps with what are called good offices.
wichtigste: Countries that are in dispute with each other often meet in Geneva.
Switzerland offers good offices: it organises meetings and mediates.
In 1954 the end of the Indochina War was negotiated in Geneva.
In 1955 the leaders of four great powers met in Geneva.
In 2013 Iran and six great powers agreed in Geneva on a first plan for its nuclear programme.
From 2012 there were talks in Geneva about peace in Syria.

abschnitte.text: Many international organisations have their seat in Geneva, for example the **UN** in the Palais des Nations and the **International Committee of the Red Cross**. That is why many diplomats work there. When countries are in dispute, they often meet in Geneva. Switzerland is **neutral** and is therefore seen as a good place for difficult talks.

Switzerland's help is called **good offices**. It organises meetings, provides rooms and makes sure things are safe. Sometimes it also mediates itself. A **mediator** does not take sides. They help both sides to find a solution that everyone can live with.

In 1954, at the **Geneva Conference on Indochina**, the end of the Indochina War in South-East Asia was negotiated. In 1955 the leaders of the USA, the Soviet Union, Great Britain and France met for the first big summit after the Second World War. In 1985 **Ronald Reagan** and **Mikhail Gorbachev** met in Geneva. In June 2021 Joe Biden and Vladimir Putin talked to each other in the **Villa La Grange**, in a park on Lake Geneva.

In November 2013 **Iran** and six great powers agreed in Geneva on a first plan for Iran's **nuclear programme**. Because of the civil war in **Syria**, representatives met again and again in Geneva from 2012 to talk about peace. Not all talks are successful straight away. Often many meetings are needed before an agreement is reached.

gewusst: Thousands of people in Geneva work for international organisations.
The Red Cross was also founded in Geneva, in 1863.

teile.einleitung: The International Telecommunication Union, ITU for short, is a specialised agency of the UN with its seat in Geneva. It makes sure that telephones, radio, satellites and the internet work together all over the world. Without its shared rules you could not simply phone someone in Japan.
wichtigste: The ITU deals with worldwide rules for telecommunications and the internet.
It has its headquarters in Geneva.
It was founded in Paris in 1865 as the International Telegraph Union.
It is the oldest specialised agency of the United Nations.
Almost all the countries in the world are members, as well as many companies and universities.
The ITU allocates radio frequencies and places for satellites in space.
Country codes such as +41 for Switzerland are also governed through the ITU.

abschnitte.text: The ITU is a **specialised agency** of the UN that deals only with communications technology. Its full name is the International Telecommunication Union. Its members include 193 countries. Hundreds of companies, research institutes and universities also take part. Together they discuss how telephones, radio and the internet should work around the world.

abschnitte.titel: From the telegraph to the internet
abschnitte.text: The ITU was founded in Paris in 1865, when messages were still sent by **telegraph**. At that time countries had to agree on how telegrams would be passed on across borders and paid for. Later the telephone, radio, television, mobile phones and the internet were added. In 1947 the ITU became a specialised agency of the UN. Since 1948 it has had its seat in Geneva.

The ITU is divided into three areas. The radiocommunication area allocates **frequencies**, so that radio stations, mobile phones and aviation radio do not interfere with each other. The standardisation area develops technical **standards**, for example for transmitting videos. The development area helps poorer countries to build good telephone and internet connections. Every few years the members meet for large conferences.

Satellites need fixed positions in orbit around the Earth and their own radio frequencies. The ITU keeps a register of which country may use which place and which frequency. In this way it prevents satellites from interfering with each other. This is important for television, weather services and navigation such as GPS. Because more and more satellites are being sent into space, this task is getting harder and harder.

The ITU's headquarters stands in Geneva, near the Palais des Nations. This makes the ITU an important part of **International Geneva**. Switzerland is a member and takes part through the Federal Office of Communications. If people can reach you in Switzerland on +41, you owe it to the ITU's worldwide numbering system.

begriffe.erklaerung: Exchanging messages over long distances with technology, for example by telephone, radio or the internet.
A particular range of radio waves on which signals are sent, rather like a channel of its own.
A shared technical rule, so that devices from different companies work together.
An independent organisation that is closely linked to the UN and has its own field of expertise.

gewusst: The ITU is older than the telephone, because Alexander Graham Bell only patented his telephone in 1876.
The emergency number 112 and many mobile phone standards were agreed in international bodies in which the ITU takes part.

tdu8fh1.t: International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination

teile.einleitung: The International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination is often called the **anti-racism convention** for short. It is a UN treaty that obliges countries to fight racism. Switzerland has also joined it.
wichtigste: The UN General Assembly adopted the Convention on 21 December 1965.
It came into force in 1969 and is the oldest of the major UN human rights conventions.
Switzerland joined it in November 1994.
In 1994 the Swiss people approved the anti-racism criminal provision with about 55 per cent yes.
In 1995 the Federal Commission against Racism was founded.
21 March is the International Day for the Elimination of Racial Discrimination.

abschnitte.text: The UN General Assembly adopted the Convention on **21 December 1965**, and it came into force in 1969. It is the oldest of the major **UN human rights conventions**. Countries commit themselves to banning and fighting racial discrimination. A committee of experts regularly examines the countries' reports.

The Convention lists features such as race, **colour**, **descent** and national or **ethnic origin**. Anyone who is treated worse because of such a feature is being discriminated against. This can happen, for example, when looking for a flat, at work or when trying to get into a restaurant or club. So discrimination means being put at an unfair disadvantage.

Before Switzerland could join, it had to adapt its **criminal law**. In 1994 the people voted on the **anti-racism criminal provision** in the Criminal Code. It was approved with about 55 per cent yes and punishes racist incitement. In November 1994 Switzerland joined the Convention. In 1995 the **Federal Commission against Racism** was set up; it advises the Confederation and informs the public.

The UN declared 21 March the **International Day for the Elimination of Racial Discrimination**. It recalls the **Sharpeville massacre** in South Africa. There, on 21 March 1960, police shot people who were protesting peacefully against the pass laws of **apartheid**; at least 69 died. In Switzerland, weeks of action against racism take place in many towns around this day.

gewusst: The anti-racism convention is older than all the other major UN human rights treaties.
The Swiss people voted on the Swiss anti-racism criminal provision themselves.

teile.einleitung: The dove of peace is a white dove, often with an olive branch in its beak, and it is seen around the world as a symbol of peace. You see it on posters, stamps and at peace demonstrations. Its meaning has a long history that goes back to old stories in the Bible.
wichtigste: The dove is seen around the world as a symbol of peace.
It is usually shown white, with an olive branch in its beak.
One origin of the symbol is the Bible story of Noah and the Flood.
In 1949 Pablo Picasso drew a famous dove for a peace congress in Paris.
Since the 20th century the dove of peace has been a sign of the peace movement.
Real doves belong to the pigeon family, which also includes the town pigeon.

abschnitte.text: The Bible tells how Noah lets a dove fly out of the ark after the **Flood**. The dove comes back with a fresh olive leaf. From this Noah knows that the water is going down and that life is possible again. Since then the dove and the **olive branch** have stood for reconciliation, hope and peace.

In 1949 the Spanish artist **Pablo Picasso** created a lithograph of a dove for the poster of the World Peace Congress in Paris. The picture became world-famous and made the dove the modern symbol of peace. Picasso went on to draw many more doves. He named his daughter, who was born the same year, Paloma, the Spanish word for dove.

Doves and pigeons are birds with a small head, a round body and short legs. The **town pigeons** you see in squares in Zurich or Bern are descended from the wild rock dove. Pigeons are very good at finding their way home, which is why **carrier pigeons** were once used for messages. For the peace symbol a white dove is usually chosen, because white stands for purity and innocence.

The dove of peace appears on flags, badges, stamps and in the logos of peace organisations. At celebrations and memorial events, white doves are sometimes released. Besides the dove there are other **peace signs**, for example the peace symbol from the 1950s or the white flag. Children often paint the dove of peace in lessons about war and peace.

abschnitte.titel: The dove in religion and culture
abschnitte.text: In Christianity the dove also stands for the Holy Spirit. Even in ancient cultures around the Mediterranean, the dove was seen as a friendly, gentle bird. The **olive tree** grows slowly and needs peaceful times to be looked after, which is why it suits peace so well. The combination of dove and olive branch is understood in almost every country today.

begriffe.erklaerung: A sign that stands for an idea or a value.
A branch of the olive tree, a sign of peace and reconciliation.
A print made with a printing technique that uses a stone.
A pigeon trained to carry messages home.

gewusst: Picasso named his daughter, born in 1949, Paloma, which means dove in Spanish.
Carrier pigeons can find their way back to their loft over hundreds of kilometres.
The expression “to hold out an olive branch to someone” also means to offer peace.

teile.einleitung: At a summit meeting, the heads of state and government of several countries come together. They discuss important questions directly with each other. Some summits have changed world history, and some took place in Switzerland.
wichtigste: In 1950 Winston Churchill coined the term “summit” for meetings of the powerful.
In 1945 the leaders of the USA, Great Britain and the Soviet Union met in Yalta in Crimea.
In 1985 Reagan and Gorbachev met for the first time in Geneva.
In 1989 George Bush and Gorbachev met off Malta.
A sherpa prepares a summit for a head of state or government.
The European Council is the summit meeting of the EU leaders.

abschnitte.text: In a speech in 1950, the British Prime Minister **Winston Churchill** spoke of negotiations “at the summit” between the great powers. Since then meetings of heads of state and government have been called **summit meetings**. Whoever prepares a summit is called a **sherpa**, like the mountain guides in the Himalayas. The sherpa negotiates the texts and topics in advance, so that the leaders can decide quickly at the meeting.

In February 1945 the leaders of the **USA**, **Great Britain** and the **Soviet Union** met in **Yalta** on the **Crimean** peninsula on the Black Sea. The Second World War was not quite over yet. The three victorious powers discussed how Europe should be organised after the war. The Yalta Conference is seen as one of the summits with the most far-reaching consequences.

In November 1985 **Ronald Reagan** and **Mikhail Gorbachev** met for the first time in **Geneva**. The meeting is seen as the start of an easing of tension in the **Cold War**. In October 1986 a summit followed in **Reykjavik**, the capital of Iceland. It ended without an agreement, but a year later they signed the **INF Treaty** on intermediate-range missiles. In June 2021 Joe Biden and Vladimir Putin met at the **Villa La Grange** in Geneva.

In December 1989, shortly after the fall of the Berlin Wall, **George Bush** and Mikhail Gorbachev met off **Malta**. The meeting took place on ships in the harbour of Marsaxlokk. Because of a storm this was not easy. The summit is seen as a sign of the end of the Cold War.

Some summits take place regularly. In the **European Council**, the leaders of the EU countries meet several times a year, usually in **Brussels**. The **Council of Europe** in Strasbourg, on the other hand, is a separate organisation. The **G7** and the **G20** also hold a summit every year. In 2024 Switzerland invited countries to a summit on peace in Ukraine on the Bürgenstock.

gewusst: In 1989 Bush and Gorbachev met off Malta on the Soviet ship “Maxim Gorky”.
Yalta is in Crimea on the Black Sea.

teile.einleitung: The accompanying measures are rules with which Switzerland protects its wages and working conditions. They have applied since 2004 and go along with the free movement of persons with the EU. In German they are called “flanking” measures: they stand, as it were, at the side of the open labour markets.
wichtigste: The accompanying measures have applied since 1 June 2004.
They are meant to prevent wage and social dumping.
The Posted Workers Act obliges foreign companies to keep to minimum wage and working conditions.
