Tripartite commissions made up of the state, employers and employees monitor the labour market.
Joint commissions check collective labour agreements that have been declared generally binding.
If wage dumping happens repeatedly, a standard employment contract with minimum wages can be issued.

abschnitte.text: Switzerland has concluded the **Agreement on the Free Movement of Persons** with the EU. It allows people from the EU to work in Switzerland, and the other way round. On **1 June 2004** the **priority for local workers** was dropped. Before that, companies first had to check whether there were workers from Switzerland. Since then the **accompanying measures** have applied. They are meant to prevent the **usual wages** in Switzerland from being **undercut**. This is called **wage and social dumping**.

Some companies from abroad send their staff to Switzerland for a short time, for example for a job on a building site. This is called **posting** employees. The **Posted Workers Act** obliges these companies to keep to **minimum wage and working conditions**. Under the previous **eight-day rule**, they had to report a job **eight days in advance**. This gave the authorities time for checks. The **EU** criticised this rule as an obstacle to the free movement of services.

In sectors with a **collective labour agreement declared generally binding** (in German, GAV), **joint commissions** carry out the checks. They have equal numbers of representatives of **employers** and **employees**. In sectors without such an agreement, **tripartite commissions** monitor the labour market. Tripartite means **in three parts**: the **state, employers and employees** work together. There are such commissions at the Confederation and in the cantons.

If the commissions find **breaches**, fines or other **sanctions** can follow. If **wage dumping happens repeatedly** in a sector without a collective agreement, a **standard employment contract** with mandatory **minimum wages** can be issued. It then applies to the whole sector. In addition, under certain conditions a collective agreement can more easily be declared **generally binding**. It then applies to all companies in the sector.

The accompanying measures are important in Swiss politics. **Trade unions** see them as essential **wage protection**. In negotiations on new agreements, the **EU** asked several times for changes, for example to the reporting deadline. Many **employers** and parties are looking for a path between good wage protection and good relations with the EU. That is why how strong the protection should be is debated again and again.

gewusst: Every year tens of thousands of businesses and people in Switzerland are checked as part of the accompanying measures.
The word “flankieren” comes from French and means “to stand at the side”.

teile.einleitung: The G7 is a group of seven large industrialised countries. Their heads of state and government meet every year for a summit. There they discuss questions of the world economy and world politics.
wichtigste: G7 means “Group of Seven”.
The members are the USA, Canada, Japan, Germany, France, Italy and Great Britain.
The European Union also takes part regularly.
The first summit took place in France in 1975; Canada joined in 1976.
From 1998 to 2014 Russia also took part, and it was called the G8.
Switzerland is not a member.

abschnitte.text: The **“G”** stands for **“Group”**. So G7 means “Group of Seven”. The G7 is not an organisation with its own building or a permanent secretariat. Every year a different member country takes over the **presidency** and organises the summit.

The G7 is made up of the **USA**, **Canada**, **Japan**, **Germany**, **France**, **Italy** and **Great Britain**. Japan is the only Asian member. Large economies such as China, India, Brazil or Spain do not belong to it. The **European Union** is present at all summits, even though it is not a country. It is represented by the Presidents of the EU Commission and the European Council.

The first meeting took place in 1975 at the **Château de Rambouillet** in France, with six countries at the time. The reason was the economic problems after the **oil crisis**. In 1976 **Canada** joined, and the G6 became the G7. From 1998 to 2014 **Russia** also took part, and it was then called the **G8**. Russia has not been part of it since 2014.

**Switzerland** does not belong to the G7. But like other countries it can occasionally be invited as a **guest** to particular talks. There is also the larger **G20**, which includes countries such as China, India and Brazil. Critics think that a small group of rich countries should not discuss questions that concern the whole world. Supporters say that solutions can be found more quickly in a small group.

gewusst: At the first summit in 1975, only six countries sat at the table.
The people who prepare a summit are called “sherpas”, like the mountain guides in the Himalayas.

teile.einleitung: The Gulf Cooperation Council is an alliance of six Arab countries on the Persian Gulf. They work together on politics, the economy and security. The Council was founded in 1981.
wichtigste: The Gulf Cooperation Council has six members: Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates and Oman.
It was founded in Abu Dhabi in 1981.
Its seat, the General Secretariat, is in Riyadh, the capital of Saudi Arabia.
All the members are monarchies.
The countries have become rich mainly through oil and natural gas.
From 2017 to 2021 there was a serious dispute over Qatar.

abschnitte.text: The Council is named after the **Persian Gulf**, an arm of the sea between the Arabian Peninsula and Iran. Almost all the members have a coastline there. Saudi Arabia is by far the largest country; Bahrain is a small group of islands. **Iraq** is not a member, even though it also lies on the Gulf. Iran does not belong to it either.

All six countries are **monarchies**. They are ruled by kings, emirs or a sultan, often from families that have ruled for a long time. An emir is an Arab prince; a sultan is a ruler in the Islamic world. Oman is ruled by a sultan, Saudi Arabia and Bahrain by kings. Their similar form of government links the countries.

In 1979 the **Iranian Revolution** took place in Iran. The Gulf monarchies feared that the upheaval could spread to their countries. From 1980 there was also war between Iran and Iraq. That is why the six countries joined together in 1981. Shared **security** was an important aim from the start.

Under the Gulf states lie huge reserves of **oil** and **natural gas**. Selling them brought great wealth. The Council wants to make trade between the members easier, for example with a customs union. A shared **currency** was planned, but Oman withdrew in 2006 and the Emirates in 2009. To this day this monetary union does not exist.

In 2017 Saudi Arabia, the Emirates and Bahrain, together with Egypt, broke off relations with **Qatar**. Borders, airspace and ports were closed to Qatar. The countries accused Qatar, among other things, of being too close to Iran; Qatar rejected the accusations. In January 2021 the dispute was settled with the **al-Ula Declaration**.

gewusst: Together with the other EFTA countries, Switzerland has concluded a free trade agreement with the Gulf Cooperation Council.
Bahrain is linked directly to Saudi Arabia by a causeway across the sea.

teile.einleitung: The Secretary-General of the United Nations is the top person at the UN. This person leads the Secretariat, meaning the organisation's administration, and speaks for the UN around the world. The office is sometimes called the most difficult job in the world.
wichtigste: The UN Secretary-General is the top person at the UN and leads its Secretariat.
The term of office is normally five years, and re-election is possible.
The Security Council proposes a person, and the General Assembly appoints them.
The first Secretary-General, from 1946, was the Norwegian Trygve Lie.
Since 2017 the Portuguese António Guterres has held the office; his second term ends at the end of 2026.
So far a woman has never been Secretary-General.

abschnitte.text: The Secretary-General is at the head of the **Secretariat**, one of the main bodies of the UN. He leads tens of thousands of staff in New York, Geneva, Vienna, Nairobi and all over the world. The UN Charter calls him the organisation's chief **administrative officer**. He has no army and cannot pass laws, but he has great influence through speeches, reports and talks.

The Secretary-General may draw the **Security Council's** attention to dangers to world peace. He mediates in conflicts and offers his good offices. Every year he presents a report on the UN's work. He also draws attention to global problems such as climate change, hunger or people fleeing their homes.

First the **Security Council** recommends a candidate; each of its five permanent members can use a veto. Then the **General Assembly** appoints the person. The usual term of office is five years, often followed by a second. Traditionally the world regions take turns, which is why the office holders have come from Europe, Asia, Africa and Latin America.

Up to 2026 there have been nine Secretaries-General, all of them men. They include Trygve Lie from Norway, **Dag Hammarskjöld** from Sweden, U Thant from Myanmar, Kurt Waldheim from Austria and Kofi Annan from Ghana. They were followed by Ban Ki-moon from South Korea and **António Guterres** from Portugal, who has been in office since 2017. The successor will be decided in 2026, and the new term begins on 1 January 2027.

Dag Hammarskjöld died in a plane crash in Africa in 1961 and afterwards received the **Nobel Peace Prize**. Kofi Annan was also awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2001, together with the UN. Kofi Annan later lived in Switzerland for many years and died in Bern in 2018. Many people hope that a woman will soon be chosen for the first time.

begriffe.erklaerung: The administration of the UN with its staff.
The period during which someone holds an office.
The right to block a decision on your own.
The assembly of all UN member states, where each country has one vote.

gewusst: The five-year term of office is not in the UN Charter; it is a custom.
Kofi Annan died in Bern in 2018.
Dag Hammarskjöld is still the only person to receive the Nobel Peace Prize after his death.

tkvjtbg.t: United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees

teile.einleitung: The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees leads the UNHCR, the UN refugee agency. It protects and supports people who have had to flee war and persecution. It was founded in 1950, and its seat is in Geneva.
wichtigste: The UNHCR was founded in December 1950.
At its head is a High Commissioner for Refugees.
This person is elected by the UN General Assembly.
The R in UNHCR stands for “Refugees”.
The UNHCR received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1954 and 1981.
Every year it awards the Nansen Refugee Award.

abschnitte.text: After the **Second World War** there were millions of refugees in Europe. That is why the UN founded the **UNHCR** in December 1950. The abbreviation stands for “United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees”. The agency has its headquarters in **Geneva**. An important basis for its work is the **Geneva Refugee Convention** of 1951.

At its head is the **High Commissioner for Refugees**. This person is elected by the UN **General Assembly**. They lead the agency's work and speak for refugees around the world. They visit camps, negotiate with governments and ask countries for money and help.

The UNHCR helps people who have had to leave their country. It hands out **tents**, **blankets**, mats and cooking pots, so that families have the bare necessities. It also helps **internally displaced people**. These are people who have had to flee but have stayed in their own country. The blue **logo** shows two hands protecting a small figure.

The UNHCR has received the **Nobel Peace Prize** twice, in 1954 and 1981. Since 1954 it has itself awarded the **Nansen Refugee Award** every year. It is named after the Norwegian **Fridtjof Nansen**, a polar explorer who worked for refugees after the First World War. The award honours people who help refugees in special ways.

gewusst: Fridtjof Nansen introduced a special identity document for stateless refugees, the so-called Nansen passport.
World Refugee Day is on 20 June every year.

teile.einleitung: The Global South is a simplified term for countries that are less well off economically, often in Africa, Asia and Latin America. Its counterpart is the Global North, with rich industrialised countries such as Switzerland. The term does not exactly describe a direction on the compass but mainly economic and political differences.
wichtigste: Global South means countries that are less well off economically, mainly in Africa, Asia and Latin America.
The term is a simplification and not strictly geographical.
Australia and New Zealand lie in the south but count as part of the Global North.
In the past people often spoke of developing countries or the Third World.
Many countries of the Global South are former colonies.
Countries such as China, India and Brazil are gaining influence worldwide.

abschnitte.text: The **Global South** groups together countries that are poorer or have less power in the world economy. They include most countries in Africa and Latin America and large parts of Asia. The **Global North** includes rich countries such as the USA, the countries of Europe, Japan, Australia and New Zealand. So the term is meant politically, not exactly according to the equator.

abschnitte.titel: Where does the term come from?
abschnitte.text: People used to speak of the **Third World**, an expression from the time of the Cold War. Later the word developing countries was often used, which some people find disparaging. In 1980 the so-called Brandt Report drew a line between the rich North and the poorer South on the world map. Today many people prefer the more neutral term Global South.

Many countries of the Global South were **colonies** of European countries for a long time. The colonial powers used their raw materials and workers. Most colonies only became independent in the 20th century, many African countries around 1960. The effects, such as poverty, borders drawn without regard for peoples or one-sided economies, can still be felt in part today.

The Global South is very varied: there are very poor countries and fast-growing ones. **China**, India and Brazil are major economic powers today. In the **G77** group, more than 130 countries work together at the UN to represent their interests jointly. The group of BRICS countries also wants to strengthen the influence of the South.

Switzerland supports countries in the Global South with **development cooperation**, mainly through the SDC. Swiss aid organisations work for education, water and health. Many products in Switzerland, such as coffee, cocoa or bananas, come from countries of the South. Fair trade is meant to help the farmers there get fair prices.

begriffe.erklaerung: Economically rich countries such as Switzerland, the USA or Japan.
An area that is ruled by a foreign country.
Help and partnership so that people in poorer countries are better off.
Trade in which the producers get fair wages and prices.

gewusst: Australia lies in the Southern Hemisphere but belongs to the Global North.
The Group of 77 was founded in 1964 with 77 countries and today has more than 130 members.
A large share of the world's young people live in countries of the Global South.

teile.einleitung: A border crossing is a place where a road, a path or a railway line leads from one country into another. There it can be checked who and what is coming across the border. In Switzerland, customs is responsible for this.
wichtigste: At a border crossing you travel from one country into another.
Customs checks goods and also people.
Anyone crossing a border should always carry an identity document.
Anyone who buys more than may be brought in without charges must declare the goods.
Sniffer dogs help customs to find forbidden things.
In Italian customs is called “dogana”, in French “douane”.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland the **Federal Office for Customs and Border Security** checks the border. It checks which **goods** come into the country and also keeps an eye on people. Some goods are forbidden, for example drugs or certain weapons. For other goods you have to pay **charges**. The money goes to the Confederation.

At many border crossings there is a **customs office**. There goods are declared and charges are paid. In the past a **barrier** blocked the road, a long beam across the carriageway. It was only opened when the check was over. Today many small crossings have no staff, but customs can carry out checks at any time.

Anyone crossing a border should carry an **identity document**, meaning a **passport** or an **identity card**. With it you can show who you are. Switzerland takes part in the **Schengen Agreement**. That is why people are no longer always checked at the border with the neighbouring countries. You still need your ID, though, because a check is possible at any time.

Many people from Switzerland go shopping in a neighbouring country. Up to a certain value, you may bring in goods without paying charges. Anyone who buys more must **declare** the goods at customs and pay charges. Anyone who does not can get a **fine**. Special limits apply to meat, alcohol and tobacco.

Dogs have a very sensitive nose. Specially trained **sniffer dogs** work with customs. They can smell, for example, drugs or large amounts of cash in luggage. The dogs are trained for a long time and work closely with their handler.

gewusst: Switzerland is not in the EU customs union. That is why goods are still checked at the border, even though people travel freely.
At border crossings into Italy you see the word “Dogana”, and into France “Douane”.

teile.einleitung: The International Olympic Committee, IOC for short, is the organisation that runs the Olympic Games. It has its seat in Lausanne on Lake Geneva. That is why Lausanne is also called the Olympic capital.
wichtigste: The IOC has its seat in Lausanne.
It was founded in Paris in 1894 on the initiative of Pierre de Coubertin.
Lausanne has been the seat of the IOC since 1915.
The IOC awards the Olympic Games to host cities.
It is a private organisation, not a government organisation.
Since 2025 Kirsty Coventry from Zimbabwe has been President of the IOC.
The Olympic Museum is in Lausanne.

abschnitte.text: The **International Olympic Committee** is the highest authority of the Olympic movement. It decides which city may hold the Games and which sports are Olympic. It is a private organisation registered as an association under Swiss law. Its members are not sent by governments but elected by the IOC itself. They include former athletes and sports officials.

The Frenchman **Pierre de Coubertin** wanted to revive the Olympic Games of the ancient Greeks. In 1894 the IOC was founded in Paris. As early as 1896 the first Olympic Games of modern times took place in Athens. During the First World War, in 1915, Coubertin moved the seat to Lausanne in neutral Switzerland. He himself is buried in Lausanne, but his heart is in Olympia in Greece.

The IOC organises the Summer and Winter Olympic Games together with the host cities. It sells the television rights and looks for sponsors. With this money it supports sports federations and athletes all over the world. It also fights against **doping** together with other bodies. Since 2010 there have also been Youth Olympic Games for young athletes.

Since 2019 the **Olympic House**, the IOC's new headquarters, has stood in Lausanne. On the lakeshore at Ouchy is the Olympic Museum, which opened in 1993. In addition, more than 50 international sports federations have their seat in the region. In 2020 the Winter Youth Olympic Games took place in Lausanne. Switzerland hosted the Winter Olympic Games in St Moritz in 1928 and 1948.

The IOC is sometimes criticised, for example because of the high costs for host cities. Awarding the Games to countries where human rights are violated also causes debate. In the past there were cases of bribery when the Games were awarded. The IOC responded with new rules. Today the Games are meant to become cheaper and more sustainable.

begriffe.erklaerung: The largest sports festival in the world, held every four years in summer and in winter.
Forbidden substances with which athletes try to improve their performance.
The city where the Games take place.
Five linked rings that stand for the continents and the friendship of the world.

gewusst: Kirsty Coventry is the first woman and the first person from Africa to head the IOC.
The Olympic Museum in Lausanne displays torches from all the Olympic Games of modern times.

teile.einleitung: The Capitol is the large white building with the dome in Washington, D.C. The Parliament of the United States works here. It is one of the best-known buildings in the world.
wichtigste: The Capitol stands in the capital, Washington, D.C.
Congress, the Parliament of the USA, meets in the Capitol.
It stands on a hill, Capitol Hill.
George Washington laid the foundation stone in 1793.
In 1814 British soldiers set fire to the building.
Today's dome is made of cast iron and painted white.
At the very top stands the “Statue of Freedom”.

abschnitte.text: **Congress** meets in the Capitol. It is made up of two chambers: the **Senate** and the **House of Representatives**. Each chamber has its own wing in the building. The laws of the USA are debated and passed here. This is similar to the Federal Palace in Bern, where the National Council and the Council of States meet.

The first president, **George Washington**, laid the foundation stone in **1793**. During the **War of 1812**, British troops attacked the city of Washington. In **1814** they set fire to the Capitol, and it was badly damaged. Afterwards it was rebuilt. Later it was enlarged several times.

Today's large **dome** was built from 1855 and finished around **1866**. It is made of **cast iron** and painted white. That is why it looks like stone. Under the dome is a round hall, the **Rotunda**. Large paintings from the history of the USA hang there.

Since **1863** the **“Statue of Freedom”** has stood at the very top of the dome. It shows a woman who stands for **freedom**. She wears a helmet and carries a sword and a shield. The figure is made of bronze. It must not be confused with the Statue of Liberty in New York.

The Capitol stands on a small hill at the end of a long park, the **National Mall**. The hill is named after the building: **Capitol Hill**. People often simply say “Capitol Hill” when they mean Congress. At the other end of the Mall stands the Lincoln Memorial.

gewusst: In the centre of Washington, buildings may only reach a certain height, which is why the Capitol stays clearly visible.
The new president is traditionally sworn in on the west side of the Capitol.

teile.einleitung: Helvetas is a Swiss organisation for development cooperation. It helps people in poor countries to improve their lives through their own efforts. It was founded in Zurich in 1955.
wichtigste: Helvetas was founded in Zurich on 18 June 1955.
Its first name was the Swiss Aid Organisation for Regions outside Europe, SHAG for short.
In 2011 Helvetas merged with Intercooperation.
Helvetas works in about 30 countries.
The principle of “helping people to help themselves” is important.
In Nepal, Helvetas is known for building suspension bridges.

abschnitte.text: Helvetas was founded in **Zurich** on **18 June 1955**. It is seen as Switzerland's first private organisation for **development cooperation**. At first it was called the **Swiss Aid Organisation for Regions outside Europe** (in German, SHAG). In 2011 it merged with the organisation **Intercooperation**. Since then it has been called **Helvetas Swiss Intercooperation**. Its head office is still in Zurich today.

Helvetas does not just want to give people things. They should be able to improve their living conditions **themselves**. That is why Helvetas works closely with **local experts** and communities. They have a say in what is built or learnt. This is called **helping people to help themselves**. This way the effect lasts even when a project has ended.

In **Nepal**, Helvetas has helped to build **suspension bridges** for decades. By now there are thousands of them. They save people in the mountains long and dangerous detours to schools, markets and hospitals. Another core topic is clean **drinking water**, for example through pipes and wells. Helvetas also works for food, education and income.

Helvetas works in about **30 countries** in Africa, Asia, Latin America and Eastern Europe. It is organised as an **association** and is independent of politics and religion. It is supported by about 100,000 members and donors. There are also volunteer **regional groups** in Switzerland, which organise events and provide information.

In its **Fairshop**, Helvetas sells **fairly produced** goods from partner countries. They include clothes, food and handicrafts. **Fair trade** means that the people who make something get a fair price and work in good conditions. So shopping in Switzerland can make a difference.

gewusst: The suspension bridges in Nepal shorten some journeys from several hours to a few minutes.
Helvetas was founded only ten years after the end of the Second World War.

teile.einleitung: The International Organization for Migration, **IOM** for short, looks after people around the world who leave their homes. It has its headquarters in Geneva and since 2016 has been part of the UN system as a related organisation.
wichtigste: The IOM's forerunner was founded in Brussels in 1951.
The headquarters is in Geneva, more exactly in Grand-Saconnex.
Since 2016 the IOM has been a related organisation of the UN.
Amy Pope has led the IOM since October 2023, as the first woman to do so (as of 2025).
The IOM works in more than 100 countries.
Every two years it publishes the World Migration Report.

abschnitte.text: After the Second World War, many people in Europe had been uprooted. In 1951 a provisional committee was set up in **Brussels** to help resettle migrants from war-torn Europe. The IOM later grew out of it. At the UN summit for refugees and migrants in 2016, the UN and the IOM signed an agreement. Since then the IOM has been part of the UN system as a **related organisation**.

The IOM's headquarters is in **Geneva**, in the municipality of Grand-Saconnex. Geneva is the seat of many international organisations. Since October 2023 the American **Amy Pope** has led the IOM as the first woman at its head (as of 2025). Do not confuse it: the UN refugee agency **UNHCR** is a different organisation.

The IOM collects a lot of data, so that help can be planned better. With the **Displacement Tracking Matrix** (DTM) it counts and describes people who have been driven from their homes within their own country. Since 2014 the **Missing Migrants Project** has recorded people who die or disappear on migration routes, for example in the Mediterranean. Every two years the **World Migration Report**, with figures and trends, is also published.

In December 2018 the **Global Compact for Safe, Orderly and Regular Migration** was adopted in Marrakesh. It is not legally binding and describes shared goals. The IOM gives it special support. At the time Switzerland did not agree to it, because the Federal Council first wanted to involve Parliament. Whether to join it was a controversial topic in Switzerland.

gewusst: The IOM had existed for more than 60 years before it became part of the UN system.
The “Global Trends” report does not come from the IOM but from the UNHCR.

to8ouzh.t: Prohibition of the use of force

teile.einleitung: The prohibition of the use of force is one of the most important rules of international law. It forbids countries to use force against other countries or to threaten to do so. It is in the Charter of the United Nations and also counts as customary law.
wichtigste: The prohibition of the use of force is in Article 2(4) of the UN Charter.
Not only the use of force is forbidden, but also the threat of force.
The exceptions are self-defence and authorisation by the Security Council.
A forerunner was the Kellogg-Briand Pact of 1928.
Resolution 3314 of 1974 defines the term aggression.
In 1986, in the case Nicaragua v. United States, the ICJ confirmed that the prohibition is customary law.

abschnitte.text: For a long time war was seen as a permitted tool of politics. An early step was the **Drago-Porter Convention** of 1907, one of the Hague Conventions. It banned the use of force to collect national debts, as long as the debtor country accepted arbitration. In 1928 the **Kellogg-Briand Pact** outlawed war as a tool of national policy. But it contained no penalties for breaches.

The **UN Charter** of 1945 contains the comprehensive **prohibition of the use of force** in Article 2(4). It forbids any **threat** or **use of force** against the territorial integrity or political independence of a state. So even an ultimatum with a threat of war is forbidden. According to the prevailing view, economic pressure does not fall under the prohibition.

The Charter allows force in only two cases. First, for **self-defence** under Article 51, when a country is attacked. Second, with **authorisation by the Security Council** under Chapter VII. **Humanitarian intervention** without a mandate, meaning stepping in to protect people, is disputed. If a lawful government invites foreign troops in, this is called **intervention by invitation**, which according to the predominant view is allowed.

**Resolution 3314** of the UN General Assembly of 1974 defines **aggression**, meaning an attack. It gives examples such as invasion, bombing or blockading ports. In 1986 the **International Court of Justice** confirmed in the case **Nicaragua v. United States** that the prohibition of the use of force also counts as **customary law**. In 2010 countries agreed in **Kampala** (Uganda) on a definition of the crime of aggression in the Rome Statute. Since 2018 the International Criminal Court has been able to prosecute this crime.

gewusst: Customary law arises when countries follow a rule for a long time and regard it as binding.
Because of this, the prohibition of the use of force also applies to countries that are not members of the UN.

teile.einleitung: Globalisation means the worldwide linking of economies, politics and cultures. Goods, money, information and people move across borders faster and more often today than ever before. Your T-shirt, your mobile phone or your chocolate have often already travelled halfway round the world.
wichtigste: Globalisation is the worldwide linking of economies, politics and cultures.
Container ships, aeroplanes and the internet have greatly speeded it up.
Since 1995 the World Trade Organization WTO has governed world trade.
Many products are made in several countries.
Switzerland earns a large part of its prosperity from exports.
Globalisation brings opportunities but also problems such as pollution and inequality.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from **global**, meaning worldwide. Globalisation describes how countries and people are becoming more and more closely connected. This concerns trade, but also music, films, food, sport and politics. As a result, what happens in one country can quickly have effects in many other countries.

There was worldwide trade even in the past, for example on the **Silk Road** between China and Europe. After 1492 the voyages of discovery linked Europe with America. A big boost came from 1956 with the standardised **container**, which made it cheap to ship goods. Since the 1990s the internet and cheap flights have speeded up these links even more.

A smartphone contains raw materials from Africa, is assembled in Asia and designed in California. Bananas come from Central America, and the cocoa for Swiss chocolate from West Africa. On the internet you can write to people on other continents in seconds. Fast-food chains and worldwide streaming services are also signs of **globalisation**.

Switzerland is a small country with few raw materials and lives to a great extent from **foreign trade**. It exports medicines, machines, watches and food all over the world. Large Swiss companies such as Nestlé, Novartis or Roche operate worldwide. The many international organisations in Geneva show how connected Switzerland is.

Thanks to globalisation, many goods have become cheaper, and in countries such as China millions of people have escaped poverty. At the same time, long transport routes produce a lot of **CO2**. In some countries people work for very low wages. Crises such as the financial crisis of 2008 or the COVID-19 pandemic showed how quickly problems can spread around the world.

begriffe.erklaerung: Selling goods abroad.
Buying goods from abroad.
A standardised metal box for transporting goods.
The World Trade Organization, based in Geneva, which sets rules for trade.

gewusst: The largest container ships can carry more than 20,000 containers at once.
The World Trade Organization WTO has its seat in Geneva.
More than 2,000 years ago Chinese silk was already being traded as far as Rome.

teile.einleitung: In June 2024 a large summit on peace in Ukraine took place on the Bürgenstock in Central Switzerland. Switzerland was the host. Representatives from around 90 countries looked for a path towards a peace process.
wichtigste: The summit took place on 15 and 16 June 2024.
It was about the war in Ukraine.
The host was the President of the Confederation, Viola Amherd.
92 countries and 8 international organisations took part.
Russia was not invited, and China stayed away.
The communiqué dealt with nuclear safety, food security and the release of prisoners.

abschnitte.text: The **Bürgenstock** is a mountain ridge above **Lake Lucerne**. A large hotel resort stands there. It is in the canton of **Nidwalden**; most of the Bürgenstock belongs to the municipality of Ennetbürgen. The place is easy to seal off and was therefore suitable for a meeting with many heads of state.

Since February 2022 Russia has been waging war against **Ukraine**. Ukraine asked Switzerland to organise a summit. **The President of the Confederation, Viola Amherd**, sent out the invitations. The aim was to find a path towards a later **peace process**. A peace treaty was never planned from the start.

According to the figures, **92 countries** and **8 international organisations** took part, around 100 delegations in all. **Russia** was not invited for this phase. But Switzerland stressed that Russia would have to be included in a later peace process. **China** did not take part and criticised the fact that the two sides in the war were not both at the table.

At the end there was a joint **communiqué**, meaning a written statement. It dealt with three topics: **nuclear safety**, **food security** and the release of prisoners and people who had been taken away. Not all the participants signed the statement. Experts judged the meeting in different ways: some saw a first step, while others missed Russia's involvement.

gewusst: For the summit, the airspace above the Bürgenstock was strictly restricted, and the army helped with security.
The hotel on the Bürgenstock had welcomed famous guests from all over the world before.

teile.einleitung: Frontex is the European Union's Border and Coast Guard Agency. It supports the countries of the Schengen Area in protecting their external borders. Switzerland also takes part, even though it does not belong to the EU.
wichtigste: Frontex was founded by an EU regulation in 2004 and began work in 2005.
Switzerland takes part because it is linked to the Schengen Area.
On 15 May 2022 Swiss voters approved the expansion of Frontex with about 71.5 per cent yes.
By 2027 a standing reserve of about 10,000 officers is to be created.
Through Eurosur the countries have exchanged situation pictures since 2013.
A Fundamental Rights Officer monitors whether fundamental rights are respected.

abschnitte.text: **Frontex** helps the countries of the **Schengen Area** to monitor their shared external borders. Within this area there are usually no checks on people at the borders. That is why protecting the external borders is important. Frontex was founded in 2004 and began work in 2005. After 2015, when a very large number of people fled to Europe, its tasks and resources were greatly expanded.

Through the **Eurosur** system, Frontex and the Schengen countries have exchanged **situation pictures** since 2013, including satellite and aerial images. In the Mediterranean, Frontex supports joint operations: **Themis** off Italy, **Poseidon** in Greece and **Indalo** in Spain. The regulation of 2019 provides for a **standing corps**, which is to grow to about 10,000 officers by 2027.

Switzerland is not an EU member, but it is **associated with Schengen**. That is why it adopts developments of Schengen law, including on Frontex. It provides **staff and money** and has a limited right to vote on the management board. A **referendum** was called against the expansion. On 15 May 2022 the people clearly approved the proposal, with about 71.5 per cent yes.

Frontex has been criticised again and again. Among other things it has been accused of **pushbacks**, meaning illegally turning back people seeking protection. The European Anti-Fraud Office **OLAF** investigated the accusations. In April 2022 Director **Fabrice Leggeri** resigned. Since then the post of **Fundamental Rights Officer** has been strengthened; this officer reviews operations and deals with complaints. Supporters see Frontex as necessary protection of the borders; critics call for more respect for human rights.

gewusst: Frontex's headquarters is in Warsaw in Poland.
Eurodac is something different from Eurosur: a fingerprint database for asylum seekers.

teile.einleitung: The guillotine clause links the seven agreements of the Bilaterals I between Switzerland and the EU. If one of them is terminated, all the others fall away too. That is why it is very important in Swiss European policy.
wichtigste: The guillotine clause applies to the seven agreements of the Bilaterals I.
Switzerland or the EU can trigger it by terminating one agreement.
Six months after the termination, the other agreements also cease to apply.
In this way the EU wanted to tie the free movement of persons firmly to market access.
The free trade agreement of 1972 is not affected.
In the Bilaterals II, Schengen and Dublin are linked to each other in a similar way.

abschnitte.text: After the no to the EEA in 1992, Switzerland negotiated individual treaties with the EU. The **Bilaterals I** include seven agreements: free movement of persons, technical barriers to trade, public procurement, agriculture, land transport, air transport and research. The people approved them in May 2000. They have been in force since 2002.

Each party, meaning Switzerland or the EU, can **terminate** an agreement. Then the other six agreements automatically cease to apply **six months** after the notice is received. This period leaves little time for new negotiations. So you cannot keep just some parts and give up others.

The EU wanted to prevent Switzerland from keeping only the agreements that were good for it. In particular, the **free movement of persons** was to be firmly tied to **market access**. The name comes from the **guillotine**, a falling blade for executions that was often used in the French Revolution. The image shows that everything falls away with a single stroke.

The **free trade agreement** of 1972 for industrial goods is not tied to the Bilaterals I. It would remain in place even if one were terminated. In the **Bilaterals II**, the agreements on **Schengen** and **Dublin** are linked to each other: if one ends, the other ends too. The other agreements of the Bilaterals II stand on their own.

In 2020 Switzerland voted on the **limitation initiative**. It demanded an end to the free movement of persons with the EU. Because of the guillotine clause, the other agreements would also have fallen away, for example the one on **air transport**. Supporters wanted to control immigration themselves; opponents warned of disadvantages for the economy. The people rejected the initiative.

gewusst: The guillotine clause has never been triggered.
The term is not the official name in the treaty but an image that has become established in politics.

teile.einleitung: The International Criminal Court, ICC for short, is a court for the most serious crimes under international law, with its seat in The Hague. Unlike the International Court of Justice, which settles disputes between countries, the ICC convicts individual people. It is meant to make sure that nobody goes unpunished for terrible crimes.
wichtigste: The ICC prosecutes genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and the crime of aggression.
It has its seat in The Hague in the Netherlands.
The ICJ settles disputes between countries; the ICC convicts individual people.
Its basis is the Rome Statute of 1998.
The court has been working since 1 July 2002.
More than 120 countries have recognised the Statute, including Switzerland.
Large countries such as the USA, Russia and China are not members.

abschnitte.text: The **International Criminal Court** is a permanent court that punishes people for the worst crimes. Heads of state, generals or leaders of armed groups can also be charged. It is not a UN institution, but it works with the UN. Its seat is in a modern building in The Hague. There are courtrooms there and a prison for the accused.

Even after the Second World War there were trials of war criminals in Nuremberg and Tokyo. In the 1990s the UN created special courts for the former Yugoslavia and for Rwanda. After that, many countries wanted a permanent court. In 1998 in Rome they adopted the **Rome Statute**. It came into force on 1 July 2002.

The ICC is responsible for four groups of crimes. **Genocide** means intending to destroy an ethnic group in whole or in part. Crimes against humanity are serious attacks on large numbers of civilians. War crimes are serious breaches of the rules of war, for example attacks on hospitals. Then there is the crime of aggression, meaning a forbidden war of aggression.

A prosecution office investigates and collects evidence. Then the 18 judges decide whether someone is guilty. The ICC only steps in when a country does not want to or cannot investigate itself. This is called the principle of **complementarity**. Because the court has no police of its own, it depends on countries arresting suspects and handing them over.

Switzerland signed the Rome Statute and ratified it in 2001. It supports the court politically and financially. Switzerland works to make sure that international humanitarian law is kept. Through the Geneva Conventions, this law has a close link to Switzerland. Swiss courts can also prosecute certain crimes under international law themselves.

begriffe.erklaerung: A crime with the aim of wiping out a whole ethnic group.
Serious breaches of the rules that apply even in war.
The treaty of 1998 with which the International Criminal Court was founded.
A court order to arrest a person.

gewusst: The ICC can only punish acts committed after 1 July 2002.
Even serving heads of state can be charged by the ICC.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland has a long tradition of humanitarian aid. The Red Cross was founded in Geneva, and today the Confederation helps all over the world after disasters and in wars. The SDC is mainly responsible.
wichtigste: Within the FDFA, the SDC is responsible for Switzerland's humanitarian aid.
Henry Dunant from Geneva is seen as the founder of the Red Cross movement.
The Battle of Solferino in 1859 gave him the idea.
The Red Cross emblem is the Swiss flag with the colours reversed.
Switzerland is the depositary state of the Geneva Conventions.
The Swiss Rescue team searches for people buried after earthquakes.

abschnitte.text: The **SDC** is the **Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation**. It belongs to the Federal Department of Foreign Affairs (FDFA). The SDC leads the Confederation's **humanitarian aid** and development cooperation. In disasters it sends experts, equipment and money. Many of the experts belong to the **Swiss Humanitarian Aid Unit**.

In 1859 the Genevan **Henry Dunant** witnessed the **Battle of Solferino** in northern Italy. Thousands of wounded men lay on the battlefield without help. He wrote the book **“A Memory of Solferino”** about it. This led to the **Red Cross**. In honour of Switzerland, a red cross on a white background was chosen, meaning the Swiss flag with the colours reversed. In 1901 Dunant received the first **Nobel Peace Prize**, together with Frédéric Passy.

The **Geneva Conventions** protect the wounded, prisoners and civilians in war. Switzerland is their **depositary state**. This means that it keeps the originals of the treaties. It receives the accession of new countries and can call conferences of the states. This gives Switzerland a special role in international humanitarian law.

**Swiss Rescue** (the Rettungskette Schweiz) is made up of experts and **search dogs**. After severe **earthquakes** it flies abroad to locate and rescue people buried under rubble. **Swiss Solidarity** (the Glückskette) was founded in 1946. This foundation collects **donations** after disasters at home and abroad. It works with Swiss aid organisations to do so.

In winter 1871, during the Franco-Prussian War, about 87,000 French soldiers under General **Bourbaki** fled into Switzerland. They were exhausted, hungry and freezing. Switzerland **disarmed** them, **interned** them and looked after them in many municipalities. The population helped with food and shelter. In Lucerne the **Bourbaki Panorama** recalls this event.

gewusst: The International Committee of the Red Cross was founded in Geneva in 1863.
The Bourbaki Panorama in Lucerne is a huge circular painting more than 100 metres long.

teile.einleitung: The Hague Conventions are international treaties that were agreed in The Hague. The Fifth Hague Convention of 1907 is especially important. It lays down what rights and duties neutral countries have in war on land.
wichtigste: In 1907 the Second Hague Peace Conference adopted the Fifth Hague Convention on neutrality in war on land.
The impulse for the conference came from US President Theodore Roosevelt in 1904.
The territory of neutral countries is inviolable.
Parties to a war may not move troops through neutral territory.
A neutral country may not supply parties to a war with weapons from its own stocks.
The Convention is still the core of the law of neutrality today.

abschnitte.text: In 1904 US President **Theodore Roosevelt** proposed a second peace conference. Because of the **Russo-Japanese War**, it only took place in 1907 in The Hague. Several conventions were adopted there. The **Fifth Hague Convention** governs the rights and duties of neutral powers in war on land. To this day it is the core of the **law of neutrality**, including for Switzerland.

abschnitte.titel: What parties to a war may not do
abschnitte.text: The territory of a neutral country is **inviolable**. Countries at war may not move troops or convoys of ammunition or supplies through it. They may not set up **radio or telegraph stations** there to stay in contact with their troops. It is also forbidden to form troops or **recruit fighters** on neutral territory.

A neutral country may not supply parties to a war, directly or indirectly, with **war material** from its own stocks. It must treat all parties to the war equally. If individual people cross the border on their own initiative to join a party to the war, the neutral country is **not responsible** for this. Only organised forming of troops and recruitment are forbidden.

A neutral country may allow **the wounded and sick** to be transported through its territory. But the trains may carry neither soldiers nor war material. **Prisoners of war** who escape onto neutral territory are free. But the neutral country can assign them a place to stay. Humanitarian aid is always allowed.

gewusst: Representatives of 44 countries took part in the conference of 1907.
Switzerland still bases its neutrality on the Fifth Hague Convention of 1907.

teile.einleitung: The Jet d'Eau is a huge jet of water in Lake Geneva. It is Geneva's best-known landmark and shoots water about 140 metres into the air.
wichtigste: The Jet d'Eau is in Lake Geneva, where the Rhône flows out of the lake.
It shoots water about 140 metres high.
It pumps about 500 litres of water per second.
The water shoots out of the nozzle at about 200 km/h.
Since 1951 it has taken its water directly from the lake.
It is switched off in frost or strong wind.

abschnitte.text: The first Jet d'Eau, in 1886, was not created as decoration. It was a **safety valve** for a network of water pipes that supplied factories with pressurised water. When the machines were switched off in the evening, the pressure was too high, and the extra water shot into the air. People found it so beautiful that the jet was later moved to a better place in the lake and made higher.

Today's Jet d'Eau has existed since 1951. It pumps water directly from **Lake Geneva**, and the water falls back into the lake. That is about **500 litres** per second, roughly three full bathtubs. The water leaves the nozzle at about **200 kilometres per hour**, faster than a car on the motorway. At any moment there are about **7,000 litres** of water in the air.

The jet reaches a height of about **140 metres**. That is higher than a church tower. You can see the Jet d'Eau from far away, even from an aeroplane. It stands where the **Rhône** flows out of Lake Geneva and is part of the picture of the city of **Geneva**.

At night the Jet d'Eau is usually lit up **white**. On special days it also shines in other colours, for example to draw attention to a cause. In **frost** or **strong wind** it is switched off. Otherwise the water would freeze or soak people walking along the shore.

gewusst: The first Jet d'Eau of 1886 was much lower than today's jet.
The Jet d'Eau began as a technical stopgap and became the landmark of a whole city.

teile.einleitung: The term International Geneva means that a particularly large number of international organisations have their seat in the Swiss city of Geneva. Diplomats from all over the world meet here. Geneva is seen as one of the most important places for peace, human rights and cooperation.
wichtigste: A particularly large number of international organisations have their seat in Geneva.
The Geneva tradition means that Geneva is a neutral place of negotiation for conferences and organisations.
The Palais des Nations houses the European seat of the UN.
The WHO, the WTO and the ICRC also have their headquarters in Geneva.
About 180 countries have a representation in Geneva.
The League of Nations, the UN's predecessor, had its seat in Geneva from 1920.
The Geneva Conventions protect people in war.

abschnitte.text: **International Geneva** is the whole of all the international organisations, embassies and aid organisations in Geneva. It includes about 40 international organisations and several hundred non-governmental organisations. Tens of thousands of people work for them there. Thousands of conferences and meetings take place every year. This makes Geneva the most important centre of the UN after New York.

As early as 1863 the Red Cross was founded in Geneva, followed in 1864 by the first **Geneva Convention**. In 1872 an arbitration tribunal in Geneva settled a dispute between the USA and Great Britain, the so-called Alabama case. In 1920 Geneva became the seat of the League of Nations. The large Palais des Nations was built for it. This long history is called the Geneva tradition of diplomacy.

Today the United Nations Office at Geneva works in the Palais des Nations. The **World Health Organization** WHO looks after health around the world. The World Trade Organization WTO governs trade. The UN refugee agency UNHCR, the International Labour Organization and the International Telecommunication Union are also here. The UN Human Rights Council meets in Geneva too.

Because Switzerland is neutral, countries that are hostile to each other often meet in Geneva. In 1985 US President Ronald Reagan and the Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev met here. Many talks about Syria, Iran or Yemen have also taken place in Geneva. Switzerland offers its **good offices**. It provides rooms, security and sometimes mediators.

In front of the Palais des Nations stands the **Broken Chair**, a giant chair with a broken leg. It is a reminder of the victims of landmines. Peacocks roam freely in the park of the Palais. The International Red Cross and Red Crescent Museum shows the history of humanitarian aid. On guided tours you can also visit the inside of the Palais.

begriffe.erklaerung: The art of finding solutions between countries through talks and negotiations.
A country does not take sides in conflicts.
Switzerland's help so that parties to a conflict can talk to each other.
The organisation that came before the UN, founded after the First World War.

gewusst: The Broken Chair is about 12 metres high and was designed by the artist Daniel Berset.
The Palais des Nations is one of the largest building complexes in Europe.

teile.einleitung: The Hague Regulations on Land Warfare contain rules on how war on land may be fought. They are the annex to the Fourth Hague Convention of 1907. Their aim is to limit suffering in war and to protect the civilian population.
wichtigste: The Hague Regulations are the annex to the Fourth Hague Convention of 18 October 1907.
A first version came from the Hague Peace Conference of 1899.
This conference went back to the Russian Tsar Nicholas II.
In war, not every means is allowed.
Pillage and attacks on undefended places are forbidden.
Since the Nuremberg judgment of 1946, the Hague Regulations have counted as customary international law.

abschnitte.text: In 1898 the Russian Tsar **Nicholas II** called a conference on disarmament and peace. It took place in **The Hague** in 1899 and adopted a first version of the regulations on land warfare. In 1907 they were revised and adopted as the **annex to the Fourth Hague Convention**. They govern the “laws and customs of war on land”.

Article 22 sets out an important principle: those waging war do **not have an unlimited right** to choose the means of harming the enemy. Many later **bans on weapons** grew out of this. The preamble also contains the **Martens Clause**. It was proposed by the Russian delegate Friedrich Martens. Where rules are missing, the laws of humanity and the dictates of public conscience apply.

Article 1 lays down when militias and volunteer corps count as **belligerents**. They need a commander who is responsible and a fixed **emblem** that can be recognised from a distance. They must carry their weapons openly and keep to the laws of war. This is meant to make combatants distinguishable from **civilians**. Captured combatants must be treated humanely.

Article 25 forbids attacking or bombarding **undefended** towns, villages and buildings. This is an early form of protection for the civilian population. According to Article 42, an area counts as **occupied** when it is actually under the authority of the hostile army. Even then, **private property** is protected. Article 47 says it short and clear: **pillage** is expressly forbidden.

After the Second World War, the **International Military Tribunal at Nuremberg** stated in 1946 that the rules of the Hague Regulations had been recognised by all civilised nations by 1939. This means they count as **customary international law**, even for countries that never signed the treaty. Many ideas from the Hague Regulations are found again later in the **Geneva Conventions**.

gewusst: The Martens Clause was later also taken into the Geneva Conventions.
Article 47 of the Hague Regulations consists of just one short sentence.

teile.einleitung: The International Health Regulations, **IHR** for short, are rules of the World Health Organization WHO. They are meant to prevent dangerous diseases from spreading across borders. They are legally binding on the states that are party to them.
wichtigste: Today's regulations were adopted in 2005 and came into force on 15 June 2007.
The Director-General of the WHO can declare a “public health emergency of international concern”.
This happened for the first time in 2009 with swine flu, H1N1.
COVID-19 was declared an emergency on 30 January 2020.
In Switzerland the Federal Office of Public Health is the national focal point.
In 2024 the new level of “pandemic emergency” was adopted.

abschnitte.text: There were international health rules before. In the end, the regulations of 1969 covered only three diseases that had to be reported: **cholera, plague and yellow fever**. In 2005 the **World Health Assembly** adopted a major revision. Since they came into force on 15 June 2007, they have applied to all events that could endanger public health internationally.

Every state party must have a **national focal point** that can be reached round the clock. In Switzerland the **Federal Office of Public Health** (FOPH) takes on this task and exchanges reports with the WHO. A country assesses an event using a decision tool. If it could be an international emergency, the country must report it to the WHO within **24 hours** of this assessment.

The highest warning is called a **public health emergency of international concern**, PHEIC for short. It is declared by the **Director-General of the WHO** after hearing an emergency committee of experts. The declaration comes with recommendations to the countries. The first time this happened was in 2009, with the new influenza A/H1N1, **swine flu**. For **COVID-19**, the emergency was declared on 30 January 2020; on 11 March 2020 the Director-General also spoke of a pandemic.

After the experience with COVID-19, the World Health Assembly adopted changes in 2024. There is now the level of **pandemic emergency** as the highest category. The changes came into force for most state parties in September 2025. In Switzerland the changes were also debated publicly.

gewusst: SARS in 2003 was one of the diseases that led to the revision of the regulations, but it did not yet fall under the new rules.
The health regulations require a focal point to be reachable day and night, including at weekends.

teile.einleitung: The Headquarters of the United Nations is the most important seat of the UN. It stands in New York, right on the bank of the East River in Manhattan. Here representatives of almost all the countries in the world meet to talk about war, peace and shared problems.
wichtigste: The UN Headquarters stands in New York.
It is in the borough of Manhattan on the East River.
The complex of buildings was built between 1949 and 1952.
The site was bought with money from the businessman John D. Rockefeller Jr. and given to the UN.
The General Assembly and the Security Council meet at the Headquarters.
The flags of the member states fly in front of the building.
There are other large UN seats in Geneva, Vienna and Nairobi.

abschnitte.text: The Headquarters lies on the east side of **Manhattan**, the best-known borough of **New York**. The site borders directly on the East River. There used to be slaughterhouses and factories there. In 1946 the businessman John D. Rockefeller Jr. donated about 8.5 million dollars so that the UN could buy the site.

The Headquarters was built from 1949 to 1952. An international team of architects planned it together, led by the American **Wallace Harrison**. The famous architect **Le Corbusier**, who was born in Switzerland, and the Brazilian Oscar Niemeyer also worked on it. The most striking building is the narrow, tall Secretariat building, with 39 storeys and a large glass front.

The **General Assembly**, in which each member country has one vote, meets in the great hall. The **Security Council**, which decides on questions of war and peace, meets in a chamber of its own. Thousands of staff work in the Secretariat, led by the Secretary-General. Every September many heads of state and government travel to New York to speak to the General Assembly.

Legally the site still belongs to the USA, but under an **agreement** it is administered by the UN. The city's police and authorities may only enter it with the UN's permission. The UN has its own post office there and issues its own stamps. Visitors can see the Headquarters on guided tours.

Many countries have given works of art to the Headquarters. The Security Council chamber was a gift from Norway and has a large mural. In front of the building stands the sculpture **Non-Violence**, a revolver with a knotted barrel, which Luxembourg gave in 1988. It is a well-known symbol of peace and against violence.

Switzerland only joined the UN in 2002, after a **popular vote**. Since then it has had its own representation in New York, the Mission of Switzerland. But much closer is the UN office in **Geneva** in the Palais des Nations, the organisation's second most important seat. In 2023 and 2024 Switzerland sat on the Security Council for the first time, as a non-permanent member.

begriffe.erklaerung: The most important seat of an organisation, from which it is run.
The assembly of all UN member states, in which each country has one vote.
The UN body with 15 members that deals with peace and security.
The administration of the UN, which does the day-to-day work.

gewusst: Before the Headquarters was finished, the UN met for some years on a temporary basis at Lake Success near New York.
The UN post office in New York issues its own stamps, which can only be posted on the site.
Le Corbusier, who was born in La Chaux-de-Fonds, was one of the architects who helped to design the building.

teile.einleitung: India is a large country in South Asia and one of the most populous countries in the world. Because so many people there are allowed to vote, India is called the largest democracy in the world.
wichtigste: The capital of India is New Delhi.
India is seen as the largest democracy in the world.
In the 2024 election almost a billion people were allowed to vote.
Voting is done on electronic voting machines.
The elected parliament is called the Lok Sabha, “House of the People”.
Mahatma Gandhi fought without violence for India's independence.

abschnitte.text: India lies in South Asia, between the Himalayas in the north and the Indian Ocean in the south. The capital is **New Delhi**, where Parliament and the government sit. **Mumbai** is a huge business city, but it is not the capital. Many different languages are spoken in India, and people of many religions live together.

For a long time India was a British colony. **Mahatma Gandhi** wanted to achieve freedom without violence, for example with peaceful protests and boycotts. He became famous around the world for this. In 1947 India became independent. Since then India has been a republic with elected parliaments.

abschnitte.titel: The largest election in the world
abschnitte.text: In the 2024 parliamentary election, almost a billion people were allowed to vote. Because there are so many, voting takes place in several **phases**. In 2024 the election lasted from April to early June, about six weeks. People vote on **electronic voting machines** and press a button next to a party's symbol. The symbols also help people who cannot read well.
After voting, voters get an **ink mark** on their finger. This ink does not come off for days. This way nobody can vote a second time. Many people proudly show their finger in photos afterwards.

The parliament elected by the people is called the **Lok Sabha**, meaning “House of the People”. The party or group with a majority provides the **Prime Minister**, who leads the government. There is also a second chamber, the Rajya Sabha, whose members are mainly chosen by the states. Like Switzerland, India is a federal state with many member states.

gewusst: In the 2024 election, more people were allowed to vote in India than the whole of Europe has inhabitants.
To make sure that really everyone can vote, a polling station has even been set up in a forest in India for a single voter.

teile.einleitung: A refugee camp is a place where people who have had to flee their homes can live for a while. Often they are large tent cities or settlements of simple huts. But some camps have existed for so long that children are born and grow up there.
wichtigste: A refugee camp is a place where people who have fled live for a while.
Camps are usually set up near crisis areas, often in neighbouring countries.
Organisations such as the UNHCR help to build and supply them.
In camps there are shelters, water, food and medical help.
Many camps last much longer than planned, sometimes for decades.
One of the largest camps is Kutupalong in Bangladesh, for refugees from Myanmar.
Schools in camps are especially important for children.

abschnitte.text: A **refugee camp** is a shelter for many people who have had to flee war, persecution or disasters. It is usually set up quickly, often with **tents** or simple huts. The camps are meant to offer protection until the people return home or find a new home elsewhere. Besides camps for refugees, there are also camps for internally displaced people in their own country.

In a camp, people above all need **drinking water**, food, toilets and protection from cold or heat. Aid organisations hand out food, blankets and hygiene items. There are health posts and often simple schools too. Even so, life is cramped and hard, and many people are not allowed to leave the camp or to work.

One of the largest camps in the world is **Kutupalong** in Bangladesh, where hundreds of thousands of Rohingya from Myanmar live. In Kenya there are the large camps of Dadaab and Kakuma, which have existed since the 1990s. The Zaatari camp in Jordan was opened in 2012 for people from Syria. It is so big that it seems like a city of its own, with shops and streets.

The **UNHCR**, the refugee agency of the United Nations, organises many camps together with the governments of the host countries. The World Food Programme, UNICEF, the Red Cross and Doctors Without Borders are also often on the spot. Switzerland supports such aid through the SDC and Swiss aid organisations. Many experts from Switzerland work in camps, for example as engineers for water supply.

Refugee camps are really meant to be only a **temporary solution**. But when wars and conflicts last a long time, people often stay for many years. Some camps, for example for refugees from Palestine, have existed for decades and have become permanent settlements. That is why today people try to make it possible for refugees to have a life with work and school outside camps too.

begriffe.erklaerung: A simple shelter made of fabric or sheeting that can be put up quickly.
The country that takes in people who have fled.
A Muslim ethnic group from Myanmar, many of whom have had to flee to Bangladesh.
A solution that is only meant for a certain time.

gewusst: Some refugee camps have more inhabitants than the city of Zurich.
In large camps there are often small markets where refugees sell vegetables, clothes or mobile phone credit.
